AN ENGLISHMAN'S HOUSE IS HIS CASTLE or, properly speaking, ought to be. This can never be the case, if unfortunately a would-be householder has to resort to the Easy Payment System. a new name for the ini- quitous Hire System. To furnish a house on the Hire System. alias the Easy Payment System, is to establish and support what is the most cruel, arbitrary extortion ever invented. The prices charged for the goods are enormous, without any regard for quality, the agreements are one-sided, being drawn with a cuteness which would do credit to a money lender, full of despotic and arbitrary restrictions, such as not to remove the mark on the furniture, not to remove the furniture, not to wear the furniture. At all times to allow the mercenaries to inspect the furniture. To pay the instal- ments regularly, and if one is missed to forfeit the furniture and all the moneys you may have paid, that is to say, although you might have paid £l9 on £2) worth of furniture. but missed the last payment by a single day, the vultures could empty your house and stick to the £l9 paid, as well as the furniture. div.p: PLEASANT PARAGRAPHS.

ALL men are not homeless, ut me are home less than others. COLD doesn't travel very fast; anybody can catch it. THERE is reason in all things; but there doesn't seem to be in all people. A ROMANCE OF THE MIDDLE AGES.—Two people falling in love when they are forty-five. Miss ELDERLY: "What would you do if I should tell you my age" He: "Multiply it by two."

" WomAN," says Victor Hugo, "is the riddle of the nineteenth century." She is. We can't guess her, but, it has been gallantly observed, we will never give her up. "A AIIDDLE-AGED young lady wants a situation" is an advertisement that recently appeared in one of the daily papers. TAKING IT Essv.—Lady :"I must tell you that we're very early risers." Irish Domestic : " Well, ye won't dishturb me, mum ; Oi slape bike a top !"
THE SCHOOLMASTER AEROAD.—A village school- master was lately found in a brook, and would have been drowned, had he not been so full of liquor that the water could not get at him.
OF HIGH RANK.—Cus,orner: "How is it your butter has such a rank flavour ?'' Bateman : "I don't know, I'm sure, ma'am, unless it is because it comes from a nobleman's dairy ."

IN INVERSE RATIO. —Wagsby "That brewer gets fatter and fatter every year." Ga,gsby : "Yes, and his beer gets thinner and thinner every year," ExrE-RIENcE TEACHES. —An Irish editor, who speaks with the air of a man who has discovered a new fact by experience, says that the way to pre- vent bleeding at the nose is to keep your nose out of other people's business.

- - MOST USEFUL —Don't you think, Mr. Bright- side, that lying is the ugliest of all vices?" " Well, I can't say I think it the prettiest; but, at least, its the best thing we have discovered yet when we don't want to tel the truth."

A CERTAIN thin man sent a shilling in postage stamps to an advertiser, who promised for that sum to impart trustworthy information how to get fat, and received the message on a post-card, "Buy it at the butcher's !"

A n.Aw Jonathan, who had been gazing at a garden in the vicinity of New York, in which wera several marble statues, exclaimed, "Just see what a waste! Here is no less than six sc q-ecrows in this little ten-foot patch, and any one of 'em would keep the crows from a five-acre field." THE popular idea of a good business man is one who can meet and beat a scoundrel at his own game. - -
INQUIRING STRANGER: "And do you get a fair allowance of vegetables on board ship ?" Old Sailor: " Taters always—an' a leak now and then."

1 SHE WANTED THE BARGAIN.—Through an error of the clerk, the sign read thus: "A great bar- gain! Last one left! Formerly five shillings. Now offered for eight." And Mrs. Bargainbyer paid eight shillings for it and went home happy. IN A DANGEROUS PLACE.—A writer of a love- tale, in describing his heroine, says: "Innocence dwells in the rich curls of her dark hair." A critic, commenting on this passage says: "Sorry to hear it; we think it stands a perilous chance of being combed out."

OVERHEARD. —First Harlem Woman (over the backyard fence) : "Mrs. Jinks told me yester- day she thought she was the most un- happy woman living." Second Harlem Woman: "That's just like her—always trying to outdo her neighbours." SHOPMAN (savagely, to agent) : "If you don't get out of my shop in double-quick time, I'll kick you out !" Agent : "Before you do so, sir, I'd like to show you a special line I've got in extra thick boots !"

FIRST MAN: "How that Mrs. Gabbel does talk ! I wonder it doesn't make her jaws stiff." Fecond Ditto: " Well, I expect it would, only she's got such an oily tongue, you know l" "WHO," says a poet, "would indite sonnets to a woman whom he saw every morning in her night- cap, and every day at dinner swallowing meat and mustard ?"

Too thicH rOlt HIM.—A Detroit man took his seat in the barber's chair. He asked the barber if he had the same razor he had used two days before. Being answered cheerfully in the affirmative, the patient man said, "Then give me chloroform." "I AM willing to split hairs with my opponent all day if he insists on it," said a very dis- tinguished Ameti: an lawyer, in a speech at the bar. "Split that, then,' said the opponent, pul- ling a course specimen from his own head, and extending it. "Ma' it please the court, I didn't say bristles." "KIND words never die." How bitterly does a man realise that truth.when he sees all the kindest words that he ever used in his life glaring at him from his published letters in a breach of promise snit. _ _

-- -- SAID an Irishman the other day to a friend: " Arrah, where will you find a modern building that has lasted as long as the ould wans ?" RUSTIC MOE.ALITY. —Rector (going his rounds): "Fine pig that, Mr. Dibbles, uncommonly fine !" Contemplative Villager: "Ah, yes, sir, if we was only all of us as fit to die as him, sir !" A COLOURED philosopher "down South" is re ported to have said: "Life, my breddern, aim mosly made up of prayin' for rain and then wishirk' it would cl'ar off.'

BIS FAVOURITE ANIMALS. - Sunday-school teacher: "Do you love animals?" Boy: " Yes'm." "That's right; I'm glad you do. What animals do you like het?" "Snakes." " G odness ! Why do you like snakes?' "'Cause it ain't wicked to kill 'em." _

SMART BOY !—Minister: "So you go to school, do you, Bobby?" Bobby: ," / es, sir." Minister: "Le: me hear you spell bread." Bobby: " B-r-e-d." Minister: "Webster spells it with an a, Bobby." Bobby: " Yes, sir; but you didn't ask me bow Wt bster spells it—you asked me howl spell it."

IN conversation with Lord Normanby, a French lady once made the oft-repeated assertion that her countrymen were the politest people in Europe, and cr,pped all her aroiments by saying, "You admit it yourselves.' "Exactly so," was his lordship's reply, with a diplomatic bow. "That is oar politeness." JUDGE: So you want a divorce simply because your wile won't speak to you when she gets angry? Mr. Growler : Yes, that's it. Judge (severely) : This is positively the most frivolous complaint I ever listened to. Don't you know when you're well off?

A RELIGIOUS lecturer told an audience in Oklahoma that if a man had sufficient faith he might pick up a rattlesnake and the rdptile could not bite him. In3tead if accepting the statement on trust, one man went out and put the matter to the test, with the result that the creature bit him and he died. An Amdrican paper which tells the story remarks, " The fools are not all dead yet, but, one of them is."

SELF-DEFENCE.— Striker: "We hos, indooced thim blacklegs to quit wurrick, an' th' mill do be sthopped." Wife : Oi hope yez did not use violence." Striker: " Violence ? No ; we only definded oursilves Av'en they attacked us fur t'yowing stones at 'em." "MA," said Master Biggs, " may I go to the circus to-night?' " No, Tom.' "Then I'll go and get the measles, that 1 wid ; I know a boy who has em prime." THE ONE THING NEEDVUL.—A Crimean soldier was one day oast ing of the praise he received from his officers, and wound up his yarn with the fol- lowing : "dist befoore the battle iv Ballyelavy the giniral came galloping up furnent our regiment and shouted, 'ls Patsey M'Callerty in the ranks?' ''Via, yer 11,•nour, 1 replied. Then,' says he, `let the battle begin.'"

RIGHT AGAIN !—" When was Rome built ?" -asked a school committeeman of the first-class in ancient history. "In the night," answered a bright little girl. "In the night !" exclaimed the astonished examinQr. " llow do you make that out ?" " Why, I thought 'everybody knew that Rome wasn't built in a day' !" PHYSICIAN (to shivering pat Tent) : "If you'd follow my prescription you'd have been warm in less than no time.' Patient : " I know it, for I threw the prescription into the tire."

div.head: "CAPITAL" CHAT.
div.p: "CAPITAL" CHAT.

Mr. Morley Roberts tells me a curious story. He has jut returned from a tour round the wOrld, during which he had the unique experience for a novelist of being received as a guest; at a house where he formerly acted as stableman. Most people know that many of the stories of Western life which Roberts tells are founded on actual ex- perience gained as a navvy on the Canadian Pacific Railway, a sailor before the ma,t, a labourer in lumber mills on the Fraser, or a worker on Western farms. He describes with con,iderabte enjoyment the surprise of the guests to whom be was intro- duced, when he mentioned how well he know them. They declared they did not remember him. "Possibly not," Roberts would say, " but I used to be stableman here, and I have taken care of your horses many a time." The Chinese cook was especially bewildered to find in the man he used to bully for not chopping enough wood a novelist and a guest of the house. It is a curious incident in a career which has been full of ups and downs, and had more close encounters with poverty and hard toil than many literary men in London can look back upon.

There is no doubt that the Unionist leaders have made up their minds for a vigorous campaign against the Government during the autumn. I have a good authority for saying that in leading Unionist quarters the belief still exists that a general election before the beginning of next session is at least possible. Up to the time of the prorogation some of the occupants of the front Opposition bench persisted,in spite of all appearances to the contrary, in predicting a dissolution in November. Now the favourite prophecy in Unionist quarters is that it may be looked for in January. It is not worth while discussing whether these speculations have any basis, but the mere existence of such an ex- pectation accounts for the marked activity in Unionist quarters.

Exeter Hall was crowded to its utmost capacity on Tuesday night by an audience anxious to say farewell to thirty-eight missionaries of the Church Missionary Society who are proceeding to India and Persia, Sir J. H. Kennaway, presided. Among the recruits going forth is Lieutenant-Colonel Free- man, who addressed the meeting on Tuesday night on "The army as a field from which supplies may be drawn." The increased activity in the army in connection with various forms of Christian work was, he thought, full of encouragement and hope. Mrs. Durrant, d sister of the present Bishop of Exeter, was also pre,4ent. She is going with her daughter to the North-west Provinces, and will subsequently be joined by her son,who is at present serving a curacy at Plymouth. Another meeting was held on Wednesday night to take leave of other missionaries who are going to China, Japan, Africa, and Palestine.

There is some talk of Mr. Asquith introducing a short bill to deal with the sale of dangerous lamps. The terrible fatality reported on Tuesday morning at Rochester is about the tenth in one week, and it is felt that if we have to wait for legislation until the Select Committee have been reappointed and have issued a final report, it will necessarily be a long time before the law can be strengthened. It is believed that the Home Secretary could get the assent of Parliament to a measure prohibiting the sale of lamps with glass reservoirs, and this would be a great advantage.

That the evil which men do lives after them is true of the late Marquis of Ailesbury in more res- pects that one. The latest illustration of it is found in the infinitude of trouble bequeathed to his successor in tracing a large number of heirlooms with which the gay marquis had made extraordi- narily free. The whereabouts of many of these is now •known, but the stops necessary for their recovery are tortuous and complicated.

An exceedingly interesting performance was given on Wednesday at the theatre annexed to the Royal Aquarium. The performers were a troupe of nnamite actors and actresses who have lately been playing at Antwerp. Of course the chief interest lies in the strong centrist between our own drama- tic methods and those of the Far East. Some further excitement lies in the fact that the European spec- tator does not in the least know whether he is seeing a tragedy or a comic opera. The drama pro- duced this afternoon is tragic in its plot, hut, there are songs and dances. Little gesticulation is used, . and there isabsolutelv no facial play. The orchestra consisted of two stringed instruments, a horn, a drum, and a thing with the tinkling sound of triangles. No attempt was made at harmony, but the singers kept accurately on tt,e same note. In timbre the prima donna's voice was not much inferior to that of the domestic cat. F'ghting was done by the performers whirling round like dervishes and carefully avoiding contact with each other's spears.. The dresses were magnificent specimens of Oriental embroidery. They are said to have cost vast sums, and this one can well believe. In their own coun- try the Annamite company do not finish a play for days, or even weeks; but here in I.ondon the performance is mercifully cut down to half-an-hour. But for that space of time the spectacle is worth seeing. It gives one quite new insights in Eastern art.

The Parnellites will honour in Dublin next Sun- day the anniversary of the death of their Into leader, Mr. Parnell. They will make a pilgrimage to his grave in Glasnevin Cemetery with a devotion that would do credit to the pilgrims of Lourdes. From all parts of Ireland will come Parnellite depu- tations or delegates to assist in the denunciation of their anti-Parnellite oppranents as betrayers of Irp- land, and to propagate their views. They believe they are growing in influenee and numbers in Ire- land, and they are powerful enough to make an im- posing display next Sunday. If they possessed the power of the anti-Parnellite section there would have been a general election long ago, or it, may even he that the Government would have been out of office by the present time. As the princ,ples of Mr. Parnell are worked by Mr. Redmond and Ilia limited following, the thread that hinds Ireland to England wou'd be of the most mieroscopic fineness, if it con inues to exist at all awl their position is so intransigent and hostile that Parliament would probably pause before putting the government of Ireland into their hands.

The ordinary male hears,almost with dismay,and the advanced woman will hear with pride, that the champion miller of America is soon likely to be a female. She must have been horn with a genius for sculling,as a person is born with a genius for music or art. Nothing short of genius,surelv, could have carried her to the summit of the sculling world of America after three months' practice. But she is not an American. She is a Norwegian importation, though she has lived in the States sin-e she was four years of age. The progressive world of America will,nevertheless.be proud of her, awl regard her as thoroughly Jona,thanised. It. is said she has deve- loped wonderful strength with her three months' practice. If so,she might publish the secret, of the art by which she has developed the muscles of her arms and back in sohrief a time. There are heroine,. in England who would follow her footsteps as if she were a patron goddess. It is said that it is all done by simple diet, long walks, and swimming. Who knows hut we may see this charming product of the debonnnir woman exhibiting her prowess in British waters?

Artists who design wall-papers and cretonnes are complaining loudly inst. now. They say that it is almost impossible to sell a good design. A wave of bad taste has come over the community, and nothing is manufactured except the most atrocious floral designs, in which flowers of every colour and description are mingled together without any attempt at conventional treatment. A glance at any furniture shop window sufficiently confirms the statement, for the wall-papers and curtains which flaunt their garish colours behind the glass would not have been looked at three or four years ago. Chintzes are great sinners in this respect, and it seems as if the revival of this material, which had ' almost gone out a few years ago, had something to do with the decadence of patterns. The manu- facturers admit that the phase will probably pass before long, hut meanwhile it is hard on our good designers who find their wares unmarketable.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATUROAY, OCTOBER 6, 1894.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATUROAY, OCTOBER 6, 1894.
Dancing is mentioned as being beneficial to health and deprement by Plutarch, Lucian, and other ancient writers.
Sewing machines driven by electric motors have been fitted up in a large costume establishment in Paris. The current is obtained from the street mains.
It's as easy to move mole hills as mountains,and most women would prefer the former to the latter, especially in cases where the mole hill is on the side of the nose.

Belfast is the great tea drinking city of the United Kingdom. Everybody, high and low, drinks tea of the finest quality. The merits of different bran as are a continual subject of discussion, and the stately mansions of tea-merchants, which are rising everywhere in the suburbs, testify to the prosperity of the trade. A hundred tons of cAts' tails were recently sold in one lot for the purpose of ornamenting ladies' wearing apparel. Assuming that an average cat's tail would weigh a couple of ounces, this would mean that no fewer than one million seven hundred and ninety-two thousand pussies had keen killed just to supply this one transaction alone.

The fortune of the late Grand Duchess, Catherine of Russia was like the riches of Sidonia, for it " could be counted only by millions." The whole of the immense wealth of the Grand Duke Michel Paulovitch devolved upon his daughter, and also his vast and very valuable e,tates in various parts of Russia, his landed property forming a considerable principality. Her Majesty's fondness for children is well known, says the "Woman at Home," and one of her life-long pleasures has been to encourage children's correspond- ence. Princess Louise resembles her Royal mother in this love for children's letters, and it was to her that a little daughter of Henschel( said, in taking leave of the Princcss, " Yes, I will often write you, but please what's your number?" _

Miss Ashley,who aspires to be known as the champion woman &Allier of Atnerica,is a Norwegian by birth, al- though she has lived in the States since her fourth year. She has practised with a shell for only three months, but she has worked so energetically that she has developed wonderful strength and skill. She thinks nothing of row- ing twelve to fifteen miles in her twenty-seven-pound shell, and keeps herself in training by a pimple diet, long walks, and swimming. In old days the Queen was very much attached to neatly all forms of spert, and, says "Red Rod" in "St. Paul's," she herself tells, in quite picturesque language, how she used to be out nine hours at a stretch ; how she was not allowed to speak a word, how she" scrambled," to use her own term, from rock to rock in terrible heat after a "Royal,' how she tramped the woods and hills in wet and muddy weather, and was carried over brooks on rough men's shoulders; how much she enjoyed the " leistering " of the salmon ; how pleased she was at the keepers' superstition that she had what they, and she, call " a lucky foot"; and she is never tired of relating the painful adventure when "Vicky "—the Empress Frederick—disturbed a wasps' nest.

Our Popular Princess. A writer in the "Young Woman" describes graphi- cally and truly the unique popularity of the Princess of Wales. In social popularity, she says, the Princess has no rival in this country. There is not a woman in th 3 country—perhaps not in the world—to whom that sincerest form of flattery, imitation, has been so unin- terruptedly offered as to the Princess. She wears her hair in a certain way, and half the women in the coun- try wear it in the same way, regardless ot the fact that what may be very becoming to one face may altoge`h, r spoil another. She patronises a certain clan tartan dr3ss, charmingly suited to her lithe and slender figure, and the plumpest little dumpling of a coman fan( ie• herself" in similar attire. This blind—and yet so very keen-sighted—admiration is carried so far that even the Princess's little infirmities are imitated. It would l be sad if it were not so irresistibly laughable, that a few years ago, when Her Royal Highness walked temporarily a little lame, quite an army of fashionable women as- sumed a limp. In order to hide some slight scars on her neck, the Princess, when decollettee, always wears either a velvet ribbon or some strings of pearls or other precious stones immediately under her chin, and close round the neck. This is not by any means a becoming arraneyment, and the Princess, with her exquisite taste, no doubt only adopted it as a pis oiler, but that did not prevent her devoted imitators from doing likewise.

div.head: LADIES' LETTER.
div.p: LADIES' LETTER.

Mr DEAREST NELLIE, I am reminded ot children's outfits by the model of a simple little frock I have just seen. One made simply of white lawn over silk of any colour is in excellent taste, and having a small gathered yoke, cape, and puffed sleeves. A pelisse for one of tender years had a cape of fins embroidery, tied at the neck with a big bow. Young people are wear- ing Tam o' Shanters made of Irish poplin in tar- tans, as well Ll 3 others made of white satin, faced with poplin, which is used also for pelisses, as it doe q not crease, and this is a great desideratum. A silk frock for a boy was smocked at neck and waist, and many little garments of mohairs, soft woollens, and printed silk are made with insertion and lace, with ribbon run through it; this trim- ming is intreducf,d e ',so at the hem of the skirt and the yoke. These styles apply to young children; older ones have white fichus in the Marie Antoinette style' carried under the arm, tied round the waist, and finished with ribbons. A simple blue serge frock and coat, with a Swiss belt, which fastened over a skirt, is made with a turn-down collar and open coat—a generally useful style for holidays when spenb in the errantry or on the boul.

Au to our millinery for the season several of the new felt toques in various .00lours are mostly trimmed with a fold of velvet and a couple of quills; some of them are of plain felt, others are stamped to imitate crocodile leather. In white felt a toque looks delightful 'resting on a few folds of black velvet, with a jet wing poised on its left side. Then, again, a successful small hat, or you might call it a bonnet, if it so please you, is in drab with green parrot's wings in tbe front, and a large bow of shot ribbon extending itself at the back. A small hat of reeeda green velvet, with a touch of copper colour, ;n a full frill at one side, through which are thrak;t two quills of copper and green, is successful, and no less attractive and quite novel in a while felt hat, somewhat in the three•corner shape, with a brim turned up and decked with an appl;que of fine black lace, caught here and there with pale blue rosettes. But these are only coming events that cast their shadows before; in any case, they merit being chronicled, for they are there for our immediate needs now, when the fhwer-decked hat of summer must bow Its head before the inevitable deoree of " worn- out," and yield place to the toque of felt.

A-serge gown that is intended for wear in the autumn months should be st.ffi.lently warm to wear without a wrap on fine days, and yet made in such a style that a cape or coat may be comfort- ably worn over it when required. A dress suitable either for blue or black serge, has the vest of white twill flannel, striped with braid, which is stitched on by machine. The vest is removable, and fastens up the back, and the front is arranged on the one lining, the top faced plain and fiat, with the flannel and braid stretched on, and the lower part shaped at the top, and drawn in full to the waist.

The sailor costume, which for the past seven or eight years has been the all but invariable dress for small boys not yet promoted to the honour of coats and vests, has been superseded to no small extent this seasan by fanciful shirts overhanging, Gari- baldi fashion, the rather close-fitting breeches, which complete a very pretty and comfortable suit. A smart little shirt, for example, is of white linen, and has a deep round turn-down collar, edged with a frill of Cash's horn-stitched frilling, an inch in width, which is headed by a feather-stitching worked in thick white washing silk. The broad flat pleat down the front of the shirt is bordered on either side with feather-stitching and frilling, and the turn up gauntlet cuffs correspond. The shirt hangs well over the top band of the breeches, which in this particular cavi are of dull green velveteen with three tiny smoked pearl buttons at each knee. _ _

div.head: BIRDS WHISTLED "THE DEAD
div.p: THE BIRDS WHISTLED "THE DEAD
MARCH."
" Even the birds On the trees learned to whistle the 'Dead March." "

It was an old soldier who was talking. "We were in camp," he said, "in a flat, nialarious part of the coun- try. Our Colonel was a splendid fighter, but didn't appear to have any idea of sanitary matters. Just then we were in nnore danger from disease than from the enemy. Presently fever broke out and the men died by the dozen. Hardly a day but we buried some of them in the swamp. In fact, we played the "Dead March" so often that I used to fancy the birds in the trees had learned to whistle it. "Awful sorry, you know, boys," said our Colonel, "but so long as we have to stay here, we can't help having the fever." Yet the Colf•nel was wrong, as another regiment camped near us almosq wholly escaped. But their commander fought the malaria with sanitation and pr eventive medicine. Tha made the difference."

In January, 1892, the influenza wi,s epidemic at Steb_ bing, near Chelmsford. Among the persons attacked were Mrs. Abram Thoro,good, of White House Farm, her daughter Annie, and her sons William and Ernest. They had terrible pains in the head, sore muscles and joints, and were very feverish. The whole four—mother and three children—were confined to their beds.

In a letter on the subject Mr. Thorogood says: "My wife became quite delirious; she did not know where she was, and could neither get in nor out of bed. I gave Mother Seigel's Curative Syrup to all of them with excel- lent results, the fever soon left them, and shortly they were well and strong as ever, and have since remained so. I may mention that many neighbours and friends had the same complaint as my wife and family, but although the others had doctors and the best attention and advice, none recovered so rapidly as i.y people did. 1 thank God that I came t- hear of Mother Seigel's Cura- tive Syrup, for although we are a family of seven,living at home, during the eight years I have kept it in the house we have not needed a doctor, thus saving man pounds in doctors' bills and costly prescriptions. "The way I first used Seigel's Syrup was this the spring of 1883 I began to feel ill and out of sorts. My tongue was dreadfully coated and a thick phlegm covered my gums and teeth. After eating I suffered from pain at the chest and stomach. I had bad nights, and sweat so much that in the morning my underclothing was soaked with moisture. In the following August car, bunc.les came on the back of my neck, on my nose, and on my cheek bone. What I suffered I cannot describe, I got so low and weak that I could barely crawl about. The doctors did me no good. And as for their physic I might as well have taken tea or water. In pain and 1 suffering I lingered on until I heard, through a neigh- bour, of Mother Seigel's Curative Syrup and got a bottle rom Mr. W. Linsell, grocer, of Stebbing. A fewthses relieved me, and soon the carbuncles disappeared. and I was well as ever. Yours truly, (Signed) ABIIAM MORO- GOOD, White House Farm, Stebbing, by Chelmsford, August 18th, 1892."

In Mr. 'Thorogood's own case the disease was indiges- tion and dyspepsia, which poisoned his blood and caused the carbuncles, which are growths on the underlying layers of the skin. After the Syrup had purified his blood they were absorbed and expelled from the system. The effect of the remedy in the cases of the other mem- bers of his family shows (what we have often stated), viz., that influenra attacks those whose blood is file with the poisonous acids thrown into the system by fer- mented food in the stomach. Mr. Thorogood says his wife had been troubled with indigestion and dyspepsia, which was no doubt the case with the children also. Don't allow your blood to become a breeding-ground of disease. On the first signs of indigestion take Mother Seigel's Curative Syrup. You know the proverb about the ounce of prevention.

div.p: EXTRAORDINARY REAL-LIFE E OMANCE.
£4,000 GOING A-BEGGING.

The following remarkable paragraph is published by the " Bristol Times and Mirror."—"l am a photographer in Bristol, and one the queerest experienccs I ever had was the following : One day a gentleman of about forty walked into the shop, purchased the photrgra ph of a young lady which was exhibited in the window, and, having inquired her name and address—which I was un- able to give him, for I had only recently purchared the bir-iness, and the hooks were muddled—left me, having previously informed me that he would give :E2O to one who discovered her. After that he took the most active steps to find her, without avail. Be died five years ago, unmarried, and in his will left a legacy of £4,000 to the nameless young lady whose photograph he had purchased, to go t,) her if she were found within seven years of his death. Money was also left to the executors to enable them to prosecute a search for her. Lest than two year; now remain, and th 3 young lady has never been discovered.'
THE DOUBLE LIFE OR, THE HAMPTON MYSTERY. By the Author of " DARKWOOD."
CHAPTER XXXV, ADLOWE DEVELOPS HIS PLANS.
How stands the great account 'twixt me and ven- geance? Though much is paid, yet still it owes me much; And I will not abate a single groan. YOUNG.

As the fears of the Lady Beatrice had told her, and as the investigation of the coachman at the station had proved, little Fay had been carried away from his home by his parents' bitterest enemy, and was now in that enemy's power. Lord Adlowe had come upon the fair-haired little lad near the garden gate, a moment after he had hurled back at Geoffrey Trevelyan the assurance of his undying hatred, and of the certainty of his complete and fearful revenge. The heart of the profligate lord was brimming over with bitterness and rage at the moment of his encounter with Fay, and the sight of the boy added fuel to the flame burning in his soul. Acting upon the wild impulse of the moment, stopping neither to reason nor reflect, seeing in the lad only an instrument by which to torture the Lady Beatrice and her hus- band, he had caught up the child in his arms, and hurried onward to the station. Not until he was on his return by train to Lon- don, himself and the weeping boy the only occu- pants of the compartment, did he realize the full meaning of his impulsive and cruel act. "I nave done a clever thing," he concluded, with a glow of self complacence. "They won't dare to telegraph to have me stopped, as that would imperil the secret ef the Lady Beatrice. They will attempt to work secretly, as I have done.. This child is a hostage which I shall carefully guard until Giralda becomes my wife and I stand again, on firm ground. Ah, I have been very near to ruin !" and he shuddered. "If Lord Trevelyan had died at any time during tho past eighteen years, there was Geoffrey ready to come forward to claim the title and estates, and leave me a beggar. And if anything were to happen to him now, he has sons to succeed him. I have been a blind, un- suspecting fool. How the Lady Beatrice must have laughed at my professions of love, at my frequent allusions to my expected inheritance !" and now the baffled schemer ground his teeth. "We'll see who will laugh now; yes, and who will win too !"'

He looked towards his little captive with an ex- nitant smile. Fay had hushed his sobs, and was regarding him curiously, a look of fear in his wide, violet eyes. Like most bad men, Adlowe was not altogether bad. He could crush remorselessly any person whom he considera to stand in his path; he could have mocked the anguish of Geoffrey Trevelyan; and laughed at the tears of Uiralda ; but he felt small and mean in the presence of this little un- offending child, and grew positively uneasy under Fay's steady, accusing gaze. "Well, what do You think of me, my little man?" he asked, assuming an air of friendly patron- age. "Who are you, and where are you taking me ? " demanded Fay gravely, his lip quivering. "I am your father's cousin, and I am taking you to Giralda," replied Adlowe, not unkindly. Fay studied the countenance of his enemy for a moment in silence. Then his brow lightened a little. His sister's name evidently brought some comfort to his sorrowful soul.
"What did you snatch me up in that way for ? " he asked, thoughtfully. "Why did you steal me from my home? Why have you been so cruel to nicV' _ _ _

"See here, my boy," said Adlowe, flushing a tittle under that childish, rebuking gaze. "We may as well understand each other. Your father and I are enemies. I love your sister, Giralda, and am going to make her my wife. By and by we shall all be friends and you shall go home again. But till then the best thing you can do is to keep quiet, and do nothing to offend me. Do you comprehend me? If you cry out at the stations—if you try to get away from me—if you make any noise or attract any attention—l shall be very hard on Giralda. Remember, you will be injuring her." The little face grew paler. "Where is Giralda ? ' Fay asked in a frightened whisper. " She is shut up in a lonely place and I am szoinst to take you to tier. You must be very quiet it you want to see her." Thus admonished, Fay sank back on his seat and wept for a long time in silence. The noise of the train, the dim light, the face of his cruel enemy, all blended together in one terrifying whole, and, stunned and stupefied, he fell at last into a deep slum Tr. -
Adlowe looked at him with a gratified smile. "I am not quite defeated," he thought, his sin- ister face brightening. "Allis not lost. By a bold and skilful effort I may yet retrieve myself."

He became thoughtful, and reviewed in his own soul the desperateness of his situation. The best years of his life had been lost in a fruitless waiting for an inheritance he would never possess. The strength and fervor of his heart had been wasted upon a woman who was secretly a wife and mother. He felt that he might not have time to woo an heiress, even should he find one willing to accept him. Lord Trevelyan might die any day, and every one would then know that he, Adlowe, was poverty-stricken man, with only an empty title to otlset a host of debts. Clearly his best course was to marry Giralda, and thus secure to himself a lov,-ly young wife and an ample fortune. And if Girabla were likely to prove obstinate, little Fay would be a lever by which to reduce her to a quiet submission. Thus musing, Adlowe neither stirred nor spoke again until the train had dashed into the London station, and come to a full stop. Then, taking up the sleeping boy, he stepped out on the platform, where he was met by his valet, Haskins. Resigning Fay to the care of his man, Lord Ad. lowe signalled a cab, and the next moment the three had entered the vehicle and were slowly moving out into the street. During their progress to his hotel, Adlowe briefly explained how he had become possessed of his little charge, and learned all that Haskins had to impart to him in return.

...... " The boy must be placed somewhere in seclu- sion at once," said his lordship, when he had gained his own room and Haskins had laid the drowsy lad on a couch. "It is out of the question for me to retain charge of him. His mother will move Heaven and earth in her secret endeavours to re- gain him." "How very like he is to Mr. Geoffrey," said the valet, in a low tone, bending over the boy, whose half-closed lids trembled over his violet eyes. Something in that fair, girl-like face touched Haskin's heart with a suhen pang of remorse for his own guilty past. "There is nothing strange in such resemblance," said Lord Adlowe, flinging himself into a chair, "since he is the child of Geoffrey Trevelyan and his wife, the Lady Beatrice Hampton. I saw Geoffrey to-night, Negwyn. He has changed in eighteen years. In place of the gay, laughing boy, I saw a grave and stately man, with black hair, and dark blue, melancholy eyes, that were as keen and cutting in their glances as blades of Damascus steel. I did not know him at first." " Alive 1 Mr. Geoffrey alive 1" murmured Has- kin' in agitaoon. Lord Adlowe eyed his man sharply. "He is alive,' he said, slowly; "and would give a fortnne for evidence which you could fur- nish, Negwyn ; but he would not pay so well for it as I will pay for your silence and fidelity to me. There is another reason for your silence: If Lord Trevelyan were to suspect your share in that affair which made him cast off his favourite nephew, he would send you into penal servitude for the rest of your life ! " Haskins sighed, and his cour tenance fell. If he had experienced any vague determination to right the wrong of years, it fled before the image of Lord Trevelyan, of whom the valet, remembering the marquis's tempests of passion, stood in profound fear. _ _ _

"You can depend on me, my lord," he said. "I will remain as secret as the grave." "About a safe asylum for this boy," remarked Adlowe. "Where can I put him so that I can find him when I want him, but where no one else can trace him ?"
--- - ------ - "There's the bluff cottage, my lord," suggested the valet. - -

"It won't do," returned Adlowe, shaking his head. "I've thought of that myself, but there's a homely and true old adage, advising one not to put all one's eggs in the same nest. The girl is there. That is enough for that place." "I've been away from England so long," said Haskins, thoughtfully, "that those peoplc I have not forgotte,i must have forgotten me. All have not such good memories as you, my lord," and he smiled unpleasantly. "Didn't you have a sweetheart once, Haskins?"
asked his lordship, ahruptly—" a Welsh mountain girl. Where is she ? " Haskin's face changed. It was evident that his employer's careless question had touched a sore spot on his soul.

"I haven't seen her since I left Trevelyan Park, eighteen years ago, my lord," he said, averting his face. "Poor Peggy Willsey ! I couldn't go to her with the guilt ot that business on my hands, my lord, but I wrote to her from Australia, and she nevei answered my letter. She was too good to mix up in our affairs, yours and mine, my lord. If she's living, she's married, of course." Adlowe knitted his brow in perplexity. At this juncture there sounded a knock on the door. Both master and man started guiltily, and Haskins hastily covered the sleeping boy with his lordship's dressing-gown. The movement was scarcely accomplished when the door opened, and Wigby, Lord Trevelyan's late valet, entered. Lord Adlowe stared at the new comer in surprise and alarm. "You here ?" he exclaimed. "You in London? Where is your master ? " "Lord Trevelyan is at Trevelyan Park," replied Wigby, coolly. "His lordship discharged me from his service this morning." "Discharged you ?" echoed Adlowe, frowning. "What have you been doing to get yourself dis- charged at the very time I neceded your services at the Park ? "

Wigby seemed to enjoy his lordship's dismay. He seated himself coolly, wiped his brows, and glanced curiously at the couch before replying. "You can prepare yourself for a shock, my lord," he said, at last. "It's all out—your per- formance of last night with Haskins. Miss Are- valo's got home from the bluff cottage, and has told her story, and my lord has raved around like a madman! He discharged me on suspicion of being a spy on him in your employ, and told me to come straight to you and tell you never to dare to set foot at the Park in his lifetime."

A wild look came into Adlowe's eyes. "The girl escaped V! he muttered. "Demons and furies ! What a fatality !" He averted his face and sat in a profound silence while Wigby narrated the facts connected with Giralda's ezeape from the bluff cottage and her return to the Park.
It was a wild and desperate face his lordship turned at last upon his two confederates. All the schemes of his life seemed blasted—all his hopes annihilated.

"I will not go under without a struggle !" he said, his eyes blazing with an evil light. " I'll make it worth your while to stand by me, my men. Geoffrey Trevelyan is alive, is married to a noble lady, and should anything happen to him, has three children to inherit the Trevelyan estates. Ile is lying off now, iu seclusion and disguise, waiting for Lord Trevelyan's death. Miss Arevalo is his daughter. That boy on the couch is his younger son. You see therefore, that Trevelyan Park is not likely to be m.ne—that I am doomed to a life of poverty—unless I move quickly and ably. I have two objects to work for—yes, thrte : I want to be revenged upon the lady who has fooled me so completely during all these years; I want to be rich; I want my cousin's daughter, with her youth, beauty, and wealth, for my bride. Aid me in these objects, and I will make you rich men." "How does your lordship expect to accomplish BO much ?" asked Wigby, cautiously. "I will hold that boy—his mother's darling—as a hostage to be heavily ransomed. I will take the girl4naptive again, and compel her to marry me. And then I can make terms with my cousin Geoffrey." The plan looked feasible to the two valets, and they signified their willingness to assist in it. "That boy ought to be taken to a secure hiding. place this very night," declared Wigby, glancing at the couch. "I know the very place for him. Does your lordship remember Negwyn's old sweet- heart, Peggy Willsey ? A few years ago she fell heir to a mountain hut, a flock of sh,,en, and a elieep-walk in the loneliest part of all Wales. She lives by herself, with no neighbour within three miles. I have kept up my acquaintance with'her, and I saw her lately. I can take the boy to her with some made-up story that he is your lordship's own son, and she will guard him as closely as if he were shut up in the Old Bailey and she was his jailer. She's a prime person to keep her word, is Peggy Willsey." Haskins listened eagerly and with a flushed face to this speech. "Then take the boy to her, Wigby," said Ad- lowe, tossing the man a bank note. "Bind her to secresy. Tell her a story that will neutralise all the boy himself may say." "You may depend on me, my lord," said Wigby, resolutely. "11l be off at once. There's an early morning train, which I shall catch. By daylight, if I should remain here so long, some one might arrive here in pursuit of the boy. Do you know the Burnt Downs, my lord?" "Yes," said Adlowe. "It's a desolate gorse- covered region in a hilly district, full of pitfalls and ravines. There are no houses there?"

"There is a hut there, my lord—the hut of Peggy Willsey," declared Wigby. "The boy will be lost In that wild region." He arose and bent over the couch, carefully lift- ing the tired boy, who moaned restlessly, and half awakened from his slumbers.

Adlowe gave his confederate a few further in- structions, and Wigby then departed, carrying Cut boy in his arms. "My affairs are not desperate yet," said Adlowe, with reviving hope. "The possession of that boy a great thing for me, Haskins. To-morrow we must take steps to recapture the girl. I feel tired. I think I'll take a nap, and get strength for to- morrow."

Be flung himself lazily on the couch and soon dropped asleep. Haskins took possession of the easy chair and reviewed the past, thin king of Geoffrey Trevelyan, of the marquis, and of the simple, honest Welsh maiden he had himself wooed and then deserted for a life of wrong-doing. He wrung his brown hands silently as a remorseful spasm rent his heart, and great tears gathered in his eyes, and he thought with vain regret if he could only live his life over again. Yet, strangely enough, he did not think of repairing his errors and be- ginning anew now. The morning deepened. Haskins slept in his chair, and Lord Adlowe slept on his couch, both as calmly as if they had been innocent. Both were aroused at last by a thunderous knocking on the door. Lord Adlowe sprang upright with a stifled shriek. Haskins leaped to his feet, and looked around him with a wild instinct for concealment.
The knocking was repeated. Haskins pushed back the thick curtains, letting Into the room a flood of sunlight, and hastened' to admit the visitor.

As the reader may have guessed, the intruder was the youg Lord of Grosvenor. He came in, grave and stern, his splendidly jiandsome face set in an expression of haughty re- suke, his hazel eyes glowing with a keen ac- cusing gaze. He swept a scythe-like glance around him' and approached the besdide, upon which Lord Adlowe sat, endeavouring to assume command of his bewildered senses.
"Lord Adlowe ?" said the young lord, inquir- ingly. Adlowe nodded crossly, exclaiming: "And who are you that intrudes into a gentle- man's bedroom in this manner, I should like to know ? '

_ "I am Paul, Lord Grosvenor," was the stern response, and the visitor's eyes flashed lightning gleams—" the friend of Geoffrey. Trey elyan, and his wife and children ! I have come for little Fay, whom you abducted last evening !" Lord Grosvenor looked around the chamber in a vain quest for the little lad, while Adlowe, re- covering his senses, laughed insolently. "So you are the champion, my lord," he said, with ill-concealed hatred, "of that assassin and robber, Geoffrey Trevelyan, and of his wife, the belle and beauty, Lady Beatrice Hampton! You are a young man te imperil your good name in this manner. Permit me, my lord, as your senior, as a man .of the world, as the former friend of your venerable father, to advise you to turn your back on that unworthy fellow whose friend you declare yourself! You should associate with none but worthy people ot the outset of your career I" "If I had acted upon such advice I should not now be in your presence, Lord Adlowe," re- sponded the young lord, with flashing eye and curling lip. "What have you done with little "I have put him where he will not be found until I chose to produce him," declared Adlowe, arising, "I will restore him to his parents on con- ditions. As you are the friend of Geoffrey Tre- velyan you can bear to him this message." "And the conditions ? " "The hand of Giralda in marriage, accompanied by a handiome dowry of half her mother's private fortune." Lord Grosvenor's dark eyes fairly b!azed. He did not dare trust his voice for a reply. ,_"thu av that t'airaida Ltit;;4llC3 1111/ W110:1

continued Adlowe, **ray snail be restored to We parents, and a general amnesty shall reign. I will even endeavour to soften my uncle's hatred towards Geoffrey—" "Stop !" commanded Lord Grosvenor, sternly. "You need base no plans of the fulfillment of your condition.' Giralda become your wife! That angel linked to a demon! Better that she were dead !" Adlowe sneered.

"Ah !" he said, his small eyes glowing.. "I see that I have a rival! Lord Grosvenor has entered into the lists against me! So be it, my lord; but let me warn you that in Fay I hold the winning card. Your love is hopeless.' "Not hopeless, since it is returned," said the young lord, quietly. "You are speaking of my betrothed wife, Lord Adlowe !"
Adlowe looked at his young rival with the look of a demon.

"You have made quick work !" he said, sneer- ingly. "The lady is easily won. But you are not married yet, my lord. My conditions remain un- altered. I can at any moment bring disgrace and death on Geoffrey Trevelyan, for he is not one to long survive a public trial and transportation. I hold the honour and happiness of that family in my hands. Lord Grosvenor will scarcely care to sully his honourable name with an alliance with the daughter of a convicted thief I It is war be- tween us, my lord." " Yes, war to the knife !" declared Giralda's love; convinced that Fay had indeed been taken elsewhere, and that further parley with Adlowe was useless. "Heretofore, Lord Adlowe, you have had it all your own way. Your career will soon be terminated. Your persecutions of the innocent and the helpless will soon cease. lam the champion of these wronged people, Lord Ad- lowe, and henceforth to harm them you will have first to battle with me. The end is surely near." He emphasized his words by a stern look, and then turning, quitted the apartment, his words ringing in Adlowe's ears like the knell of approach- • in doom.

WHAT DOES IT MEAN?

A great sensation followed the recent rumour that the Czar of Russia was a victim to Renal disease,or Bright'S disease of the kidneys. We can read with evanimity ' attempts to assassinate the Czar, relying upen the strength and assiduity of his attendants to protect him, hut to learn that he is attacked by this " octopus Of diseases," stirs our deepest, heartfelt sympathy. CAN HE ESCAPE ? or will he become another Royal victim to this painful malady? Kidney disease knows no distinction. All born of woman are liable to its encroachments. Napo' leon the Great said : " I fear ne foe that I can see,'' but this unseen, insidious foe (kidney disease) struck his name from the living roll. Yes : of all diseases that menace the human race, this is the most dreaded, for it so quickly brings its victims to the grave. This ruthless malady has caused the death of more noted men and women than diphtheria, smallpox, and typhoid fever cornbined. No class is exempt— kings,q seens,presicients, lords, dukes, professionals, littesateurs, and laymen; •palaces and squalid hovels are alike invaded—no respeC- t,r of ace, position, wealth, or surroundings. The late King of Holland, Napoleon 111., Rev. Charles Haddon Surgeon, and Chester A. Arthur, ViceTresident of the United States, are prominent examples from the many trieht lights that have been extinguished by the breath_ _ of this poisonous disease. Must we calmly fold our hands because a few bisisoted physicians claim it is incuaable,ancl make no endeavours ti check its progress? No ; for many of the foremost scientists on the Continent, and in America, have givers this question serious thought-, and agreed that there is ts force mighty to prevail which successfully combats even with Bright's disease of the kidnests. Unimpeachable and living evidence proves that Warner's Safe Cure doeS permanently cure all diseases of the kidneys (including' Bright's disease), and unprejudieed physicians the world sver now recognise the value of this remedy and pre- scribe it.

Dr. Fisher says, A GERMAN GOVERNMENT PHYSICIAN, Neuenbuerg, Wurttemberg, Germany, says :—" I have nieasurein saying that a lady patient who was suffering from Bright's disease of the kidneys, and ti whom I pre- scribed and gave Warner's Sate Cure, after having tr.'ated her,in consultation with eminent colleagues,witn all (tiler known therapeutic remedies, has been coifl. pletely cured through the use of M'arner's Safe Cure." Dr. R. A. Gunn, Professor, New York Medical College. writes :—" In severe cases of Bright's disease, where all other remedies and treatment failed, I have effected per- manent cures with Warner's Safe Core. Furthermore, am convinced that. in all ailments where the blood is ie an unhealthy condition,and the general health impaired, the advantage gained from the use of Warner's Safe Cure is remarkable."

But we need not go abroad for proof, the recent ex" perience of a lady living in our midst, Mrs. W. Priest, 4. Magdala Cottages, Wellington-road, Houn.dow, corto- - b,rates the.,e scientists, and can be easily verified. Dur- ing the early part of last year she was suffering front Br4,Yht's disease of the kidnevs,originating from a simple rol, , and after being attended by her family doctor in Hounslow for some time, he informed her that he could nut do her any good. She then became an in-patient of the West London Hospital for eleven weeks, one of the physicians of that institution telling her that he could do nothing for her. She was then discharged as incur- able, and her family and friends gave up all hopes of her ever again being well. By this time dropsical swel• ng was such that no one who saw her thought her re' covery possible, extending from her ankles to her entire body. To make matters worse,after her return from the hospital she caught a fresh cold, which brought 00 bronchitis and pleurisy. She again called a local doctor, but derived no 1-enefit, from a month's further treatment. She suffered excruciating pain in the should-hlades,painiS shooting through her even when sitting ~nd lying, an" her strength seemed exhausted. At this period, het father (Mr. A. Brown, mace-bearer of the Corporation Chequer, Devizes), who can vouch for her statements sent her a bottle of Warner's Safe Cure, and after taking the second dose she felt relief ; bv the time she had finished the contents of the bottle She felt quite another woman. She continued taking it, the relief being se marked that she eagerly looked for the time to conV round for each succeeding dose. And after taking 1° bottles she is completely cured. "Facts," said Frederick the Great, "are Divine things." It is only the foolish man who doubts facts.

WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL.

A meeting of this Council was held at the Town Hall on Tuesday evening. The Mayor (Alderman Greenali) presided, and there were also present— Aldermen Blackhurst, Harrison, Sutton, Wright, Bolton, Francomb ; Councillors R. T. Fairclough, Shaw Green, Hill, Smethurst, Longton, Bennett, Greening, Shillcock, Roberts, Evans, Wilkinson, Garner, Baird,Muir, nkelton, Woods, Davies,Monks, Shaw, Heaton; Messrs. J. Lyon Whittle (town clerk), Longdin (borough surveyor), Fairhurst (borough treasurer), and Stanley Wilson (deputy town clerk). STREET IMPROVEMENT COMMITTEE-THE WIDENING OF
B RIDGE-STREET.

, The adoption of the minutes of this committee, which appeared in our last issue, was proposed by Alderman SUTTON, seconded by Alderman BLACICHURST. Councillor BENNETT broucrht up the question of re- letting for a term of three years of the premises recently . occupied by the lee Mr. R. W. Marsh. He said that Many were of the opinion that it was a mistake to do anything of the kind. He believed that the lower end of Bridge-st. was simply waiting the expiration of the late tenancy, and that as soon as they were able to get hold of the property they would pull the shop down. Be 1 therefore thought that it ought to be deferred no longer, as there was no necessity for futher delay. He considered -? that the present proposal was on a par with the pro- ' crastination which seemed to be characteristic of all the street improvements. There was a chance of having a nne open space in Arpley. (Hear, hear.) There was the , same tendency reflected with reference to the Town Hall 'wall. The Street Improvement Committee were delay- ing the widening of the streets by their procrastination. (Councillor SHAW GREEN : '• Find the money.") He hoped r hat the committee would consider the matter. Councillor BILL said that he was going to speak about the same thing. It Was a great mistake to set the pre- mises for three years more. They had been looking for- ward to the improvement of the bottom of Bridge-st., and there never was a better time than now. He be- lieved that if the Corporation took the-matter up there would be no difficulty. He, therefore, proposed that the minutes of the committee pass with the exception of the resolution in question. Councillor ROBERTS said that it seemed to him that the resolution explained itself, as the committee could secure possession las making an abatement in the rent. Alderman WRIGHT said that he had not much abjec- tion to the withdrawal of the resolution. He did not think it was likely that they would let the buildings to any great advantage. But before they proceeded with the scheme they must keep their attention to the scheme in connection with the widening of Warrington bridge. Councillor LONGTON contended that the resolution was ambiguous as it did not provide for the premises being taken up. Councillor Woons, as a member of the committee, said that he would like to refer to the matter mentioned last meeting with reference to the bridge. He spoke about the question being in the hands of the county "people," and the borough surveyor two or three months ago: He therefore thought that something should now be said of the decision or what had been done. After further remarks by Alderman BOLTON, Alderman Burrow said in reply to the various criticisms said that he did not think it was necessary for him to say any- thing. With reference to the premises of the late Mr.R. W. Marsh, it had been thought it would be best to re- _ . _ . _ _ _

let them until it was decided what should be done with the bridge. They had not yet paid for the property, and it was therefore premature to ask them to pull it down. Councillor HILL expressed his willingness to withdraw his amendment, and tne minutes were passed unanim- ously. HEALTH COMMITTEE. PROPOSED SMALLPDX HOSPITAL.

The minutes of this committee which appeared in our last issue were moved by Alderman Sutton who said ex- planatory of the resolution to send a deputation to Pres- ton on Friday to attend a meeting to discuss the subject of a joint smallpox hospital for Warrington and Leigh, that the question of the provision of a joint small-pox hospital was discussed sometime ago by Dr. Gornall,the Town Clerk,himself, and Dr. Sergeant. It was suggested that the County Council should be asked to obtain Powers to erect a suitable building. Subsequently a Bill was introduced and passed as the Isolation Hospital Act. Alderman Sutton then read a letter which had been received from Dr. Sergeant, inviting a deputation from the Corporation to attend the Conference, and he said it had been decided that a deputation should attend. Councillor BAIRD seconded the 'motion which was Passed unanimously. SANITARY WORKS COMMITTEE: THE LONGFORD DESTRUCTOR.
Councillor MONKS in moving the adoption of this Com- Inittee's minutes referred to the visit paid ..by himself,

and Councillors Beaman, Smethurst, and Wilkieson.and Deas to the Sanitary Congress in Liverpool. He said that speaking for himself and the other members of the deputation, they had derived a great deal of information Which would he very uqeful ts them, from their visit to Liverpool. More especially was he satisfied after seeinw the work which was being done in Liverpool in similar departments to those at Longford. He had recently had .

there were destructors, but not one he had seen was do- ing such excellent work as that at Longfcrd. The new furnace of Mr. Dees and Mr. Beaman was the best that had yet been turned out. Of course there was a con- eiderable amount of opposition from persons who had Other patents, and who were interested in other arrange- tnents fordealing with the refuse, but an inspection of Of the furnace would convinee those who were interested in the matter that it was the best of the kind which had Yet been brought out. (Hear, hear.) The committee Was, therefore, justified in proposing to erect another destruct or in place of the one which was worn out. Councillor SMETHURST said he could endorse e7ery- thing which had he-n said with regard to the visit to Liverpool. The visit had been the means of giving the Inembers of the deputation much valuable information. Some ot the members of the committee had never pre- viously seen other destructors at work. He believed that after the experience which had been gained they would be able to dispense with a great deal of the smell at Longford ; even that which came from the working de- Partment. (Hear. hear.) The minutes were agreed to. PAVING AND SEWERAGE COMMITTEE.—COMPLAINTS ABOUT THE SEWERS. This committee's minutes were published in our last issue. Alder:Tr-4n WRIGHT moved and Alderman kiUTCHIN;ON seconded the adoption of the minutes. Councillor BENNETT, with the permission of the Coun- cil, asked the following question " Whether having regard to the fact that an extensive sewerage scheme is now in prospect, the committee will consider the feasi- bility of ventilating the 'sewers of the borough by a aYstem of ornamental shafts in suitable positions which Would carry any effi IVia that might be generated into the air,instead of by the existing grids,which allow them to escape in the middle of our main thoroughfares ? " Councillor WOODS complained of the condition of the rids in Cherch-st. and Manchester-lane. The grids had been sufficient to breed any amount of fever. The smell Which was exnQripnrpi every day was sickening. The MAYOR riled that Councillor Woods was out of Order, as the sub:pet was not mentioned on the minutes. , Councillor LONGTON asked if it was intended to pave in front of the Town Hall gates? He understood it was intended to widen the street. Alderman HARRISON asked for the explanation of the term cement liaes," which were mentioned in the leinutes as being intended for paving in front of the 'rown Hall gates. Aldernaan SUTTON said they had been in use in War- rington for a lone. time.

Alderman WRIGHT said he could not give Coune,illor tennett any definite answer to his question.but he would consult his committee and the Borough Surveyor, and tio so later on. With regard to the Town Ball gates,they Would leave the road as it was, but pave the whole of the area from the present curve. The minutes were passed. • SCHOOL ATTENDANCE COMMITTEE. This Committee's minutes which were published in Our last is;uo, were passed without comment on the trlotion of Councillor Slikw GREEN, seconded by Coun- cillor SHILLCOCK. MUSEUM, ETC. He ktid that it, applied also to every other department of the Technical School. Councillor GREENING seconded the motion which was Dassed unanimously. tovrx HALL ETC. up to the Town Hall steps no such difficulty would have existed. Had he been at the meeting he should have voted against the plan adopted. Alderman BOLTON said Alderman Haßnisos waS at the meeting. Alderman HAnnisoN did not remember being there. Alderman HUTCHINSON said Mr. HARRISON spoke in favour of a straight drive up to the Town Flail. Alderman HARRISON, who appeared surprised to find he attended the Committee meeting, said that if he had spoken against it at the committee meeting he could speak again there, and he was convinced that the plan adopted was not the best one. Alderman HUTCHINSON said he hoped the Council would decide the matter. He thought they might do away with the side walks. Alderman FRANCOMB supported the committee. Until the stables at the Town Hall were removed he would prefer to see the plan suggested by the committee carried out.

_ Councillor DAVIES obj,..cted to the cutting up of the beautiful ornamental grass plot. There were few towns of the size of Warrineton which could boast of such an excellent plot in the centre of the town. (Hear, hear.) Councillor RoBERTs expressed a similar opinion. The grass should be kept as intact as possible. As a matter of taste and restfulness to the eve,near a crowded street there was nothing like grass for giving pleasure and effect.

Alderman SUTTON, Councillor WOODS, and Councillor H. T. FAIRCLOUGIT also spoke in defence of the grass be- ing untouched. The latter said it would be an act of desecration to cut a walk through such beautiful grass. Gamcillor BOLTON said that in a landscape he did not like to see a straight walk when there were no trees. The minutes were agreed to.
GAS COMMITTEE.-COUNCILLOR WOODS AND THE GAS AGAIN.

Councillor R. T. FAIRCLOUGII moved, and Councillor SKELTON seconded, the confirmation of the minutes, which were of a formal character. Councillor Woons asked if the committee had noticed the remarks that were made by the Revising Barrister on the quality of the gas. Be (Councillor Woods) did not want to frighten them, hut he would only suggest that the barrister might strike their names off the list if they did not make it better at the next revision. (Laughter.) Councillor R. T. FAIRCLOUGFI : The lights were not turned up when the Revising Barrister was here. (Laughter.) The minutes were passed unanimously. RIVERS COMMITTEE.—THE OPENING OF WALTON LOCK.

Councillor R. T. FAIRCLOUGH proposed the adoption of the minutes, which appPared in our last issue, and stated that the new lock at Walton was completed, and on Monday was formally opened. Traffic could now b. carried on between Liverpool and Warrington at all times, whether neap or spring tides. Councillor ROBERTS seconded.

Councillor DAviEs said he read in the newspapers that there was a meeting of the Ship Canal directors and the Warrington Corporation at the lock, and he wanted to know if the Corporation had been invited, or only the committee. He understood that the Corporation had been invited to attend, having been told that the steamer Olga, which he saw in the lack on Sunday, was far the purpose of conveying the corporation and the directors. and he was at a loss to see why he had been passed over, If it had been the openino, of a 'Town Hall he should think that the whole of the Corporation would have been represented. At any rate he thought they should attend on such occasions.

Alderman Surrox : On this occasion it was only the intelligent members of the Council. kLaughter.) Councillor DAVIES : I looked through th.. list and I failed to see any excopt cour-s !Councillor Roberts whops an intelligent member. (Redewed laughter.) The TOWN CLERK explained that the Rivers Committee decided to wake an inspection of the lock, and a para- graph appeared in a local newspaper saying that there would be a formal opening. Mr. Whitworth said he had seen the paragraph, and was very glad that the Rivers Committee were going there. Be asked if the directors might meet them there. He (the Town Clerk), after consulting with the Mayor and the members of the com- mittee, replied that they would be pleased to meet the directors at the lock.
The discussion then dropped and the minutes were passed.
GENERAL PURPOSES COMMITTEE.-PROPOSED STREET
IMPROVEMENT.

The MAYOR proposed, and Alderman FRANCOMB seconded, the ad2ption of the minutes which were in last week's" Examiner." Councillor BENNETT asked what the effect of the reso- lution would be with regard to obtaining a provisional order for the widening of Bridge-st. from Friars'-green ,to Hylands-st., how long it would be before they could get it, and when it would become operative. Alderman FRANCOMB suggested, seeing that they were making an application to the Local Government Board, whether it would not be well to delay a little until the deputation had waited upon the County Council to see what part they were going to take in the widening of the bridge. If they had to pay any portion of that would it not be well to include it in the one application ? Councillor Woons said he was going to remark that as deputations to London cost about £6O, whether they might not obtain a provisoual order at once for the widening of the whole of Bridge-st. He did not see why that should not be done for one £6O instead of three sixties.
The MAYOR said the reason why they had only taken a certain part into consideration was that they had only three years to do it in,and they could not do the whole of the street in that time.

The TOWN CLERK, in reply to Councillor Bennett, said the Corporation were obliged to give notice in October or November of each year of their intention to apply for a provisional order, and that was the reason they were giving notice now. They would not be able to get it con- firmed until June next year, and then they would pro- ceed. They would have power to acquire property by compulsory purchase.
The minutes were carried and the Council rose.
