div.head: SHOCKING NEGLECT OF CHILDREN AT
div.p: SHOCKING NEGLECT OF CHILDREN AT
RUNCORN. A FATHER SENT TO PRISON.

On Monday morning, at the Runcorn Petty Ses- sions, before Messrs. P. Speakman, C.C., and F. J. Norman, Benjamin and Eliza Moore, 22, ason-st., were charged with unlawfully neglecting their four children, Wm.lienry Ridgeway (illegitimate), Sarni Moore,Fanny Moore,and Thomas Moore, in such a man- ner as to cause them unnecessary suffering and injury to health.—The father pleaded guilty, but the mother denied the charge. Mr. J. 17. Knowles, who prosecuted on behalf of the National Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Child- ren, said that-the eldest boy,Wm. Henry Ridgeway was illegitimate. through being born out of wedlock. Be was aged eleven,Samuel was seven,Fanny,who was a cripple, was five,and Thomas was two years. On the 24th Sept. Inspector McAteer accempanied by Dr. Dunn, locum tenens for Dr. McDougall, visited the defendant's house. The eldest boy was found wearing an old pair of pants, fastened up with a piece of rope; a portion of an old dirty waistcoat and some pieces of shirting comnleted the boy's clothing, with the exception of an old pair of boots about four inches too long for him and a pair of dirty old stockings. All the children's hair was matted and filled with vermin. Fanny and Thomas were in a very emaciated condition, and were at the time of the visit lying upon some rotting rags with excrement ad- hering to their flnsh.Both the Society's inspector and the doctor would support him in saying that the emaciated state of the children was owing to shortness of food. He had often prosecuted in such cases as this one, and had generally found that if children had been well fed they would keep fat notwithstanding how dirty their sur- roundings might be. In this case the children had not had sufficient bread to eat, and had been starved. The father earned 225. per week, but went home only once a fortnight, lodging most of the time in different lodging-houses in Runcorn. • Inspector McAteer, of the N.s.r.c,c., stated that an the 24th September. he, in company with Inspector Hicks, visited 22, Mason-street, where, in the kitchen, they found the female defendant, and her four children, all of whom presented a pitiable appearance. Be exam- ined the children and found them all in a deplorable state of filth. The eldest boy was dressed as described by Mr. Knowles. His flesh was crusted with dirt, his hair was matted and covered all over with vermin, and he looked as though he had not been washed for some considerable time. The boy Samuel was in a similar condition. The child Fanny, who was a cripple, was seated on the floor. She was dressed in a few old rags of a filthy nature,and her body was covered with excrement. She appeared as if she had not been washed for some days. Her body was completely eaten, as it were, with vermin bites and she looked very much emaciated and neglected. Thomas was alsrs very emaciated. The weight of the child Fanny was 14Ibs. The normal weight of a child her age was 331bs. 9 ozs. Thomas weighed 10 lbs., the normal weight of a child his age being 24 lbs. 8 ozs. He could not find any fond in the house, neither any coal. Vermin sixre everywhere crawling about. In the room where fM children slept was a parcel of dirty rags, saturated with urine, which served for the purpose of a bed. The walls of this room were in a very filthy state, dirt being smeared over them. Witness asked the mother how she

accounted for the dirty state of the house, and she said she was obliged to work hard and could not pay the attention to the children that they required. 5,1 had not seen a more dirty house since he joined the Society. Inspector Hicks supported the statement made by the last witness.

P.C. Gregory also deposed to visiting the house on the 24th September by himself and to finding it in much tho same condition as already described. The male defend- ant witness knew to be an idle man and helped his wife very little. The wife, however, he had always seen at work whenever he passed the house. She had an old mangle and earned a little money by mangling clothes. AA hen witness served the male defendant with the sum- mons he said he would not support either his wife or his children any longer. Dr. John Dunn, locum tenens for Dr. McDougall, deposed to the filthy state of the house, furniture and children. The latter were very badly clothed, and Thomas very evidently had not -had sufficient to eat. Witness bore out further, the testimony of Inspector McAteer.

The female defendant, in appealing to the bench said that her husband had neglected her and thE children and she was forced to work hard to keep the little ones alive. Ple came home at times, after long periods of absence and always brought dirt home through his sleeping in lodging houses in the town. She kept the house as clean as she could, but her husband came home and brought the dirt with him. She coul4 call witnesses to prove that food was sent to her for the children and that when- ever it came they had it. She worked hard all thy at her mangle in order to get food for her children and herself. _ _

_ The mother of the female defendant (Mrs. Taylor), testified to sending a man from Lostock with food for her daughter and children several times. She had, in fact, almost kept them since their marriage as the male defendant would not work. Some times he came home and gave his wife a b.w coppers, but that was not very often. Her daughter had not a change of clothing for her children and consequently could not wash them very often. Her daughter was also subject to fits, and on some occasions remained unconscious for two days or more.

Other evidence having been given the magistrates committed Benjamin Moore to three months' imprison- ment. With regard to the female defendant they felt that while she was to a certain extent guilty of neglect, •and particularly of cleanliness, yet they would give her another trial, and she was discharged.

IHE 1-4:XAMINFP, SATURDAY, OCTOBER 6 1894 DI. OS THE DEE RE-VISITED. BY MR. JOHN PEERS. (Continued from last week.) Unfortunately—for the Duke that is—wit; Grace of Westminster was from home—Scotland and the 12th had claimed him for their own—otherwise things might have been different. Besides that, it would be very troublesome to have too many Peers bothering around; although one would not wish to appear too exclusive and unneighbourly. And lam sure,t hat the descendent of the Da Clare's—County family in Irelaud—&c., &c., &c., would have wel- comed his brother aristocrat, presented him with freedom of the" tub "—and set apart for his use and benefit one of our three pint cups. But per- haps some difficulties might have arisen as to the proper division, of the eels we had for breakfast— the captives of our night-laid line.—Grace before meat may be all very well—but when the meat is so scarce it is as well not to put the meat before the grace. Perhaps it would be as well if Earl Gros- venor never knew the loss he sustained by his ab- sence at this time:; it would be a pity to grieve him by acquainting him of his lost opportunity. Had he seen the announcement of our advent in the papers, things might have taken a different turn. But it is always alike. When we first arrived from the sea—we found Chester en fete—flags flying, bands playing, and general air of holiday-making. " Well, said we to ourselves, "how have they got wind of our coming ?" "And so early too ?" It all gave us a high opinion of the Cestrians and their ability and willingness to do the right thing at the right time. Bali ! After all, this tom-foolery—this itenseless display was actually, only on account of a confounded Musical Festival or some such trifle ! After this we determined strictly to preserve our incog. and not let this benighted people know of the greatness that abode upon its waters or rubbed shoulders in the thick of its crowds ! On a river like that above Chester from whence the in- habitants draw the kirban water supply, one feels a sort of reluctance in using it for common boating purposes—an indefinable feeling of trespass and im- propriety in thus polluting even to thesmall extent of washing decks—the water which the citizens drink. And this adds another anxiety to boating on these waters—the fear of polluting the water by getting drowned in it, noth withstanding that the Chester people effer a reward for the recovery of bodies from the river; cats and dogs a shilling each.

At what I should be estimated I never yet have teamed, As I wish to be cremated And quietly inurnA. Particular as the Cestrians need to be to avoid riparian pollution, they .are not sufficiently so in my estimation. The sanitary arrangements below the weir are not admirable if ancient ; and if, as often occurs this polluted water is carried by the high tides over the weir and reaches the source of the city water supply, if this is t i .he care t Wants remedy- ing with despatch. Be this as it may—the change is great to one used to navigate the waters of the Mersey, where the fear is not that you might pol- lute the water, but that the water should pollute you. By the generous contributions of Manchester Salford, Stockport, Warrington,and Widnes, a some what fluid compound which I imagine would quickly fix • the flint of old Charon if he left his old Styx and came to re-visit the glimpses of the moon—to see if the Mersey still "dared to emulate a classic tide." Not now would he find it creeping "inglorious, like a vulgar stream." No! vulgar no longer, but unique in its nastiness, and the number and variety of its riparian abominations. "Our Poetess" waxed enthusiastic upon the subject of" his rushy banks (" no poets theme)." But I find more dead dogs and cats than rushes lining his banks, while sewer slime has foully displaced the eel-fry which, in the pleasant spring-time of Academic days, formed a living fringe to his shoaly sands. "No poet's theme "; alas; the literature of the Mersey is now chiefly that of the Sanitary Inspector on its insani- thry state. If ever a muddy minded versifier should arise, let him try his prentice hand upon this lethal stream, and tell in mournful numbers how the deso- lating steps of ruthless tiade have turned what was a pleasant and a healthy region into a land of deso- lation, and the river into an open sewer. Enough ! let us return to Earl Grosvenor's bridge which here spans the Dee in one arch and adds to the interest, if not the beauty of the landscape. In my opinion it does the latter. Breakfast over—the ilb. of eel having been successfully negotiated—we prepared to continue our return trip. Perhaps,as this has been called a fishing trip, ne curious reader would like to know what results we had to show? That ilb. of eels and one small dace filled the bill. The most satisfactory item in this poor showing was the eel part—l had 'em. The dace was returned to its native element. It is to be hoped that it would take its experience as a warning and avoid in future the piscatorial blandishments so plentifully held out to compass its destruction. And indeed, these same are numerous, if not deadly. It is safe to say that wherever the river side can be conveni- ently approached—there, the picture of piscatorial patience stood—lay or sat—underterred by the great lexicographer's sneer, a Waltonian devotee absorbed in the anticipati-m of g:orious nibble, or feasting upon the sweet recollection of the last one, some fortnight previously. Such fidelity is the best corroboration of the poet where he says that • Hope sprints eternal in the hunvin breast, Man never is—but always to be—blest." I do not know whether it was one and the same poet who said these things, nor do I know how men can go on hoping for that which never comes. But I do know that fishermen sometimes catch what they never bait for. Colds, coughs, and , rheumatics, what a sport! To spend weary hours damply dangling nndelustive worms before the inappreciative noses of undeluded fish. It would be interesting to know how the fish of this part of the Dee regard the seasons. Do they prefer the winter or the summer ? Which will they regard as their holiday time? The winter when anglers cease fr,m troubling and fish-books have a rest? The summer season must however have its com- pensations for the teasing endured. For the tyro who Comes to catch, oft, but remains to feed the evasive fish. Again I have seen Di. literally "cast his bread upon the waters" baiting the hole he called it—a gratuitous feast for the fishes. So on the whole I think perhaps the summer has the pre- ference with such of the fish as like cheap feeds, to say nothing of the fun there must be in winking the other eye at the rows of TFIROIt'S disciptsa who are learning how very unsatisfactory—both .41k)istol- ary and piscatorially—to he dropping lines to which no answers are vouchsafed. Eaton is the usual terminus of the rowers on the Dee; but some of the nicest bits lie above this. The river is charm- ing in the variety of its direction its trees and flowers; whilst the slowness of its current equalizes the labour of an up and down row.

But now "Tom" lifts his peak on high with the intention of leaving these pleasant scenes for good and for ever so far as the present trio are concerned. "But stay." I fancy I can hear an elderly female exclaim—which he! name is " Grundy "—" What about the flail?" "Nothing, 'my dear madam." "What ! leaving Eaton without going through the flail ?" "Quite so, that is just what we did." Although, as you very truly remark, the place was thrown open to the public, we did not join the miscellaneous gang who were streaming over the bridge on that mission." On the contrary, 0 Ron- torix Mundi, I hold an Englishman's house to be his castle, a place of all places to be sacred from unin- vited intrusion,notwithstanding that its owner may be a peer of the realm.vvho is the victim of a sanc- tion which has hardened into a' custom—' a custom,' in my opinion, more honoured in the breach than the observance." "I believe you,madam,you doubt- less would have been on the jo'-‘ rejoicingly, the custom is kept up by and for you and your child- ren." As for me, as his Grace of Devonshire has not yet specially invited me. I have not, yet seen Chatsworth; and, as his Grace and I are perfectly content with things as they are, T do not think I ever shall. But on the other hand—as Di. said, it would have been only a neighbourly cour- tesy, had he of Westminster looked us up in a friendly way. But distance, St. Grouse, and other

things stood in the way. So our third pint cup was still a spare one. So, owing no man anything,being free of ground rent, tithes, and taxes, we determined to " flit ' downwards to the city. We had again a fine breeze and glided merrily along by this impelled and' the help of the favouring stream. Below Eaton the river is enlivened by frequent passenger ' steamers, notably "Bend Or" and "Or- mond" charged with sight-seers going to "do " the Hall, and the too-too vacillant oarsmen, who, all unused to the seemingly erratic waltzing of a sailing boat beating against the wind, are apt to get flustered and put themselves into place from which they wish themselves absent, to which they add the mistake of talking inconsequent rubbish about the Rule of the Road—which here is to keep to the right! Thanks to the luck which seems to attend drunken men and incompetent oars- men, we managed to get through without the green ones suffering further than a slight fnght. But Di. took compassion upon the innocents and ordered the sails down, so down they came and the boat was drops, under oar, to her berth. After which while, my "heaven born" friend busied himself in prepar- ing the evening meal, 1 rushed off to the P.O. to seek news from home. Blank; no news is good news. So again we drew on the hatches and retired but not to rest on my part; a racking headache made a recumbent position and the confinement ot the cabin, unbearable. So about eleven o'clock, I stole quietly out and leaped ashore, the better to wrestle with ray distracting tormentor. The night was beautifully fine and clear—the moon about full. So, leaving Di. to his slumbers, I picked my way over the rough ascent to the now deserted but still beautiful suspension bridge, through the interven- ing part of the city and on to the walls. Round ancisnt circumvallations I had determined to lead my persecutor such a" traipse" as to sicken him of my company and free myself of his most unwel- come attentions. Well! apart from the purpose that brought me here at such an untimely hour, it was a most glorious sight to see the city calmly sleeping in the bright moonlight—sleeping in perfect security both without and within those protecting walls. Not always was this so not in the bad old times that necessitated these restraining walls. But the moon, riding high in the azure, looked down from among her silver lined clouds upon a scene so much contrasted with some she must have witnessed—scenes of ruthless- ness and wrong—of reft misery and murder. What hopes and fears have been felt and frustrated behind these ancient parapets And now in these happily degenerate times and at this witching hour of the night, with the moon, after her ancient wont, throwing chequered patterns in silhouette upon the pavement, my only thoughts are of peace —its arts and aspirations. For instance, see what a glorious place the fitful light of the glancing moon makes of the nooks and corners of these old walls! Built for the sterner purposes of war how admirably adapted for the whispered- tale of love. The clank of armour and sounds of strife have given place to the soft nothings breathed by languishing swains into the ears of ostensibly reluctant maids. Where the clang of mailed feet were wont to ring —falls the softer patter of the modern shoe— whether worn by the inappreciative English or curious Yankee. Nevertheless the glamour of old times still haunts the place at this time, so appro- priate to the raising of the ghosts of ancient memories. The active fancy is ready to people each shadowy corner with the sentinel guardians once so familiar with these stories. Roman, Briton, Saxon, Dane, or the resulting amalgam of these and the later Normans, might each have a shadowy presence here. So much so that the mail-clad hand of one of these long byegone mural defenders might almost be expected to protrude from the darkling nooks so plentiful here, and arrest the dis- turber of his solitary watch! And me with nothing save mine innocence to defend me! Nothing how- ever more harmful did arrest me than the amorous inharmonious cat and I continued my walk in peace without encountering any greater " boggart " than myself. Silence and slumberous peace seem to reign in the city below me. Only in one place did I hear the sound of human voices—that of some belated reveller proclaiming to the world his love "Daisy "and that for her he was "half crazy." I thought the man very considerably understated his "case "—that he had not successfully diagnosed his own symptoms; this Daisy might be a very enchanting person, but she need not drive folks who are already half crazy to further extremities. Near the part of the walls skirting the Roodee I came upon the projecting ledge of the buttress on which Di. and I sat when first we came, to partake of a most memorable meal. It was noon and we were hungry. After quite a number of restaurants had been rejected by Di. as being too dear, too dirty or too grand, we compromised the matter by the pur- chase of two pennyworth of bread,and cheese to the amount of twopence halfpenny. And this Spartan meal we ate and enjoyed upon this very ledge. I was much amused by the side glances we had from the much struck passers by. The rotund well fed minister of him who had a place wherein to lay his head, and the lean but be-dollared Yankee with a curiosity that struggled through their politeness, furtively regarded us, wondering possibly if our necessities were as real as appeared on the surface. I suggested to D!. that. we might test the sincerity of all this commiseration by holding out the hat. But the pity went by untested, and so this truly philosophic meal came to an'end without eleemosyn- ary aid being extended to us. A draught at the fountain in the street below brought to an inexpen- sive end this frugal feast. But. this was in the hot noontide of sunny July, whilst now the smiling moon looks out from among her iridescent clouds on the deserted grandstand and the desolate Roodee the scene of the annual Saturnalia where some grow rich by the losses of others. And away to the far N.W. she is illuminating a scene which recalls far pleasanter memories the wide spreading estuary of the Dee, through whose intricate maze of sands we might have to lead our willing " Tom." Having completed the circumambulation of the walls I thought a change to the street might be agrseable,so along the deserted Rows echoing to the foot fall I paced, an object of suspicious observation to the be-buttoned guardians of the peace. I hastened to assure " Robert" that I had no felonious intentions—no burglarious designs upon the com- modities hidden by the shutters of the Rows. Then again I sought our home upon the river, but first stood watching the tide striving to overcome the rippling water of the weir, the current of which it silenced but did not reverse. I left my philosophic friend in the afternoon and returned by train, with the promise on my part to come over again and accompany him in the boat on the seaward and homeward route if need be. But this need not arise, for Di informed me by letter that he had scud his tub So "Tom Bowling," like his namesake, had "gone. aloft" finally and, let us hope, for good.

"DISFIGURED FOR LIFE " is the despairing cry of thousands afflicted with unsightly skin diseases. Do you realiza what. this disfiguration means to sensitive souls ? It means isolation, seclusion. It is a bar to social and business success. Do you wonder that despair seizes upon these sufferers when doctors fail, standard reme- dies fail, and nostrums prove worse than useless ? Skin diseases are most obstinate to cure or even relieve. It is an easy matter to claim to core them, but quite another thing to do so. CIITICDRA REMEDIES have earned the right to be called Skin Specifics, because for rears they have met with most remarkable success. There are cases that they cannot cure, but they are few in- deed. It is no inn-drawn-nut expensive experiment. One shilling invested in a tablet of CIITICURA SOAP will prove more convincing. than a nacre of advertisement. In short, CUTICURA WORKS WONDERS, and its cures are simply marvellous.

div.head: INFLUENZA. APPROACHING.
div.p: INFLUENZA. APPROACHING.

The icifluenza season is at hand now, and already the monster is reported in our midst. This terrible scourge seems to have settled down into a regularly recurring epidemic every autumn, and returns punctually to carry off its unresisting victims.

There has been consequently considerable excitement over the announcement that the monster's secret has been surprised, and that a Canadian doctor (hailing, however, from Edinburgh University), has broken the back of the coming terrcr by discovering a simple means by which the epidemic may be set at defiance. It is all, he says, a matter of resistance. Build up and fortify the system by the one needful combination, and laugh at the influenza ! This combination he has discovered, and it proves so safe and so handy for various uses in the improvement and restoration of health that it has been issued for general use, without even a doctor's pre- scription, under the name of Dr. Williams' Pink Pills for Pale People, and the newspapers are already full of the results. The "Star of Wales " (Seren Cymru), a Welsh paper, repprts the case of a Carmarthenshire man, Mr. J.Thomas,of Cwmduad,near Conwil, who was seized with influenza, and by this, and the awful pains of rheuma- tism which accompanied it, incapacitated from work and compelled to remain indoors, but who was promptly cured and re stored to perfect health by Dr. Williams' discovery. He said to the reporter (who saw him and bears witness to his case) : "I was very bad. The pain was all through my body and my limbs. I had a dread- ful pain in my back; and my appetite quite gone. I was languid and depressed, and unable to move from the house. Looking one day over a Welsh newspaper,! read of the wonderful scientific discovery given to the wend unchr the name of Dr. Williams' Pink Pills for Pale People; and I determined to try them. The first box did me much good. Afterwards I bought another box, and this second bcx completely cuted me. I have not lost a day's work since. I have a splendid appetite. Dr. Williams' Pink Pills cured me of all my troubles." To avoid fraud, owing to the great celebrity of Dr. Williams' Pink Pills it is important to note that they are genuine only as manufactured by the Dr. Williams Medi- cine Company, 46, Holborn-viaduct, London, at 2s. 9d. a :, or six box es 13s. 9d. Never sold bulk, or b,

div.head: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

Mr. John Mclntyre presided over the fortnightly meeting of the Runcorn Board of Guardians on Tuesday afternoon at the Dutton Workhouse. There were also present—Major Fox (ex-officio) ; Messrs. Joseph Knowles, J. Brandreth, H E. Hey- wood, J. M. Williams, E. Aaron, T. Handley, J.P., S. Yarwood, T. Lea, A. R. Norman, S Taylor. J.P.. J. Stokes, S. Woodward, J. Weir, C. T. Whitley, J. L. Jones, J. W. Baguley, E. Bratherton, A. Greenway, J. Ashton (clerk), and G. Ashton (deputy clerk).

div.head: VOTE OF SYMPATHY.
div.p: VOTE OF SYMPATHY.
On the motion of the Chairman a vote of condolence with the Rev. J. W. N. Tanner, on the death of Mrs. Tanner, was passed by the Board. THE LOCAL GOVERNMENT ACT, 1894.

An order. fixing the number of guardians and parish and district councillors for the various townships in the Union was forwarded by the Clerk to the Cheshire County Council. The number of guardians was un- altered, namely, 45, and the district councillors 38. For Runcorn there were seven guardians : two for the central ward, and one each to the other wards. The Parish Councils were consTituted as follows :—Acton Grange, five members; Alvataley, seven ; Antrobus, eight. Appleton : Stockton Heath ward, seven; Appleton ward, seven ; Great Budworth, eight ; Dutton, eight; Frodsham. fourteen ; Frndsham Lordship, twelve; Gra.npenhall, ten ; Halton, twelve ; Batton, seven ; Helsby, eleven ; Kingsley, eleven ; Latchford Without,eight ; Moore, eight; Norley, nine ; Norton, eight ; Preston o'th Rill, eight ; Stretton, seven ; Sutton, eight ; Thel wall, nine ; Walton Inferior, eight. Weston : Weaver ward, five; Weston ward, eight ; Whitley Superior, seven.

div.head: POOR LAW CONFERENCE.
div.p: POOR LAW CONFERENCE.

Mr. Williams submitted the report of the deputation which attended the Poor Law Conference at Souttiport,the previous week. The Chairman, clerk, and himself had attended and were impressed by the good results to be derived from such gatherings. Papers were read on various subjects, and the decisions arrived at were that old age pensions would be an enormous expenditure to the ratepayers without any good results ; that trained nurses ought to be employed in workhouses, instead of payper nurses who frequently undertook that work. It was also held to be very desirable that means should he provided for training workhouse boys for sea service. A discussion took place on the county rate, during which it was explained that it was made much heavier because of the great expenditure that the County Councils had incurred on repairs of roads and bridges, and it was stated that the county rate would probably becon.e less rather than increased. There was a concansus of opinion that some drastic and uniform method would have to be adopted for dealing with the large increase of tramps that had taken place of late. The speaker instanced how Cheshire stood lowest (~n the list of percentages of pauperism compared with southern counties. The con- ference also resolved that from a ratepayers point of view good sanitary dwelling houses ought to be insisted upon.

div.head: COMFORT FOR THE AGED INMATES.
div.p: COMFORT FOR THE AGED INMATES.

Mr. Yarwood said that in going the rounds of the Workhouse he had decided to ask the Board to provide cushions for the aged inmates, those who were over 70 years of age, to sit upon. He had seen some of the poor old creatures that day, about 80 years of age, and they had seemed very uncomfortable sitting upon their hard seats. It appeared to him to be inhuman that these old people, with their feeble limbs, should sit upon the ordinary hard benches. Only about two dozen of the cushions would be required he thought, and if they were purchased for such a purpose he would be very glad.—Mr. Lea seconded the proposition.—Finally It was decided to refer the matter to the House Committee, who would make a recommendation to the Board at their next meeting.

div.head: PROPOSED COUNCIL OF THE EVANGELICAL CHURCHES.
div.p: PROPOSED COUNCIL OF THE EVANGELICAL CHURCHES.
CONFERENCE AT WARRINGTON.

A conference was held in the band-room of Bold- stree t Wesleyan Chapel, on Thursday last aeEk, in order to consider the question of forming a council of the Evangelical Churches of Warrington, and also the details of the Parish Councils Act, which will shortly come into operation. The objects of the Council are stated to be-1. Primarily and chiefly to promote the spiritual life of the churches by (a) cultiva- ing.a closer fellowship, (b) adopting united evangelistic action.-2. To consider questions affecting the moral and social welfare of our fellow-citizens.-3. To furnish opportunities to Evangelical Nonconformists for taking concerted action upon questions affecting their common interests.-4. To discuss such other matters as may appear to the Council to be desirable, it being understood that all party political questions should be rigidly excluded.
Invitations had been sent out to the various Non- conformist churches of the town, and a good number of the members of those churches attended the conference.

Among those present were the Revs. T. Law (Bir- mingham), J. Yonge, Owen Watkins, G. D. Mason, D. W. Roberts, W. J. Kirkland, E. Moore, E. T. Reed, J. Warnock, J. Gunnell, J. S. Hughes, and Clay (Lymm) ; and Messrs. R. Garnett, J.P., E. J. Guest, J.P., Davies (Hollins Green), Whitley. J. Titchett, W. Brough, J. Bennett, W. Roberts, Winstanley, J. S. Garland, and G. L. Wellford (Lymm). Tne Rev. G. D. MAsoN explained that the Rev. J. Kirt- lan,who should have presided, was unable to be present, and he therefore proposed that the Rov.J. Yonge occupy the chair.—The Rev. OWEN WATKINS seconded, and the motion was carried unanimously. The CHAIRMAN said that he regretted that there was a disawointment in store for the meeting. He had re- ceived a letter from Dr. Mackennall that morning, which stated that he had just been called to Coventry where his brother had been found dead in his bed, and therefore he could not attend the meeting that day. Proceeding to explain the object of the meeting, he said that during the visit of Messrs. Fullerton and Smith, the churches of Warrington were drawn more closely towards elch other. It was a matter for thankfulness and congratulation that they had been coming together for some time,but on the occasion of the visit of the two gentlemen named, they

were drawn much nearer than ever before. He could re- member the time during his residence in the town, when there was a very marked distinction between the churches of the town. But by the united• prayer meet- ings, and still mare by meetings round the Lord's Table, the churches were becoming reore united. (Hear, hear.) After the mission of Messrs. Fullerton and Smith was over, a meeting of the delegates who had charge of ;he mission was held and a discussion was held upon the subject, which really led to the present meeting, and it was thought deeireele to form a council of the evangeli- calchurches of Warrington and the district. Mr. Mason I and himself were appointed secretaries pro ton in order te make the necessary arrangements. In this work,they , were following the spirit of the time. Sometimes they gathered encouragement from those with whom they widely differed, and he had strong sympathy with the sentiment of Cardinal Vaughan who, speaking at a Catholic conference at Pres- ton, said that one of the best signs of the times was the longing for the reunion of Christendom. They cordially agreed with Cardinal Vaughan, and it was a matter of great encouragement to Christian people to see the move- ment for union and co-operation which appeared to be extending. This movement was spreading allover the country, and he was glad to see in Glasgow, one feature which he scarcely hoped to see realized in England, and that was the establiseed church cf Scotland working along with the free Presbyterian churches in this move- ment. The proposed council would be of great use in Warriegton. Vast numbers in Warrington went to no place of worship. (Hear, hear.) Then were many matters in the town and district to work with united action upon. Among others were the Parish and District Coun- cils. It was very desirable that suitanle persons should elected upon these councils and also the Boards of Guar- dians, the election e for which took place in November. The Rev. G. D. MASON then read letters of apology he had received from persons unable to be present that afternoon. The following are the names, Rev. S. W. Varley, Messrs. Edwin Richardson, William Bennett, Councillor Shaw Green, Edwin Brown (Lymm), R. Cook (Penketh), J. Plinston, W. H. Bradford. S. B. Stringer, J. Therpe, G. Wells, T. Wallington, F. 0. Mostyn, and the Captain of the Salvation Army. The Rev. T. LAW, of Birmingham, gave an address, explanatory of the movement in other towns and cities. He said that there were now many oppor- tunities of asserting their streegth, but before the coun- cil became a power in the town, there were many things to be done. House to house visitations at Bradford at which place he worked until recently, had grand results.J Many congregations had been doubled as a result. He believed that the parochial system would have to be the system of the future, and each chapel or church must be the " parish " church of a district. This had worked with great success in Bradford, at which there were 80 Nonconformist parishes. At Birmingham also, where the systeni had recently been adopted, there were 154 parishes. There was no doubt a prejudice against the parish system among Nonconformists, but, if it worked well, then there was no reason whatever why they should not adopt it. Cf course it need not be upon the hard and fast lines of the Church of England, but still he always noticed that when a place of worship was responsible for a certain district, the people at that chapel always worked much harder. Mr. Law went on in a most interesting speech, te indicate ether fields of labour, in which the council could work. The Rev. J. YONGE thanked Mr. Law for his interest- ing discourse, and said that he thought it was highly desirable that a council on lines indicated in his speech be formed. He deprecated taking part in party politics, and he consideeed that whatever might be their poli- tical opinions, they ought to do everything they pos- sibly could to preserve the new departure in local legis- latures from the hands into which municipal cor- porations had fallen. He thought that they should vote for the best man or woman, whatever their political creed plight be. At the present conference he suggested that a motion similar to the following be passed, as it would not tie their hands, but leave them free to work out their plans in the future :—" That in the opinion of this meeting it is highly desirable to form a free evan- gelical church council fer Warrington and district, and that the churches represerted in this conference be invited to consider the scheme indicated in the constitu- tion now submitted.and that they proceed to elect mem- bers as speedily as possible to sit upon the council." The following is the constitution which was proposed: "That the membership consist of the minister or minis- ters in charge of any associated church ; representative members elected annually, in the proportion of two for every 100 church members or fraction thereof above 30. To ensure as wide representation as possible, churches having less than 100 members, but more than 30, will be allowed te send two representatives.and churches under 30, one member. The council, so constituted, shall have power to elect annually (by ballot if desired) 25 ladies or gentlemen, members of any free evangelical church in Warrington and district, as personal members, on their written application. That regular meetings shall he held quarterly. Sneeial meetings may be convened by the executive, or upon written requisition of 40 members of the council. 'f he executive committee shall consist of 30 members, in addition to a President, 3 vice-presidents, treasurer, and two honorary Secreta,ries,to be elected annually by ballot after nomination at the council meeting." The Rev. G. D. MASON moved the resolution sug- gested by the Rev. J. Yonge. ' The Rev. OWEN WATKINS also spoke in approving terms of the scheme. He said that he was glad that they had nothing to do with party politics. They as Wesleyans belonged to no party, but that did not prevent them from acting in questions of temperance, social purity, and parochial questions amongst which were the Parish Councils. They weuld vote for the hest man be he church or chapel, conserva- tive or radical. He hoped that the council would present a united front on the subject he had enumerated. A desultnry discussion ensued, in which the Revs. J. Warnock, Clay, and others took part, and the motion of Mr. MASON was carried unanimously. Mr. G. L.WELLFOED of Lvmm,then gave details of the Parish Councils Bill. After sketching out the scheme, an article upon which appeared in our columns in our last issue, he pointed out that there would only be one man, one vote, and that there would be no property qualifica- tion necessary. The only objection he had to the bill was that the voting in the first instance was by a show of hands. Many men would not be free owing to that reason to vote for the man they wished to support. He could not think how that could have got into the bill. He pointed out a great number of complexities in the manner which the charities were dealt with.

The Rev. W. J. KIRKLAND also spoke upon the same subject. He said that the Act was one to make further provision for Local Government in England and Wales, March sth, 1894, commonly known as the Parish Coun- cils Act. It was a worthy attempt to do justly to the people by restoring to them their rights of Local Govern- ment. This may be regarded by some as an invagion of the rights of the parson, warden and sqaire, but on this point even history was on the side of the people. The parish vestry, which meant all the parishioners anciently had power to hold land, also to make bylaws for their own locality and,rnere, even to levy taxation. Doubtless the diminution of " common " land by enclosure had curtailed the rights and powers of the vestry, also the transfer of the care of the poor to the Boards of Guar- dians, and of roads t. the Highway Boards had also diminished the power and importance of the vestry. The private parishioner could not call a parish vestry meeting. It was called by the churchwardens by permis- sion of the Incumbent and votes could not be by ballot. The Parish Council (except in matters ecalesias..ic) would supersede the vestry, becoming possessed of its powers and additional powers, and would elect its own chairman, as provided by the Act. The Parish Council became the recognized and authorized voice and power of the people to deal themselves with local interests. England and W.ales were divided into three classes, first the Metropolis, second Urban Sanitary District, and bird Rural Sanitary Districts. In London the property qualification was abolished, also the mode of electing the London vestries and chairman. In Urban Districts new duties, power and name wet- imposed on authori- ties already existing. But their interest centred in the rural section, where the Parish Council, District Council, and County Council formed a grand system of Local Government. What more natural than that those on the spot should know most intimately and be interested most deeply in local concerns, whether of roads, commons, allotments or the squires encroachment° on the green, To all the elections the Corrupt Practices Act would apply, and each will be by ballot. Doubtless in some places there would be attempts to put pressure upon particular men to keep them back and push others forward, like a case in this neighbourhood where a servant of the squire being at the top of the poll, he was ordered to resign or leave his situation to make way for the parson. Several questions were put and answered by Mr. Well. ford and the Rev. W. J. Kirkland, after which a vote of thanks was accorded them and the Rev. T. Law for their lucid explanations of the Nonconformist cannel' scheme and the Parish Councils Bill. A tea was subsequently held in the Bold-street Wesleyan schoolroom at which a good number sat down.

div.head: EVENING MEETING.
div.p: EVENING MEETING.

There was a fair attendance at the evening meeting. when the chair was occupied by Mr. E. J. Guest, J.P., and he was supported by the Revs. G. D. Mason, E. T. Reed, D. W. Roberts, W. J. Kirkland, T. Law, J. Youge, and J. S. Hughes. The CHAIRMAN said that his time had been so fully occupied by business, and in another place where he considered that they had done good service to the town —(applause)—that he thought they would excuse him if he read his remarks that night. They were met that night to promote an important scheme—the co-operation of the free churches in all tiuestions affecting the well being of society in Warrington and its neighbourhood. In that, there was no thought of organic; union, which seemed to him a beautiful dream, not likely to be real- ised in the near future. They were met in the interests of Christ's kingdom, by promoting united action of the various denominations. The Rector of Warrington, preaching the other Sunday, was reported to have said, referring in his definition of " one body," that the Non- conformist view was,that the one body was the society of all who loved the Lord Jesus Christ in sincerity. (Hear, hear.) That was a beautiful definition, but he

said that it was modern, unnatural, and unscriptural. He (Mr. Guest) thought that it was the rector who was unscriptural. It was scriptural to compare the church to the body of Christ, but it was not scriptural to say that the body was the Church of England exclusively. (Hear, hear.) Surely if the body of Christ was to be one uniform, visible church, the Roman Catholic had the prior claim to that definition. (Hear, hear.) He did not find, however, in the Holy Scriptures, any distinct definition of a church, or holy orders, or of a liturgical service: Wherever two or three are Diet:together in the name of Christ,there was the church—(hear,hear)—representing the one universal, invisible church. Schism aid not consist in leaving the church in which one could not work. Schism meant causing quarrels in the church. The Nonconformists were rather peace makers as they left the church in which they could not work. If there had been an organic unity with the Church of England, they would have missed all the open air preaching, and all the grand work which the Nonconformists had done. The Rector also said that the definition was unnatural, but he thought that the charge of unnaturalness was on his part. The body had many members. There was a diversity of administration and in work to be done. There was run one uniform manner of working. There were many regiments, but only one army. All those present were Englishmen,and he hoped they were all Christians. He thought that if the free churches of England united in action, and work with ,ot jealousy a great improvement of the town would result from the scheme inaugurated that night. . - •

The Rev.T Lew said that he believed that mnch good would result from the council which would be inaugu- rated. The churches ought to work among the demo- cracy, because without Christ the democracy was very dangerous, and socialism was dangerous and empty without the Lord Jesus Christ. They ought to wage war against gambling. They ought to capture the Press. The Press was a mighty power, and in years to come it would be much more powerful. They, ther -fore, ought to have it in their power. They ought to boycott all the papers which were filled with sportin! news, and those which contained matter which they would be ashamed of their children reading at the breakfast table. (Ap- plause.) If the Nonconformists would unite, they could revolutionise the Press. He also considered that the churches should be political. It was a great mistake for any church to identify itself with any political party but that should not prevent them protesting against any Government of this country which for instancrs went in in for compensation of the liquor tr tae. (Applause.) Every one ought to be a politician, for if a man had a vote and never used it, he was enjoying his privileges and neglecting his responsibilities. The Rev. IV. J. KIRKLAND then moved the following resoluti "That this meeting heartily endorses the recommendation of the conference held this afternoon, inviting the free evangelktic churches in this town and district to establish a council to promote co-operaiion in Christian work, and to further the interests common to them all." Speaking of the drink traffic, Mr. Kirkland said that he was glad and rejoiced at the success which had been achieved that day in Warrington. (Applause). His friend Mr. Roberts (loud and continued applause) had spoken to him that morning when coming frotn the police court and had said to him, " We have won all along the line." (Applause). He had no doubt the parties concerned would appeal, but he hoped they would find their appeal in vain. They had accomplished that day what would have a lasting impression for good. He was sure that a blow could be struck at gambling also if the churches showed a united front in it. The Rev. E. T. REED seconded the resolution. He said that he had heard his people called worse thaa dissenters,but he and his people had always taken active interest in Christian woak. His church was a protest against ritualism in the Established church, and it had been brought into existence, he believed, not by the desire of man merely, but by the guidance of the Holy Spirit to combat that error which had risen amongst them They could therefore hardly call themselves Noncon- formists, although they co-operated with those who called themselves by that name. They claimed to be an episcopal church, and that being so they had to consider the feelings of the church people. But he could heartily join with his brethren in the present movement, and I had great pleasure its seconding the motion. The motion was carried unanimously.

A.;ote-iif thanks was proposed to Mr. E. J. Guest for presiding, by thP Rey. G. D. MASON. The Rev. J. YoNati in seconding, said that he was always pleased to meet Mr. Guest. He was anxious that the movement for a united council wauld be taken up heartily by the churches. Warringtonians did not as a ru!e take to a now thing at once, but when they did lac hold of a thing they took it up heartily. He believel that that after- noon, they had kn,icked one nail at any rate into tolerably large coffin. (Laughter.) He hoped that soon they would knock a few more.
The vote was pissed, and after Mr. Guest had briefl7 replied. the meetinz was brought to a closo, by the. pro- nouncing of the benediction.

THE EXAMINER
SATURDAY, OCTOBER 6, 1894.
THE sudden calling together of the A Disquieting Cabinet this week was a disquiet- Incident. _
ing circumstance which was bound to give occasion for a plentifnl crop of rumours of a more or less alarming description. It was clear
that even the ministers themselves had not

expected that there would be any cause for such a summons. Lord ROSEBERY was enjoying a partial retirement at Dalmeny, his seat near Edinburgh, Sir WILLIAM HARCOURT had', but a few hours previous to the notification, left Loudon for the Continent,the LORD CHANCELLOR was away in Cornwall and Mr. MORLEY in Ireland, Lord TWEEDMOUTH and Mr. ARNOLD MORLEY had be-
taken themselves to the far north of Scotland,
while as to Mr. ASQUITH and Mr. Ilnycz their movements were not generally known and had certainly not been regulated with a view to a
sudden call to London. The other members of the Cabinet were also scattered far and

near, all, apparently, being of the opinion that the vacation would be disturbed by no Un- toward event. Then, late on Tuesday, suffdenly came this" bolt from the blue" as one writer has termed it. What could be the cause of this per- emptory meetirg of the statesmen who.are respon- sible for the conduct of the nation's affairs ?"rt
was, of course, clear that there was nothing in

domestic politics to call for any Cabinet meeting out of the ordinary course. But abroad affairs are, both in the East and the West, in an un- settled state, and rumour at once declared' that the relations between England and France had reached an acute and even threatening stage. There are several outstandinr,, questions. between this county and France. They relate to New— foundland, to Siam and Madagascar, to

Egypt, and to other parts of the African mainland. At the present time the question of Madagascar is most in people's minds The French claim some thing in the nature of a protectorate over that country, and,unfortunatery, Lord SALISBURY when foreign minister, seems to have agreed so far as England was concerned to practically hand over Madagascar to the French- men. Yet, as a matter of fact, English interests in Madagascar are vastly more importatit than those of France. The bulk of the trade of the island is- in English hands, and English missionaries have been particularly active and particularly successful in converting and civilising the natives. The complete conquest of the Madagascar which the French now seem disposed to attempt would probably mean the almost total extinction of English trade, and the rapid decline of English missions. In addition to that, there appears to be some reasons for be lieving that the French intend to establish a strong naval station in Madagascar which would be a decided menace to the trade routes to the East. This being the , state of affairs with regard to Madagascar it was naturally assumed that there had been develop- ments which were so serious as to call for the con- sideration of the united Cabinet. Fortunately, later information tended to discredit this assump- tion. It soon leaked out that it was no question of peace or war between the two most advanced and democratic countries of Europe that was under consideration, but that of protecting foreigners,— Frenchmen just as much as Englishmen—in China. The"Celestral Empire" has been demoralised by' de- feat. Its troops, such as they are, have been drawn away from the cities and provinces in which small colonies of Europeans have been formed, and the result is that the hatred of " foreigu devils "which - has always been a characteristic of the Chinese rabble has again broken out to the imminent danger of the foreign residents. The Chinese imperial government being r_o longer able to repress lawlessness and outrage it falls upon civilised governments to protect their own sub- jects, and most of all upon the English- Govern- ment as this country has the largest interests at stake. Hence the sudden calling together of the Cabinet.

.. THE Liberal "Twelve. Hundred" ' A Municipal Programme. of Manchester have set an example which similar organisations in other , towns might profit by. They have adopted a !mini- t' eipal programme which is in harmony with the tendencies of the times in which we live, and - which, in a word, contains something " worth fighting for." The Manchester Liberals have „ recognised the fact that no party which has only a policy of negation can fight a winning battle irk this country. The programme contains thirteen points, some of which, however, are of only local application. Those of a more general bearing relate to the paying of a standath rate of wages to Corporafion workmen ; a working day of not more than eight hours where practicable ; the election of a considerable number of worl6ngmen to public bodies; and the demolition of slum property and the provision of workmen's dwellings and open spaces. The elimination of contractors and the direct employment of labour is a policy which is I now followed by several progressive public bodies : and the Manchester Liberals declare in favour of

it. In Warrington, unfortunately, them appear° to be a tendency in the other direction. It is only a few months ago that one of the committees 01 the Corporation decided to. have its cartage done through the medium of a contractor, and even the meeting of the Town Council held on Tuesday the Sanitary Works Committee asked that a, tender for cartage--the"lowest tender"doubt- less—be sanctioned. It seems clear that Warring- ton Corporation does not aspire, like some other Corporations, to fill the role of model employer.

infected with warlike ambitions. He is credited with having on more than one occasion during his reign used his influence for smoothing over diffi- culties between European powers which might easily have led to armed conflicts. The CZAR'S illness, which is now reported is, therefore, a matter of the weightiest importance. It is said that he is suffering from advanced Bright's disease and neurostenia, and that his once herculean form has been reduced almost to a skeleton. When in full vigour he was a man of extraordinary physical strength—a veritable Samson in fact—yet now he can hardly use his arms. The illness is compli- cated with a domestic sorrow. The CZAR, writes one correspondent, " spends whole nights sleepless in a chair, weeping about his consumptive favour- ite son, the Grand Duke GEORGE, for whom there is no hope of recovery. Heartrending scenes are reported to have taken place at a recent meeting between the CZAR and his dying son."

ACCIDENT TO A LABOURER AT RUNCORN. Whilst engaged on Monday morning at the Runcorn -43olpery, John Riley, of 63, Church-st.' Runcorn, was struck on the head with a brick which had fallen a dis- tance of about twenty feet. A serious wound was in- flicted on the man's scalp, and Dr. McKenzie was sum- moned to attend him. SO,sequcnt inquiries elicited the information that the injured person was recovering. COLLIER'S sell everything for the smallest possible profits.

Advt. ST. LTJICE'S CONGREGATIONAL SABBATH SCHOOL, RUNCORN. The harvest festival in connection with this place of worship was held on Sunday. Mr. Philip France, of Malpas, preached afternoon and evening to large con- gregations, special hymns being sung by the children to the accompaniment of Mr. Paul Cartwright. The Rev. J. Simpson preached on Monday evening, and after the service the fruit was distributed to the sick people of the district. COLLIER'S BREAD is the best money can buy.—Advt. A NEW LIGHTER FOR THE SHIP CANAL AT RUNCORN. The second of a number of lighters to be constructed at the Old Quay yard for use on the Ship Canal, was launched successfully on Monday afternoon at Runcorn. Its dimensions are almost identical with those of the first lighter floated two months ago. It is 102 feet long. 21 feet wide, 8 feet depth of hold, and will carry 250 tons when drawing only five feet four inches of water. Mr. F. Wiswall is the designer of the barges, and Mr. J. Dykes, foreman of the Sprinch Works has superintended the building ef them.

HARVEST FESTIVAL AT RUNCORN. Harvest thanksgiving eervices were conducted on Sun- day at the Primitive Methodist Chapel, Greenway-road, Runcorn.The decorations were carried out by the ladies of the sewinw class and the members of the Christian En- deavour Society. The Rev. W. Albert, formerly of this circuit, but now of Winsford, preached in the morning, and the Rev. J.St4fford,Methodlst Free Church minister, was the evening preacher. At each service the choristers rendered anthems and special hymns, Mr. W. Gittens, sun. ,being the conductor. On Monday evening a coffee supper took place in the schoolroom, at which a large number attended. COLLIER'S FRESH IRISH DAIRY BUTTER, 10d. per lb. is excellent—Advt.

• On Sunday last service;- Were conducted in the above place of worship in commenoreien of its anniversary. The Rev. W. S. Slater M.A., professor in Biblice litera- ture and exegesis,Theelogicel College, Didsbury,occupied the pulpit and delivered two very instructive sermons. The anthem rendered in the morning by the choir was "The Lord is my Shepherd," and and in the evening. "The Lord is my Bing." Miss Clara Taylor, R.A.M. assisted the choristers, and the various pieces were ren- dered in a very praiseworthy manner. The choir was • conducted by Mr. T. Johnson whilst Mr. G. S. Frith presided at the organ. The offertories,which amounted to nearly £8 were to be devoted to trust funds. COLLIER'S is. BUTTER is tha gem in the market.—Advt. INTERESTING LECTURE AT RUNCORN. The members of the Brunswick Mutual Improvement Society met on Wednesday evening in the Brunswick - School and reopened the winter session. The attendance was a large one, and the Chairman was Mr. T. otmlster. After this gentleman had made a few appropriate intro- ductory remarks, Mr. Thomas Sanders, one of the society's secretaries, delivered an interesting lecture on the subject "How popular periodicals are produced." The lecture was copiously illustrated by means of a num- ber of slides which had been forwarded by Messrs. George Newnes and Co., Limited, the productions of this firm being those principally referred to in the course of the lecture. The lantern was managed by Mr. Pick- thall,assistant secretary. At the close of the proceedings, votes of thanks was accorded the lecturer, Mr. Pick- thall, and Messrs. Newnes, and Co., who had supplied the illustrative slides. COLLIER'S BLACK BLENDED TEA. 21-d. per quarter lb.—Advt. SERIOUS ACCIDENT TO A 4BOY AT RUNCORN. A youth named Samuel Walker, fifteen years of age, and residing at 75, Percival-lane, Runcorn, met with a serious accident on Monday morning last. It appears that shortly before nine o'clock he was crossing the canal bridge at the bottom of Percival-lane when by some means he fell over the side on to the canal bank, striking his head with great force. So intease was the shock that the lad was rendered unconscious, and was found in this condition by a passer-by who picked him up and afterwards had him conveyed home. Here he received every attention until the arrival of Dr. MacLennan who found the boy suffering from shock and a large wound on the head; from the quantity of • blood which the patient emitted came to the conclusion that the lad had also been internally injured. He is faring as satisfactorily as can be expected, and his recovery is hopeful. COLLIER'S sell the best quality goods at lowest possible prices.—Advt. PLUCKY RESCUE FROM DROWNING BY • BOY AT RUNCORN. An act which is certainly worthy of recognition by the Royal Humane Scciety is accredited to a lad named Henry Green, fourteen years of age, who resides in Fryer-st., Runcorn. The circumstances of the case are that on Sunday at noon, Arthur Worrell, the seven year old son of Jcseph Worrell, 28, rridgewater-st., was playing on the hanks of the Ship Canal near Runcorn Bridge, when in trying to pull something out of the water he overbalanced and fell into it. Owing to the tide being up, the current was strong and the unfortu- tunate boy was carried into mid-stream. The occurrence was noted by several persons. the lad Green being one of them. Without hesitating he threw off his coat, jurneed into the canal, and reached the drowning boy by the heels, just as he was sinking for the last time. He then swain with him to the side of the waterway where willing hsnds relieved him of his burden, and he was himself assisted out of the water. Worrall was in- sensible' his face being much discoloured. Several men resorted to means to bring about respiration and they were at last successful. He was then conveyed to a house close to the spot and afterwards was taken home by his parents. Green has now been the means of sav- ing three persons from drowing. A WIDNES VIRAGO. At the Widnes Police Court on Monday morning, a young woman named Catherine Haynes, 18, Nelson-st., was charged in custody with wilfully breaking the plate glass windows o? the White Star Hotel, West Bank-st., on Saturday night, doing damage to the extent of £3O. —John Gerrard, thelandlord of the house, said he closed his house as usual on Saturday night at eleven o'clock. Twenty minutes later, when he was in the bar, he heard a noise of breaking of glass. He went out of the house and saw prisoner standing and throwing stones at the windows of the Pear-st, side of the house. Six windows Were brolrea on the West Benk-st. side, and the windowi in the corner deor was smashed. Altogether there were thirteen panes of piers broken. The prisoner ran off down Pear-street. Witness followed, but when he caught hold of her she beck me very violent and kicked and struck him.—Mr. Lewin (deputy magistrates' Clerk) : I believe she has done this before, Mr. Gerrard ? --Witness Yes.—Prisoner (smiling) : Yes and I'll do it again, too.—Mr. J. H. Lea, painter and glazier, Fern- -worth, said the damage amounted to £3o.—The prisoner was further charged with doing damage to the-police tell to the extent of £2, and was committed for trial on the first charge, and on the second charge she was sent to gaol for twenty-one days with hard labour. There vere thirty-nine previous convictions against the -Prisoner.

DEATH OF Mns. T. TIIOIIIPSON. , We have this week to record the death of Mrs. Thompson, wife of Mr. Thomas Thompson, of Crow- lane, Enrlestown, secretary to the Vulcan Foundry tompany, which took place at his residence on Sunday afternoon. The deceasedlady was 46 years has age, and for a period extending over 15 months nas been in ill-health, but during the last few raonths the malady from which she was suffering had assumed a more acute form, and very faint hopes of her recovery were entertained ; she gradually sank and died as stated. She was in- terred in theiCongregational Churchyard on Thurs- day.

div.head: RUNCORN RURAL SANITA.RY
div.p: RUNCORN RURAL SANITA.RY
AUTHORITY.

On Tuesday afternoon the fortnightly meeting of the above authority was held in the Board room, Dutton Workhouse, Mr. J. Mclntyre occupying the chair. The remaining gentlemen present were Mr. Joseph Knowles, vice-chairman, Major Fox, (ex- officio), and Messrs. John Weir, H. E. Heywood, J. NI. Williams, E. Aaron, C. T. Whitley, J. Brandreth, S. Woodward, J. L. Jones, J. Stokes; J. Ashton, clerk; G. Ashton, deputy clerk; J. Farrington, nuisance inspector; and Dr. Adams, medical officer of health. THE MEDICAL OFFICER'S REPORT. Dr. Adams submitted his report for the past fortnight which stated that a fatal case of typhoid fever had occurred at Moore. The patient, a plumber,had recent- ly been engaged in removing old sewers and relaying sewers, and it had been further ascertained that he had occasionally drunk water from a brook which was contaminated with sewage at Walton. No defects existed on the premises. Two eases of scarlet fever had occurred at Lower 'Walton, both of whom attended Stockton Heath Schools. The first case was probably due to infection from another child, and the second case appeared to have derived infection from visiting at a friend's house. Two cases of scarlet fever had occurred at Stockton Heath, Appleton. One case appeared to have been very doubtful, there having Veen no rash or peel- ing; but the other one had been evidently contracted away from home. Several fresh cases had occurred at Kingsley. He had visited all the above and had issued the necessary preventive orders. Several cases had also been reported to him from Weston.—The report was adopted.

POLLUTION OF BECKWICK BROOK. Mr. C. L. Evans, of Norton Hill, writing on October Ist relative to the above matter, said :—" This brook is continually being polluted from the tannery at Preston Brook. To-day the water was a purple colour and was about as thick as pea-soup, and the stench from it was , something dreadful. I should be glad if the Sanitary Authority can take steps to prevent its pollution which must be most detrimental to cattle."—Mr. Brandreth considered that it was for Sir Richard Brooke and Sir G. Greenall to take action. The brook ran through their property. He proposed that the Clerk should write to Mr. Evans saying if the brook was polluted he should take action.—Mr. Aaron seconded.—Mr. Farrington re- marked that they had nothing to do with the health of cattle, but of human beings.—Mr. Heywood thought that the health of human beings depended to a great extent upon the health of the cattle. —Mr. Weir said the water was very bad and unfit for cattle to drink.—Mr. Farrington said that the brook had been used before the introduction of the Rivers Pollution Preventive Act, and therefore was exempt from the powers contained therein. THE POOR-LAW CONFERENCE. Referring to the recent Poor-Law Conference at Southport, to which a deputation from the Board of Guardians had been sent, the Chairman said that Dr. Rhodes read some interesting papers showing that if Sanitary Authorities did their dauy in dealing with un- sanitary property there would be a considerable reduc- tion in the poor rate.

On Monday evening in the Greenway-road Board School Mr. J. Pritchard, Chairman of the Runcorn School Board, dirtributed the prizes and certificates to the successful scholars of the last session attend- ing the above school. He prefaced the ceremony with an address,in the course of which he said that they were assembled that evening for a two-fold purpose— firstly to distribute the prizes for the work done during the past session, and secondly to inaugurate the new session which was the fifth for the boys and the second for the girls. With regard to the work of the past it had proved eminently satisfactory and successful'. The grants and fees had been sufficient to pay for the work- ing of the school including the teaching staff, lighting, and heating, and also for the prizes. That, in itself was very satisfactory. Beyond that the educational work accomplished was very gratifying, and as a proof of this he might state that the number of certificates received for excellent work from the Union of Lancashire and Cheshire Institutes was seventveight : 28 for arithme- tic ; 27 writing; 12 geography ; and 11 grammar. In addition to that they had a very excellent report from Her Majesty's Inspector which said of the boys' depart- ment "This school continues to do an excellent work. It is conducted with marked zeal, energy, and intelli- gence." Another matter proving the efficiency of the work was the full grant which had been obtained in the boys' school on every subject taught. With regard to the coming session, the Board stated, last year, with promising results,a girls department, and they trusted this also would be successful. The imp Jrt- ance of those continuation schools seemed to be recog- nised throughout the country and he hoped that Run- corn would be able to hold that position in the future which it had held in the past. In order to give every encouragement the Board had reduced the fees this year and they trusted that the young people of the town would resolve to attend regularly so that they might get the greatest possible benefit, and also prevent any loss to the Board. He then proceeded to distribute the prizes to the following :—Girls' department, first class: Lilian Wharton, Alice Charleston, Ada Hitchmough,Fanny Hill, Gertrude Jones, Clare Pilgrim. The Chairman further reported that the Board had received the order from the Local Government Board with regard to the District Councils, and the modes of electing them. The election would take place between the 15th and the 19th.—After some discussion, in which several members seemed inclined to suggest to the Coun- cil to select the 17th as the day for the election, it was decided that nothing should be said on the matter, but leave it entirely in the hands of the Cheshire Council.

div.head: MARRIAGE OF THE VICAR OF FRODSHAII.
div.p: MARRIAGE OF THE VICAR OF FRODSHAII.

On Wednesday morning the marriage of the Rev. Henry Birdwood Blogg.vicar of Frodsham,Cheshire, second son of the late Colonel H. Savil Blogg (Mad- ras Cavalry) to Miss Annie Maria Allen, second daughter of Mr. George Afien,of Strange way s,Marn- hrill, was celebrated at Marnhutl Church, Dorset. The harvest f6stival decorations were allowed to remain up for the occasion, and thus the edifice had a joyous appearance. The villagers took great in- terest in the wedding,Mr. Allen and his family, and especially the bride, being very highly respected in the locality. Bunting was flown from several of the private residences, and a couple of evergreen arches spanned the road at different parts taken by the bridal party. One arch was an especially fine on", and bore the inscriptions in white letters on a red ground of "Health and Happiness,".and " May Blessings attend You." Over the gates at the en- trance to Strangeways, the home of the bride's father, evergreens had been tastefully arranged. By the time fixed for the ceremony, 11 a.m., the church except that portion reserved for the guests, was crammed, the aisles being filled with persons who were glad even to stand to get a look at the bride and her maids.As the bride entered the church leaning on the arm of her father, and escorted by , half-a-dozen bridesmaids and a couple of pages, the choir sang the hymn, "The voice that breathed o'er Eden,' and later on, after a special psalm, "Oh, perfect love, all human thought transcending" was sung. The ceremony was performed by the Right Rev. the Bishop of Chester, assisted by the Rev R. Bruce Kennard (the rector of Marnhuli), and the " Rev. Fowler Blogg (rector of Great Mongeham), Kent, and brother of the bridegroom). Whilst the register was being signed Mr. Parsons (Stalbridge) improvised a little melody on the organ,and as the wedding party left the sacred edifice he rendered Mendelssohn's " Wedding March." On leaving the church the bride and bridegroom were received in the approved fashion with showers of rice. The bride's dress was of the richest ivory satin duchesse, the bodice Was draped with chiffon and orange blossom, and she wore a long tulle veil. Her only ornaments were a diamond brooch, the gift of her father, and moonstone, ruby and diamond bracelEt, the gift of Lord and Lady Stalbridge. The brides- maids were Miss Rosamond Allen, Miss Jessie Allen, sisters of the bride ; Miss Winnie Blogg, Miss Lilian Blogg,nieces of the bride4room ; Miss Pauline Bennett, Miss Ruth Gravent-r, the last ;four being children; and Mmter Sam Gravener and

DROWNING MYSTERY AT RUNCORN.

An inquiry was held at the Cemetery Offices, Green- way-road, by Mr. J. E. Worsley, coroner, on Thursday afternoon, relative to the death of Patrick O'Brien, aged 37 years, whose body was found in the Frances Dock, Runcorn, on the previous morning.& verdict of "Found drowned" was returned.

div.p: FitODSHAII.

FRODSIII3I LADIES AT LOGGERHEADS.—At the Frodsham Police Court on Tuesday evening, before Messrs. C. Reynolds and A. Thomas, Mary Butters, a married woman, residing in Volunteer-street, was summoned by Mary Moores, of the same street, for using threats towards her on the Ist inst., whereby the latter feared that the defendant would do her some bodily harm.— Prosecutrix said that the affair originated through defendant losing a hat and accusing her of stealing it. The defendant struck her in the mouth and threatened her violence.—The defendant repelled this accusation saying that she simply pushed Moores in order to eject her from her (defendant's) house.—Defendant was to pay 3s. costs and was bound over to keep the peace fur six months in her recognizance of £5.

ALAN BAG 1J LEY . —ThP members of the Young Men's Bible Class, connected with the Hal- ton Wesleyan Sunday School,presentod Mr. Alan Baguley on Sunday afternoon last with a handsome comprehen- sive te4cher's bible and hymn book. The ceremony took place at the close of the Sunday school,when many re- marks of a eulogistic naturo were made with reference to Mr. Baguley's connection with the class. The inscrip- tion on the bible was "flatten Wesleyan Church. Pre- sented to Mr. Alan Bag,uley by the members of the Young Men's Bible Class as a token of their esteem. September 30th, 1894." Mr. Baguley left Stockham this week for Bangor University College to follow a course of study for two years, he having won a scholarship a few , weeks ago, offered by the County Council.

Master Montague Bennett acted as pages. The bride's sisters wore costumes of yellow shot silk, draped with embroidered lisse, and the bodices were veiled with guipure and finished with rosettes and sashes of black satin ribbon, and they wore large picture hats of black velvet. They carried shower bouquets of Marechal Niel roses and autumn leaves, and were bangles, the gifts of the bridegroom. The little pages wore charming suits of golden brown plush, of the Fauntleroy design, with yellow silk blouses and sashes. They each wore a gold and pearl horseshoe pin, the gift of the bridegroom. Sir John Hanham, Bart., fulfilled the duties of best man. The breakfast was served in a capacious marquee, the followi_ig amongst other guests sitting down : Lord and Lady Stalbridge, Sir John Elanharn, the Hon. Elsie Grosvenor, the Hon. TI-1E GRAVING DOCK: FIRII ATTITUDE OF THE BOARD.

The monthly meeting of this Board was held on Thursday morning in the Town Hall, Runcorn, Mr. S. Taylor J.P. presiding. The remaining gentlemen present were Messrs. W. Collier, F. Wiswall, J. Meadowcroft, J. Pritchard, E. Imison, W. Leach, H. J. Grice, D. Bisbrown, R. Abel, F. A. Lake, law clerk ; E. Marshall, secretary ; and M. Barker. surveyor. HIGHWAYS AND BUILDINGS COAEMITTEB. The recommendations of this committee were that £25 be paid to the owners of the " Vine " Hotel,Low- land-road, for land required for the improvement of the footpath in that road, and that the Board make the foot- way seven feet wide, remove the weighing machine and refix it leaving it in the same working order, reduce the machine house making all good, and build a brick wall with stone coping; also that application be made to the Local Government Board for their sanction to a loan for 60 years to carry out the above-named works. That a nine inch sewer pipe be laid down in Highland-road at an estimated cost of £100; a twelve inch pipe in Wes- ton-road at the estimated cost of £5O ; a twelve inch pipe (about 130 yards) in Moughland-lane, and a nine inch (310 yards) from Moughland-lane to Heath-road, at an estimated cost ef £l6O ; about 300 yards of eighteen inch piping from the bottom of Balfour-street to Holloway Bridae, estimated cost £150; contingencies £4O; making a total of £5OO. Also that application be made to the Local Government Board for their sanction to a loan of £5OO for 60 years for the above-named works.—That the pro- posal of Mr. Reynolds to pave a passage between Light- burn-st. and Curzon-st. with bricks, be approved.—That Pentnaenmawr Channel stones be substituted for the boulder stones in Bridge-st., and that Messrs. Brundrit and Co.'s price for the supply of the required channel stones be accepted. Mr. Wiswall proposed the adoption of the minutes.— Mr. Collier seconded the passing of the minntes and this was agreed to.

TRH GRAVING DOCK. The Parliamentary and General Purposes Committee recommended that the Manchester Ship Canal Co. be informed that the Commissioners will insist on the per- formance of the agreement of Ist September, 1890, and that unless the work of providing a graving dock be pro- ceeded with legal preceedings will be taken to obtain specific performance of the said agreement. Mr. Pritchard in proposing the confirmation of this minute said that all the members were aware of the importance of the subject. There were a number of conditions in the documents, several of which had been carried out by the company. The only one over which the direcrors had displayed hesitation in carrying out was the one referring to the provision of a graving dock. According to the agreement the dock should be com- pleted within twelve months after the ope ning of • the Canal; so that it should be finished at the end of this year if that agreement was rigidly adhered to. But solar there were no signs whatever, or any hope of its being completed at the end of this year, inasmuch as no steps whatever bad been taken by the company to commence the work. The Board had addressed many communica- tions to the company, but the replies had not been satis- factory.
