div.head: NEWTON BOARD OF COMMISSIONERS.
div.p: NEWTON BOARD OF COMMISSIONERS.

At the monthly meeting of the above Board held at the Town HtLL Earlestown, on Monday, there were present, Messrs. J. W. Emmett (chairman), T. Ormaud, G. R itcliffe, E. T. Evans, P. McMahon,P. Thompson, J Smith, J. E. Worsley (law clerk), R. BrieTley (clerk and surveyor), and Dr. Watkins (medical officer). COLONEL MCCORQI7ODALE'S RESIGNATION.

Mr. Emmett said that he had received a letter from Colonel McCorquodale with reference to his resignation, in which he said that he off ,:,red his sincere thanks for the kind letter in reply to his letter of resignation. It would afford him much pleasure to continue in office until all the Commissionersyesigned in November next. He would be glad if Mr. Emmett would offer to the Commissioners in general, his sincere thanks for the considerate re- ark PerCti nhim.—The Clerk also read the follow- ing letter Colonel McCorquodale :—" Dear Sir,—l re- marks res from acknowledge the receipt of yours of the 4th inst., in which you mention that a resolution was passed by the Board desiring me to remain as a Commissioner until its dissolution in November or December. I have much pleasure in agreeing to it,and I embrace the opportunity of thanking the Commissioners for the kind considera- tion in which they have passed the resolution." MEDICAL OFFICER'S REPORT.

Dr. Watkins gave his quarterly r-e-p-o—r.t ending Sept. 30, in which he said that the birth rate had been male, 53 ; female,s2 ; total, 105; the death rate had been,male, 15 ; female, 21 ; total, 36 ; excPss of births over deaths wag 69. The birth rate was 30.6, and the death rate 103 per 1,000 of the estimated population. He might remark that the death rate of children under five years of age was 416 per cent. of the whole. With such a marvellous'y low death rate, the infantik, mortality had been relatively high.—Mr. Emmett considered that the doctor's report was a very satisfactory one. He was glad that the Board was ending with such a good one.—Dr. Watkins said that it was the last report he would make to them as a Board. Thev did not know how many changes there were to be in the near future. He himself did not know whether he would keep his post,but if not he sincerely hoped that his successor would have as good furl une in his year Of office as he and the Board had had in the last one. He hoped that the Board which succeeded the present one would also have the same good fortune. 9 that at the end of the previous(Hear,hea r. li week) there eas saodb been say ease of fever inaported into the township from Ashton-under-Lyne, but he be- lieved that by that time it would have been removed. PROPOSED SMALLPOX HOSPITAL. Mr. R. Brierley read a letter from Dr. Sergeant,county medical officer, stating that a conference was arranged to be held in the county office at Preston on October s,at two o'c'ock re the formation of a Warrington and Leigh joint hospital district for smallpox purposes, which would emhrace the Leigh district, the Warrington borough ,and the Warrington Rural Sanitary district,and Newton-in-Makerfield. An invitation was given for a member of the Newton Board to attend the meeting.— Dr. Watkins thought that it would be better to join the St. Helens district, as they had a hospital at Haydock. After a short discussion, it was decided that Messrs. Ratcliffe and Ormand be appointed to attend the con- ference.

GAS COMMITTEE. At a meetina of this committee several accounts were paQsed to the Finance Committee for payment,including EV for deposits to be returned to property owners on gas accounts.—Mr. Ormand and Mr. Mahon moved and seconded the adoption 'of the minutes which were passed.

div.head: BIGHWAY COMMITTFE.
div.p: BIGHWAY COMMITTFE.

At a meeting of this committee the question of right of tolls for Newton Common enclosures at May festivals and other similar occasions was considered and ordered to stand over to next Board meeting when the Law Clerk should be present. It was resolved that Messrs. R. Davies and Co., Warrington, be informed that the Com- missioners would not make any claim against the estate of the late W. Chambers re night soil contract from which they were now released.the Commissioners having made other arrangements. Mr. Gregory's report was read and approved. Plans for 24 cottae..es in Athol-at. for Mr. W. Cross and alterations to cottages at Warring- ton for Mr. C. T.Whitley were submitted and approved. Several accounts were passed to the Finance Committee for payment.—Mr. Ratcliffe moved and Mr. Thompson secorded the adoption of the minutes which were passed unanimously.

div.head: TOWN HALL MEETINGS.
div.p: TOWN HALL MEETINGS.

Mr. Emmett then read the f,,llocring letter he had received from Mr. S. Harvey, with reference to meetings to be held is the Town Hall during the coming District Council elections :—" Dear Sir,—At a meeting of the general committee, which has to select candidates for the coming elections for the Newton division council, the following resolution was passed, That the Secretary write to the Chairman of Commissioners asking him to put before the commissioners, the question whether they would allow the use of a room in the Town Hall free for meetings of this committee, and requests him to be so good as to lay that resolution before h:s colleagues.' I may state for your guidance that a nublic meeting was held, and the committee was constitutA solely in the public interest, being free from any political, sectarian or party character."—Referring to the letter, Mr. Emmett said that seeing that the meetings were in con- nection with the election to the District Council, he was of opinion that they oug.ht to be held in the Town Hall, and that no charge should be made. Fletook it, that the Town Hall was for the benefit of the,public. (Hear, hear.) He understood that a charge had been made for the last meeting—about 15s. he thought. He, therefore, thought !that that sum should be refunded.— Mr. Ratcliffe, Mr. Smith. Mr. Ormand and Mr. Evans, spoke in support of Mr. Emmett's suggestion.—The Law Clerk, however rules that notise was required to alter, the scale of charges, and that in the meantime if any meetings were held the money would have to be deposited, but it could afterwards be refundeJ.—Mr. Ormand accordingly gave notice that at the next meeting of the Board, he would move a resolution that on the written application of ten ratepayers to the Chairman of C )mmissioners,the use of the Town Hall be allowed free for the purpose of meet- ings for the election of District Councillors and Poor Law Guardians. _ _ _ _ _ _ _

EARLESTOWN AND NEWTON.

EARLESTOWN DISTRICT SCHOOLagt/EEN'S SCHOLARSHIP EXAMINATION. Miss Adams, who has completed her term of apprenticeship at the above school has, we are pleased to learn, been placed in the first class at her last and most important examination. The result is equally gratifying to Miss Adams and her instructors.

EARLESTOWN WOMEN'S LIBERAL ASSOCIATION. The first of the series of monthly meetings, held daring the winter months, in connection with the above association, took place on Thursday after- ncon at the Co-operative Hall. Mrs. G. W. Rawlins presided, and there was a large attendance of mem- bers, fully 100 being present. After Mrs. Rawlins had extended a welcome to the members, Miss E. Marrow, who was a delegate to the affiliated society in London, read a paper, containing a summary of the various matters which were dis- cussed at the meetings of the society which she at- tended. The members afterwards partook of tea, and the gathering terminated. It is proposed to hold a meeting shortly, when an address will be delivered by a London lady on the question of , Parish Councils. YEOMANRY DINNER AT NEWTON. The annual dinner of the "C "Troop Lancashire Hussars, was held at the Red Bull Hotel on Satur- day evening, when about 80, including the members of the troop,and the tenant farmers who supply the horces , sat down to an excellent repast, prepared in nice style by Mr. J. Dorman. After dinner Mr. J. E. ,Pardey (steward) presided, and was supported by Messrs. R. Stewart, W. Balharry, Pimblett, F. A. Frost, and Livesley. The usual loyal and patriotic toasts were duly honoured, the ocher toasts being "Lord Newton," "The lion T. W. Legh," captain of the troop, "The tenant farmers," and "The non- commissioned officers." Songs were given by Quartermaster Howard, Sergeant Farrier,T. Ritchie, Corporal Swann. Private W. Turner. and Mr. J. Williams, an ex-member of the troop.

div.head: GOOD TEMPLAItS.

The weekly session of the of Earlestown lodge of Good Templars was held in the Co-opera- tive Hall on Monday evening. Bro. Joseph Anderton p-esided, and there was a very large attendance of members. Six new members were initiated and several candidates were proposed. The digest of business for the meeting of No. 1 Convention to be held at Wigan on 6aturday was read 14 Sister Mrs. Warburton, and representatives were duly in- structed. Arrangements were made tor a viit to the Hope of Vulcan lodge on Thursday night. The meeting was afterwards declared open, and an ex- cellent, programme of songs, readings, recitations, was given by the following : Sisters Blair,Newman, Cordingley, Clarke, Wilkinim, F. Holliday, Willis, Bros. Clarke, Willis, W arburton and Haynes.

div.head: DEBATE ON POLITICS AT EARLESTO WN.
div.p: DEBATE ON POLITICS AT EARLESTO WN.

At the mutual improvement class connected with the church meeting in Queen-street, Mr. B. Harri- son read a paper on Tuesday night dealing with the question of Christians and their political activities. Defining politics as the science of government on behalf of the governed Mr. Harrison showed how the same root principles applied to both local and im- perial politics in respect to the character, standing, and capability of those whose services were given to the community, and upon the principle that like produces like the question was put who but good men should be entrusted with the making of the nation's laws? And likewise, who so likely to perceive the good or to detect the hollowness and falsity of any public question as the Christrian ; therefore it was much to be desired that Christian people should use the powers now given and so hasten on the "good time coming." With regard to

party politics he thought there was room for both ' Radical and Tory Christians, wittily using the text "Prove all things, hold fast that which is good." Mr. Harrison drew a fine picture of the active operation of Christian men in the sphere of politics whose timely in: : terference, whose eloquent pleading, whose heroic forti- tude and whose persistent efforts have left us such a noble heritage in the abolition of despotism, the freedom: of the slave, the liberty of the press and the rights of conscience.—Mr. Broster thought that much needed to he done in the way of purifying the political machinery of our country, a work that Christians were far more qualified to do than those who sought t,) use the organizations existing for their own selfish purposes. —Mr:Sirett animadverted in regard to woman's position in politics, averring that her sphere was not in the fore front but like the Christian church, her usefulness was best attained in a somewhat obscure position.—Mr. Holdsworth gave prominence to the thought that the political arena was not the place for the Christian, his duty being to quietly abide all issues and trust to the leavening influence of his principles in contact with individuals.—Mr. Evans contended that while it was quite true that an end was more surely secured by devot- ing a life time to it, yet that course would tend to make individuals one-sided, while the Christian should be an all-round man.—Mr. King characterized the monastic view as "other worldliness" and pleaded for a thorough treatment by Christians of all public questions. With regard to Christians filling public offices he thought that often a man even distinctly opposed to Christianity in his thought and advocacy possessed undoubted qualifica- tions fora political career, and if of blameless life, such ought to be accorded the hearty support of all Christian people.—Master JeAse Harrison, Mr. Mellor and others also took rart and contribute I their share to what proved to be a most enjoyable debate.

div.head: MORE NEGLECT OF CHILDREN AT WARRINGTON. SHOCKING DESTITUTION.
div.p: MORE NEGLECT OF CHILDREN AT WARRINGTON. SHOCKING DESTITUTION.

At the Warrington Borough`Court Friday, on the adjourned case of Job n and Alice Clare, 8, Stamford- street, Warrington, for neglecting their two children was again brought before the magistrates. Mr. Buckton, solicitor, who prosecuted on behalf of the N.S.P.C.C., stated that the case was before the magis- trates a fortnight ago, but the male defendant was unable to appear owing to illness. He was still unable to appear and it was a question whether he was likely to get better. The Bench told the female defendant that the children shculd be taken to the Workhouse. She promised that she would do so, but when she got outside the court she refused. The children were still being neglected. Inspector McAteer said thc children were being starved, and the man was dying en a mass of rags. ; He had visited the house on four or five occasions, and it contained no food or furniture. The magistrates ordered that the children he taken to the Workhouse,and the woman was told to see the relieving officer about her husband.

John and Catherine Knight, 3, Silver-square, were charged with neglecting their children. Mr. Buckton said that the defendants were husband and wife,and the three children who had been neglected were Mary Ann, aged 7, John, aged 5, and Catherine three years of age. They were ntither clothed, fed, nor kept clean. The rags they wore and their bodies were filthy, and covered with vermin. The house was very much the same. In one bedroom where a lodger slept there was nothing hut two old sacks on the floor. The husband WAS a puddler and earned about 30s. a week. Out of that he gave his wife 18s. a week to buy food and clothing. Drink was the cause of a great deal of the neglect. The children did not attend school.—lnspector McAteer stated that on the 15th inst.in company with Detective Monaghan he visited the dt-fendant'i, house at 3, Silver-square. The girl Mary Ann was very badly dressed,her clothing consisting of two tattered garments, which were very dirty. She had no boots or stockings to wear. Her hair was matted and alive with vermin. The boy John was sitting in a corner of the kitchen undressed, having nothing on but a dirty shirt. His body was pricked all over from ver- min bites, and his flesh was very dirty. Catherine,ag,ed three,was in a similar condition. He found the kitchen a a dirty condition. In the room where the defendant and their family slept together the bedding consisted of an old bedstead, two mattresses, and a dirty sheet, and the room stank. In the front room there was nothing but two old sacks, upon which a woman lodsrer slept. He again visited the house on the 19th and 27th insts., but found no improvement what- ever in the condition of the children. D.S. Monaghan and P.C. Bruen gave corroborative evi- dence. The male defendant stated that he was not a puddler but an underhand. His wages were ss. per turn and he had not worked above three turns a week since the coal strike. Be was unable to buy the children clothing, but contended that they got sufficient food Mr. Fluct said the defendants were sober people, The magistrates decided to adjourn the case for one month to see if the defendants made any improvement in the condition of the house and children.

div.head: CoLLISIQN DTIVEN YEFIICLES,
div.p: CoLLISIQN DTIVEN YEFIICLES,
CLAIM FOR DAMAtiEg.

At the Warrington County Court, on Thursday, befow his Honour Judge Wynne Ftou:kes, John Massey, tripe dealer, Wilderspool-road, sued Edward C3nnor, cab proprietor,for G. damages by reason of his driver Thomas Perdue negligently driving a 'bus in Marshall's Cross-road, Peaslay Cross, St. Helens, on June 22nd. Mr. A. Browne represented the plaintiff, and Mr. Percy Davies defended. Mr. Browne, in opening the case, said a man named Taylor had been driving Massey's trap down the brow at Peasley Cross, and he stopped at the proper side of the road to let two boys get out. While they were getting out the 'bus belonging to Mr. Connor, which was in the charge of Perdue,eame down the brow at a fast pace and was swinging from one side of the road to the oth( r. One of the boys thereupon shouted to him "Look out, You are driving into us." Thereupon Perdue, who was drunk, turned his horse round, and the wheel of the 'bus caught the wheel of the trap, and turned the trap right round, smashing it against the lamp post. He would produce witnesses to prove that the trap was quite visi- ble, as the lamp against which the trap was standing was alight. Evidence for the complainant was given by Albert Taylor, 122, Liverpool-read, St. Helens. Reuben Taylor, 12, Leonard-street, the driver of the trap, said that when the 'but was stopped, the driver complained that there was room enough to pass, but witness replied that the 'bus had had three parts of the road. Witness afterwards measured the road and found that there was eight yards and three quarters from the off-side of the trap wheel to the opposite side of the road. By the way Perdue talked, witness considered that he was under the influence of drink. He was not capable of driving a 'bus and four horses. Thomas Pemberton, Mersey Mount, said that he had bees with the last witness in the trap to St. Helens. He corroborated the previous witnesses. Evidence was also given toy Wro.Henry Taylor.brother of the witness, Albert Taylor, William Taylor, 14, Mar- shall's Cross-road, St. Helens, Thomas Williams, 7, Peel- street, St. Helens, John Massey, son of the plaintiff, Charles Stuart, Pinners-brow, and Mr. Massey, the plaintiff,the latter of whom said that the horse had never jibbed with him. He had had it nine months. While the trap was being repaired, witness was obliged to hire a horse for his business.
The case was adjourned until the next court day.

div.head: ST. HELENS.
div.p: ST. HELENS.
A PENSIONER AND_ HIS WIFE.

At St. Helens Cni-14-71-n-d-a-y,William Travis, a pensioner, of 20, Market-st., was brought up charged with being £4 is. in arrears towards the maintenance of his wile. Travis said he had been out of work for nine weeks, but he had 21s. on him when he was arrested, and he was willing to give that to his wife. It was stated that Travis had received his pension of between £3 and £4 that morning.—Mrs. Travis was willing to take the 21s. and withdrew the warrant on those terms. THE SELLING IN STREETS BY CHILDREN. At St. Helens on Monday, Uriah Walker, a chimney sweep, of 6, Lard-st., and his wife, Annie Walker, were summoned for causing their child Angela,aged five years, to be in Greenfield-road at 8.55 on Monday night last for the purpose of selling firewood. The male def,!ndant said he was ignorant of the law, and would like to know what he was summoned for.—The Clerk (Mr. Brewis) said the charge was on the summons. No parent was allowed to send out a child under the age of eleven years on the streets for the purpose of selling at any time of the day.—Defendant said it would be a good deal better if the law was made known.—He was fined 2s. including costs, or seven days, and no fine was inflicted in the case of Mrs. Walker.

div.head: DESPERATE AFFRAY WITH ALLEGED POACHERS NEAR RUNCORN.
div.p: DESPERATE AFFRAY WITH ALLEGED POACHERS NEAR RUNCORN.
TWO CONSTABLES WOUNDED.

On Wednesday aftermoon at the. Runcorn Police Court, before Messrs. P. Speakman, C.C., and F. J. Norman, nine men named William Nixon, Thomas Jennion, Joseph Oakes, John Latham (Frodsham Bridge), Charles Percival (Bradley, near Overton), Frederick Woodcock (Ashton), John Ellis, David Aston (Overton), and Robert Garner (Main-street, Frodsham), were charged with assaulting Acting Sergeant Benfield and P.C. Juett, OR the 29th September, whilst in the execution of their duty at Norton.—Mr. Joseph Burton, solicitor, prosecuted on behalf of the police, and Mr. J. ' W. Knowles, solicitor, Widnes, defended the prisoners, all of whom pleaded not guilty to both charges. Mr. Burton, in his opening statement said that on the morning of the 29th ult., at about a quarter to four o'clock, the officers named were on duty at Norton. They were coming down Norton-road and were passing " Ptcken's wood" when they heard a noise. They stood in the road and turned their lamps in the direction of the , wood. No sooner was this done than a shower of stones assailed them from the wood. They were struck in various parts of the body with the stones, and the dog which was with Sergeant Benfield had its leg broken and skull fractured. The officers got over the fence and went into the wood. As soon as they reached the wood they were confronted by several men. Some of the men Sergeant Benfield knew by name and sight, and the whole of the nine prisoners now in court were recog- nised by the officers. More stones were thrown and the men were seen by the officers to throw them. About five of the men closed upon Benfield with sticks. He (the officer) struck at some of them and hit one. Benfield was then knocked down and kicked. He became insen- sible. Both officers had wounds upon their bodies caused by the stones and sticks. Eventually the men went away and Benfield afterwards came to his senses. He then got up and went to Frodsham Bridge where he arrested Jennion soon after six o'clock. Oakes was also arrested the same morning. The remaining seven men were apprehended at subsequent periods in the day. the officers did not interfere with the men at all before the stones were thrown. They were simply on duty and if they had not been stoned they would not have done anything. If their worships were satisfied of the guilt of the prisoners he (Mr. Burton) would ask for severe pun- ishment to be inflicted.

Acting-Sergeant Benfield supported the statement of Mr. Burton, supplementing it by giving evidence of the arrest of the prisoners. On the clothes of several was found mud and grass as though they had recently been out. The mud corresponded in colour to that fcund on the tunics of the officers, whilst several of the prisoners when called upon said that they were not at Norton be- fore the officer; told them at what place the assault was committed. In repl7 to Mr. Burton witness said that when he and his brother officer reached the wood he heard the men say, "Kill the B---3." _

Examined by Mr. Knowles: It was light at the time of hearing the noise, and he identified the prisoners without any difficulty. The reason why they turned their lamps upon the men was because they were in the wood, and for the moment their sight could not pene- trate the trees. Afterwards they saw very clearly all the men without the aid of the lamps. All the prisoners were three or four miles from their homes.

P.C. Juett gave corroborative testimony. He recog- nised all the prisoners as being in the wood on the morn- ing alluded to. Mr. Knowles submitted that their worships could not convict the prisoners on the charge read out, or to be more correct upon the informati,.n laid by Superintend- ent Atherton. He argued that the prisoners know noth- ing whatever of the assault. And even if they were proved to be the right men who were there, or some of the number, there was not a tittle of evidence before the court that they had assauite.-I the constables whilst the latter were in the execution of their duty. It had been elicited in examination that the officers were in the possession, at the time, of large dogs and sticks. Did they rrquire these? In his opinion they were not on duty at all but were acting in concert with gamekeepers to watch for any poachers who might be prowling about They were acting not as policemen, but as game assis- tants. The very action of the men in the wood went to show that they did not intend to harm the officers. They evidently used the stones to keep the dogs away. It would have been a terriblo thing if one of the dogs had bitten any of the men and the men had afterwards gone mad. The officers were exceeding their duty in inter- fering with these men whom they had evidently taken for poachers. He would call evidence which would prove beyond question that Aston was in bed at the time of the assault. In the cases of Ellison and Nixon he would call strong evidence to establish their innocence.

The witnesses called for the defence were John Aston, father of David Aston ; James Hague, hamper maker,of Overton; Frederick Aston, nephew of David Aston ; Dizibeth Hague, William Worrall, a neighbour of Ellis's, Mrs. Worrall, ‘Vm. Aston, of Overton, and Geo. Garner. John Aston and Frederick Aston said that David Aston came home on the night of the 28'h ult., went to bed, and was awakened at about six o'clock the next morning to do some shoe repairing. Both wit- nesses said that they had been asleep between twelve a-d six o'clock, but the noise in the bedroom of anyone , aetting up would have awakened them. Neither of them were aware that David was out at the time stated Iby the officers. Mrs. Hague deposed to hearing Ellis grumbling at his wife early on the morning of the 2.9:11 oh-. She afterwards went to sleep again and between five and half-past the same morning she knocked at her wall to awaken Mrs. Ellis according to her usual custom. The knock was answered. She could not say what time it would be when she heard Ellis grumbling at his wife. George Garner testified to leaving Nixon in a drunken condition at ten minutes past ten on the night of the 2811 ult. Nixon was too drunk to go poaching in wit- ness's oninion. He (Garner) knew what poaching was —(laughter)—and he had gone poaching hundreds of times but never when he was drunk, (Renewed laughter.) The magistrates afterwards retired to consider their decision, and returned at the end of about fifty minutes. The Chairman stated that the Bench had decided to con- vict in all the nine cases. Woodcock would be fined 203. and us. 81. costs for the asAault oil BAnfield Pr 21 as;cl and 203. and us. Bd. costs or 21 days for assaulting a Juqt, All the remaining prisoners would be fined 103. COstil for asigaulting each policeman, or in default of payment 21 days' hard labour. Continuing, the Chair- min said that the reason why the fine of Woodcock was heavier than the others was that on reference to the police books they found t'Aat he had been convicted ten times.

div.head: WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

A meeting of this board was held in the Board- room at the Workhouse on Wednesday morning. Mr. Wm. Houghton (occupied the chair) and there were also present—Rev. G. F. Roberts, Messrs. S. Davies, G. l'illing.W.Balharry,J. Clarke, J. Dignum, R. Heaton, J. Rill, A. Jolley, A. J. Jolley, W. Fair- dough, J. Muir, T. Smith, J. Turton, E. Aukland, G. Ratcliffe, Dr. Paterson, H. J. Longton, J. C. Sutton (clerk), S. Sutton (assistant clerk), C. H. Ward (master), H. M. Mines (superintendent of Padgate Schools.)
MB. JOLLEY OBJECTS TO CONTRACTS. -AN IMPORTANT POINT.

The House Committee recommended that the tender of Messrs. N. B. Percival and Company for groceries and provisions be accepted,alsl those of Messrs. Fletcher and Lon' for drapery, and Mrs. Chester for brushes.—Mr.A.J. JOLLEY moved an amendment that the contracts be referred back to the committee.—Mr. HILL said the matter had been before the Board before and was then referred back t 9 the committee. :He did not think it was wisa to again ;send it back to the committee. As no seconder was found for the amendment, Mr. JOLLEY said he would move another resolution that Messrs. Furness's name be substituted for Messrs. Percival in the contract for groceries, and also that of Mr. Fern for Mrs. Chester for the supple of brushes. He stated that it appeared to him that certain personal considerations were taken into acccunt in accepting contracts by the committee. He saw that there were two or three members who were quite determined to oppose any fresh tender for groceries whatever tenders were sent in. The proper way was t) ascertain whether those who tendered were bone fide tradesmen, and then accept the lowest tender,and not t," accept the highest tender from personal motives. The tender of Messrs. Furness was lower than Messrs. Percival, but the argument used was that they could not supply goods of suitable quality at the price. That was a con- sideration which should not have been allowed to have any weight at all. They had no right to assume that Messrs. Furness were g.ing to attempt to swindle and cheat the Board. With regard to the tender for brushes considerations were allowed to have weight in that case which ought not to have had any weight. The only reason for giving it to Mrs. Chester was that she was a widow. That ought to have no weight in settling a public contract. It ought to have been given to the lowest tender. He therefore moved that Mr. Fern's name be substituted.—Mr. DIGNIIM asked whether it was not usual to state on the notice that the lowest tender was not necessarily accepted.—The CLERK replied in the affirmative.—No person seconded Mr. Jolley's resolution, and it was therefore dropped. The minutes of the com- mittee were then passed.

div.head: GIFTS.
div.p: GIFTS.

The Worlihouse Master (Mr. Ward) reported that he had received a box of tobacco from Mr. H. Toft per Mr. Aukland ; a quantity of fruit and flowers from Holy Trinity Church ; and flowers from Councillor Skelton.

div.head: CASE OF SCARLET FEVER.
div.p: A CASE OF SCARLET FEVER.

_ Mr. Ward (workhouse master) further reported that there were several cases of ehieken-pox amongst the in- mates, and also one case of scarlet fever. Mr. Ward stated that he was unaHe to trace the case of scarlet fever, his opinion was that the infection had come over the wall from the Fever Hospital.

THE COMING ELECTIONS. The CLERK stated that he was in receipt of orders from the Local Government Board in connection with the election of Parish Councils and District Councils, the date of which had been fired. There were three stated

times at which the poll could be opened. One from 8 a.m. until 8 p.m., as at present in Parliamentary elec- tions, another from 12 noon until 8 p.m., and another from four o'clock until 8 p.m. He thought that having regard to the fact th tt tile election would tlke place in the dark months of the year they would be justified in taking from twelve o'clock until eight in the rural dis- tricts. In the urban districts he thought they would have a full days poll. The object of taking the election for the two councils on the same day was to save ex- pense. The day fixed was December 17:h.—Mr. Rat- cliffe wished to know who would be the returning officer in the urban districts.—Mr. sutton said if the Clerk of the Union took it up he was the returning officer for all elections in the Union.

PROPOSED JOINT SMALL-PDX HOSPITAL. The ASSISTANT CLERK (Mr. S. Surt )11) informed the members of the Rural Sanitary Auth)rity that he had received a commtmicition Irons Dr. Sergeant, Preston, county medical officer of healtli,stating that a conference was to be held at Preiton on the sth Oc*ober f4r the pur- pose of considering the subject of a joint small-pox hospital. He asked that a deputation from the Rural Sanitary Authority be present —lt was decided that the Chairman and Cl.!rk of the Authority and Air. A. Jolley form the deputation.

div.head: OUR LOCAL CLIURCHES-WARRINGTON.
div.p: OUR LOCAL CLIURCHES-WARRINGTON.

BOLD-ST. WESLEYAN CHAPEL. The third of the series of services for the people was held on Sunday afternoon, in the Bold- st. Wesleyan Chapel. The service was opened by the band rendering a minuet and trio from one of Flaydn's Symphonies. After prayer had been engaged in, the Rev. J. Kirtlan, superintendent, read a passage of scripture. The Rev. G. D. Mason pre- sided, and gave a description of the Slate Club, which, he said, was for members from 18 to 50 years of age, and the subscription was sixpence per week. The benefits to be derived from the society were these: In cases of sickness each member would receive 103. per week, with special grants in the case of the death of a member or his wife. The unique feature of the society was that, unlike other friendly societies, the accounts were audited half-yearly,and the money in hand divided amongst the members of the club. There being no work- ing expenses a,sured a higher dividend than any similar society. Mr. W. C. Nicholson gave the weekly address, taking for his subject the great force of little things. He pointed out that small things took place in their lives which they did not expect would happen. Some people arrived at a certain point in their lives, after which they could not make any headway. Some time ago, in America, they were raising a piece of statuary, when one of the links of the chain gave way, and the work of art was destroyed. So it was with them. They must I put certain links in their career together in such a manner that nothing could destroy it. He would like to impress upon them that in that service there was work for all of them. The greatest ideal they could have in life was to rescue, or help to rescue, those who had fallen. He trusted that all present would assist in the good work being done. Mr. A. Bates gave a fine rendering cf the violin solo, with accompaniments, " I know that my Redeemer liveth," from "The Messiah." The service was brought to a conclusion by the band playing Mendelssohn's "Cornelius March." The playing of the orchestra reflected credit on the conductor, Mr. Pendle- bury.

THE P.S.A. AT WYCLIFFE CHURCH. Sunday last was the half-yearly prize day in connec. tion with the Wycliffe P.S.A. Society, and over 600 members received a book prize on their entry into the church. Mr. T. &Kent, president of the P.S.A. at the Young Men's Christian Association Rooms, occupied the chair. In the course of a short address he spoke in approval of the movement which had for its ob- ject the gathering in of those who had been outside the churches. It meant that many of the old ways of looking at things were departing, and they were begin- ning to take a brighter and broader view of them. Al- though the methods differed from those in the past the ' aim was the same. The address for the afternoon was delivered by Mr. Bibby, of Liverpoel,who most impres- sively gave his hearers some realistic pictures which he had seen during his work in the slum* ! I and common: lodging-houses of Liverpool. He asserted that from a long experience he bond that the chief causes of the widespread poverty and distress were traceable to drink and gambling. In ' conclusion, he made an earnest appeal to young men to ' keep clear of these evils. Miss Roberts exceedingly well sang a solo. The Rev. J. Yonge, Messrs. G. Brown, and 1 J. Porritt, also took part in the meeting.

div.head: OPENING OF WALTON LOCK.
div.p: OPENING OF WALTON LOCK.

An event ot considerable importance took place at Walton on Monday, when the lock which will eventually be the entrance to the Warrington docks was opened. The lock will form the entrance for all vessels from the Mersey to the Ship Canal and rice versa. The Ship Cdr.al steamer" Olga" was requi- sitioned to take the members of the Rivers Com- mittee through the lock, and there were also on board representatives from the Ship Canal. The following were the members of the Rivers Com- mittee present. The Mayor (Alderman Greenall), Aldermen Francomb, Wright, Sutton, Hutchinson, and Bolton, Councillors Roberts, R. T. Fairclough, F. W. Monks, Heaton, and Bennett. The following officials were also present: Messrs. J. Lyon Whittle (Town clerk), Stanley Wilson (deputy town clerk), J. Fairhurst (borough treasurer), Dr. Gornall (medical officer of health),and T. Longdin (borough surveyor). The following gentlemen represented the Ship Canal Company : Sir Leader Williams (engineer), Mr. Bythell (chairman of the company), Councillor Southern (chairman of the executive , committee), Mr. Marshall Stevens, Alderman J. Thompson, and Walton Smith,and Councillors Ping- stone and McDougall. The party boarled tbQ "Olga "at a temporary land • log stage near Arpley railway bridge,and steamed up thak new cutting past Walton Arches to a point near to- nks'd Forge, when the vessel grounded. On the way, the dredging Opeiations could be seen' and the nit% were busily at work at various points. After getting in the deep water again, the" Olga " returned up the river and steamed up the old branch of the river to Walton Lock, where there was a large concourse of spectators, and a plentiful display of bunting. The ceremony of opening the lock consisted of holding a piece of tape across, and the Mayor should have cut it in two. Before the steamer however reached the tape, one of the men who was holding it let it fall into the water, and the ceremony was thus spoiled. A long stay was made in the lock to await the tide which raised the' Olga" to the level of the top of the lock. A large portion of the party got off here to examine the sluices and ether parts of the I work, and it will not be out of place to give:herea few ' particulars respecting the lock. The work was com- menced on November 9th,1893,and completed on August 16, 1894. The contractor was Mr. Jackson, who has been assisted by Mr. Golightly and Mr. W. Jones. The length of the lock is 229 feet and the breadth 30 feet,and it has ten feet six inches of water at low tide. The coping and hollow quoins are of Bramley Fall sandstone and the walls of Runcorn red sandstone. The gates are of. greenheart, and have been erected under the superin- tendence of Mr. Raby. The locks, were under the super- intendence of Captain Waring, who lathe superintendent of that portion of the Canal. When the tide had risen almost to its height,t he "Olga" steamed past Wilderspool Brewery, along the old portion of the river, and the party landed at a point near to the embankment which now forms the main road from Warrington to Moore. After leaving the steamer, the members of the Rivera Committee, and representatives of the Ship Canal Com- pany, proceeded to the Town Hall. where luncheon was served.

div.head: PEN KETH
div.p: PEN KETH

COTTAGE GARDENING.—A meeting of the committee of the Penketh and Sankey Window and Cottage Garden society was held in the Wesleyan Infant's School on Monday evening. The accounts for the past year were presented, and showed a balance of £2 Os. id. in the Treasurer's hands. Votes of thanks were unanimously passed to the managers of the Infants' School for the use of the room in which the show was held, and to Mr. G. H. Bolton for the plants used for decoration. A. general meeting of the members and committee will be called in February for the 'purpose of carrying on the society. HARVEST THANKSGIVING AT SANKEY—On Sunday the annual harvest thanksgiving services were held in St. Mary's Church, Great Sankey. The church as usual was splendidly adorned with fruit and flowers, which had been presented by the farmers and families about. A very pretty effect was given by large baskets of fern from Mr. Bolton's gardens, and which were suspended from the beams in the roof. Two mettoes, " Holy is the Harvest," and "Thou crowne?t the year with Thy Goodness," were placed in approprtite positions. Three services were preached during the day. The Vicar, Rev. E. S. Jackson, conducted the morning and evening services, and preached two impressive and appropriate sermons. In the afternoon a children's flower service was held and was conducted by the Rev. J. R. Jones. The offerings of flowers by the children were numerous and varied and will be given to the hospital and Infirmary. The collections amounted to £25 55., and will be devoted to church funds. The following ladies had charge of the decorations i—Misses Tinsley, Misses Jeans, Misses Pennington, Miss Bolton, Miss 'Standish, Misses Warburton, Miss Daisy Owen, Miss Smith and Miss Annie Jones. Miss Mary Standish presided at the organ. An anthem "Praise ye the Lord," was rendered at the evening service, the solo being taken by Miss Standish.

div.head: TIMELY WAttivlNG.
div.p: A TIMELY WAttivlNG.

'Never trust those who promise too much at a time. The patent medicines which pretend to cure " at once," in " asingle dose," or in " ten minutes," convince us that they are unnatural in their oper4tion, and that, therefore, either the promise made is a false one, or that the remedy is worse than the disease. It is not "at once " that a man becomes Consumptive; it is not " at a single meal" that you acquire Indigemion and Dyspepsia ; it is not in" ten minutes " that your Liver becomes sluggish and out of order. No. These com- plaints and others which might be named are gradual in thelrh,ld to release you" at once," "in ten minute " or" at a single dose." As the disease, so its cure. div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.

DEFRAUDING A RAILWAY COMPANY.—HEAVY PENALTY, A respectable noking man named Samuel Cohen, who stated that he resided in Manchester, was charged at Newton Petty Sessions on Saturday with having on the 1.9. h July travelled on the L. and N. W. Railway from St. Helens Junction to Earlestown without a ticket with intent to defraud the railway company. Mr. Fenna, solicitor, Liverpool, who prosecuted on behalf of the L. and N. W. Railway Company stated that on the 19tta July the defendant got out of a train from St. Helens Junction at Bank Quay Station, Warrington, and told the ticket collector that he had travelled from Earles- town, and paid him fivepence for the fare. The guard of the train which the defendant had travelled on made a communication to the ticket collector, whereupon he stopped Cohen and asked him whether he had not travelled from St. Helens Junction. This the defendant denied, and stated that he had been all night at Earles- town. He also made the same statement to Detective Dipple. It would be proved that the defendant got on the train at St.Belens Junction.—William Bennett,ticket collector, Warrington, gave evidence bearing out Mr. Fenna's statement. John Richardson, guard of the 9.20 p.m. train from St Helens Junction to Warrington, stated that the booking clerk at St.Helens Junction made a communication to witness, in consequence of which he watched the defendant. He saw him get in the train at St. Helens Junction, and at Warrington witness com- municated the fact to toe ticket collector.—Detective Dipple stated that he was called to the defendant at Warrington who stated that he had only travelled from Earlestown. The defendent who is a Jew, made a long but unintelligible statement to the magistrates. The Chairman (Captain NN Abington) stated that they found the defendant guilty, and fined him 403. and costs, £3 3.83. (id. altogether. ANOTHER SHOP-DOOR THEFT. At the Borough Court, on Wednesday, Isaac Smith, of Garden-row, Cockhedge-lane,was charged with stealing at 2.15 on Tuesday afternoon, from the shop-door of Messrs. Baker and Sons, Sankey-st., two pairs of chil- dren's boots, value 51. 3d. He was sent to gaol for one month's hard labour. The Chairman of the Bench (Mr. John Faitclough) expressed his dissatisfaction at the practice of hanging articles outside shop-doors. He thought it was putting temptation in the way of people.

div.head: MINOR CASES.
div.p: MINOR CASES.

WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT. YRlDAY.—Before Alderman Harrison (chairman), Coun- cillor H. Roberts, Dr. Gornall and Mr. S. Wright. CHARGE OF CRUELTY TO A HORSE.—Joseph Rigby or Dobbins, Duke-street, Ditton, was charged with cruelly Iltreating a horse by working the same in an unfit state in Sankey-street the previous night. Sergeant Cheney stated that he met the prisoner in charge of a horse the previous night, which was very lame on the off fore leg. the prisoner told him that he was taking the animal to Chester. Witness saw that it was unfit to travel and brought the man and orse to the Police Station. Insp-c- -or Luff stated that he had seen the horse. It was very lame, and totally unfit to travel. The case was remanded until Friday next. SHOUTING IN THE MARKET.—Harkes Blenkinsop, 1, York Place, St. Helens, was summoned for cryingfish in the market on the 22nd September, contrary to the bye- laws of the Borough. Mr. Place, market inspector stated that the defendant was shouting very loud in the market on Saturday night. Witness asked him to desist but he would not. A fine of 10s. including costs was imposed. A NEGLIGENT EIUSBAND. —Joseph Ma.ybnry, last from Middlesbrough, was charged with having on the 20-h ,August unlawfully neglected to keep his wife and children, causing them to be chargeable to the funds of the Warrington Union. Mr. Shearer stated that the de- fendant's wife applied for relief for herself and children GH the 20th of August. He wrote to the defendant who was working at a wire mills at Middlesbrough, and he had been continually promising to send money to his wife. All the money he bad sent was 16s. 6d. The de- fendant earned more than 30s. per week. He asked the magistrates for a commitment. On the defendant pro- mising to support his family,the magistrates decided to give him an opportunity,and adjourned the case for one month. CRUELTY TO TlORSES.—William Armstrong, carter, 1, Dakins-5 ard, was summoned for having on the 11th of September ill-treated a horse by working it in an unfit state, and Richard Miller, Bridge Foot,was charged with causing the same to be so worked. Mr. A. Browne re- presented the defendants. Seageant Cheney stated that he met the defendant Armstrong in charge of a black horse attached to a cart laden with sand. The horse was suffering pain from a wound on the near shoulder. Mr. Miller told witness that he ordered the man to take the horse out but he did not know it was suffering rotn a wound. Inspector Luff stated that he saw the horse the following day. The horse was suffering from an abcess on the near shoulder, which had broken. Blood and matter were running from it A special collar had been provided for the wound,but when the horse turned round the collar would rub against the wound. Mr. Browne, for the defence, stated that the collar was alteredlor the expresspurpose of protecting the wound, and that therefore the defendants did not intend to cause the animal any pain. The lump had not burst when the horse was taken out, or the animal would not have been allowed to work. Mr. Wilkinson, saddler, spoke as to altering the collar in order to protect a lump en the horse's shoulder. The defendants were ordered to pay the costs.—John Dutton, farm labourer was charged with working a horse in an unfit state on the 15th inst., and William Bean, Island Farm. Acton,Cheshire was charged with cawing it to be worked Inspector Luff stated that on the date lamed the defen- dant Dutton was leaving the market with a horse attached to an empty cart,when Constables Delatey and Bruen noticed that sweat was running off the horse, and that it was only able to stand on three legs. They ques- tioned Dutton who said that the horse was not in pain and that he would bring the animal again to the market on the following Wednesday. He (Inspector Luff) went to Acton and found the horse working on the following Tuesday, and when P.S. Chantler went to serve the summons he also saw the horse working. The hors was certainly lame and unfit to work. When he exa- mined it he found one leg very hot. The horse was un- able to keep it to the ground. Evidence for the prosecu- tion was also given by P.C. Delahey and Bruen, and Sergeant Chantler. Duttcn was fined 2s. 61., and Bean 10s. and costs. ASSAULTS.—Thomas Green, 229, Knutsford-road, was charged with assaulting Mary Coggan on the 21st Sept. Mr. A. Browne defended.—The complainant who resides at 239,Knut5f0rd-road, deposed that she and the de- fendant's wife were having a quarrel when the defendant interfered, knocked her down, and " puncned " hp;. In cross-examination witness admitted that she threw a bucket of water on the defendant's wife, but stated that Mrs. Green was the aggressor. Evidence in sunnort of the complainant's statement was given by Mrs. E. Holmes, Mrs. J. Smith. two neighbours.—Mr. Browne

Fults' SEALSKIN JACKETS AND FURS of every desc,iption CLEANED or RE-DYED and ALTERED. FUR SKINS dressed and made up into rugs. itc.—B COOKE, Manufacturing Furrier, 11, Upper ish-wing- ton, and 21, Renshaw-street,: Liverpool. Established 20 years.

stated that the defendant admitted pushing the com- plainant but contended that she deserved it, inasmuch as the complainant drenched the defendant's wife with a bucket of water.—James Heesom, Mersey View, Latch- ford, gave evidence for the defcnce.—The magistrates imposed a fine of ss. and costs.—Ellen Green, 28, Haydock-street, was summoned by Eliza- beth Ashton, 2, Selby-street, for assaulting her on the 25th inst. The evidence adduced by the complainant was that on the night of the date named, the defendant caliie to her in Flaydock-st. and after a few words between them, the defendant struck her on the breast with her fists. Three witnesses were called to support this statement. The defendant denied the assault, and two witnesses stated that no assault took place. The magistrates fined defendant 10s., in- eluding costs. SATURDAY.—Before Mr. J. Burgess (in the chair) and Mr.

L. Voisey. - THEFT OF A FACE-PLATE.—Thomas Pemberton, carter, Glass-house Row, Bank Quay, was charged with stealing from the head of a horse, standing outside a tavern in Factory-lane, a face-plate, value is. 6d., the property of John Barker, a carter, employed bv Messrs. Buckley and Co., contractors, Church-street. Defendant was fined ss. or in default seven days. MONDAY.—Before Mr. F. Monks (chairman), Alderman Harrison, Messrs. T. Birchall and S. tiright. THEFT FROM THE MARKET —Ann Newns, 138, Orford- lane, was charged on remand with stealing on the 22nd ult. a boy's sailor jacket, value 63., the property of James Halliwell, stall-holder in the market. Defendant pleaded guilty. The Clerk stated that the case had been remanded from the previous Saturday in order that enquiries might be made from Dr. Adams as to whether the defendant was responsible for her actions. The defendant's husband stated that she was not. Inspector Spinks saw Dr. Adams, who had been attending the defendant for some years, and he stated that the woman was perfectly sane and was not suff -ring from any form of kleptomania. Mr. Hunt then detailed the facts relat- ing to the case, in which he stated that on the 22nd Sep- tember, the defendant was seen by a boy, in the employ of Mr. Halliwell, to take a sailor jacket from the stall. The boy told Mr. Halliwell, who went to the defendant and found the jacket in her possession. Information was afterwards given to the police. D.S. Monaghan stated that he had previously cautioned the defendant. The magistrates imposed a fine of 103. including costs. DRUNK.—Mary Phcenix, 17, Lord Nelson-street, was discharged on a charge of being drunk in fluttermarket- street ; Ellen Terry, 20, Silver Square, was fined 2s. 6d. for a similar cffence in Silver Square on the 23rd ult. DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—For this offence the follow- ing were fined :—Thomas Gallop, clogger. School Brow, 5.. and costs ; Isaac Bickley, labourer, Dutton-street, 55.; Elizabeth Kearns, 18, Silver-street, 55.; Thomas Knock- ton, labourer, 27, Erwood-street, 53. and costs; Maria Nottingham, 3, Bakehouse-yard, ss. BREACH OF THE PEACE.—For committing a breach of the peace by fighting in St. James'-street, on the 24th September, Ellen Price, lodging at 3, Bakehouse-yard, was bound over to keep the peace for six months, and ordered to pay the costs, 53. A LODGING-HOUSE KEEPER FlNED.—Patrick Warlow, 10, Percivals Fold, was charged with having on the 18th September, allowed two married couples to sleep in a room without having a screen fixed, as required by the bve-laws of the borough. Inspector Powell, who proved the case, stated that en the day of his vinit he found in one bedroom two beds occupied by two married couples. There was only a screen of thin material which you could see through, instead of a wooden one as required by the byelaws. A fine of 103. including costs was imposed.

Mr. E. J. Guest.

AB9ENTER FROM TRAINING.—Martin Quinn was re- manded to Strangeways Gaol to await escort.for absent- ing himself from training in the First Liverpool Militia in May last. Sergeant Chantler who proved the case applied for, and received the usual reward. WEDNESDAY.—Before Aar. John Fairclough (in the chair) Mr. J. Geddes and Mr. J. H. Fleming.

DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—Joseph Dobson was charged with having been drunk and disorderly in Sankey-street at 2.15 on Tuesday afternoon. P.C.F. Cooper proved the case. Mr. Hunt (chief constable) said he thought there was a more serious charge against the prisoner as he was concerned in a felony. The magistrates inflicted a penalty of ss. and costs or seven days. Thomas Dono- ghue was fined for the same offence, committed in Bank. street, on Tuesday night, a like amount. P.C. Evans gave evidence in this case. Charles K. Sawer was charged with being drunk in Church-street at 9 p.m. on Tuesday Inspector Spinks in proving the case stated that defen- dant had fallen from a cab and cut his head. He was taken te the infirmary to be attended to and afterwards locked up. Prisoner is a Liverpool man and has been up at Warrington before. Fined ss. and costs or seven days. THURSDAY.—Before Major Rid gway (chairman) and Mr. J. H. Fleming. CHARGE OP STEALING A COTIISS was charged with being found in possession of a driving whip, and being unable to give a satisfactory account of the same. Detective Monaghan stated that he saw the prisoner carrying the whip produced. He questioned him as to how he became in possession of it, and the prisoner replied, "A lad stole it out of a cart and I took it from the lad, and am eting to take it to Mr. Chelmsford, a butcher." Detective Monaghan stated that they had been unable-to find an owner for the whip, and asked for a remand until Saturday.—The magistrates therefore remanded the prisoner. THEFT FROM A PIIDLIC-HOUSE.—Michael Ryder and Mary Coyne were both charged with stealing or receiv- ing from the "Old Crow "in Fennel-st. about 10.30 on Tuesday evening a two gallon jar containing finings, value 25., the property of Janes Mather. Mr.A. Browne, solicitor, prosecuted on behalf of the landlord. He stated that en the night in question Ryder was refusad drink. Eventually Mrs. Mather, the landlady, saw him run out of the house, and a two gallon jar of finings was missed from the house. The next morning the female prisoner Coyne brought the bottle back and asked them if they called that beer. Information was given to the police, and Detective Monaghan apprehended the pri- soners. On being charged with the offence, Ryder re- plied, " I took the bottle and gave it her (Covne),,but she took it back this morning." Evidence in support of Mr. Browne's statement was given by Mrs. Mather,Miss Smith, D.S. Monaghan, and P.C. Meacock.—Ryder was committed to prison for seven days hard labour, and Coyne was dismissed. ANOTHER MARKET THEFT.—Alexander Sherwood, a lad living with his parents at 52, Chorley-street, was charged with stealing from the etall of Mr. A. Peacocke in the market place the previous evening, a silk hand- kerchief value 39: From the Chief Constab:e'a state- ment it appeared that the lad was given into the cuQtadv of P.C. Chrimes by Mr. Peacocke. The han6kerchief was found in till lad's possession and Mr. Peacocke identified it as his property. On being charged with the theft the lad replied " No." He afterwards stated that a lad named Dean gave it him. Evidence was given by Mr. Peacocke and P.C. ChrimeF. The magistrates ordered the boy to receive six strokes with the birchrod, and the Chairman said they were very sorry they could not punish Dean as they believed he was quite as bad as the defendant.

WEDNESDAY. —Before Captain Withington (chairman), and Major Pickmere. DOGS AT LARGE.—Borace Ncirman, renketh, and Catherine Topping, Burtonwood, were each fined 75.6.1. for allowing their dogs to be at large unmuzzled. DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—For this off..qice John Quinn, Poulton, was fined 53. and costs ; Ralph Hart, Burtonwood, 23. Sd. and costs ; John Hull, Burtonwood, 23. 6d. and costs ; Joseph Beddard, Sankey, 25. 6d. and costs.

THEFT OF WASTE.—George Poulson was charged with stealing a quantity of waste, valued is. 10s., the pro- perty of John Jackson, from the locks at Walton.— Horace Gordon, warehouseman, gave formal evidence of the waste being stolen.—William Golightly, foreman, said that from information given by the last witness he made a search for the waste, and traced it along the rails from the warehouse to the engine upon which the defendant was working. He gave the defendant in charge of the police as a warning to others. Ho did not wish the defendant to be severely punished as he had been a good workman.—The magistrates in considera- tion of Mr. Golightly's appeal treated the defendaot under the First Offenders' Act, and bound him over to appear when caned upon. He was also ordered to pay the costs.

ALLEGED THEFT OF FOWL .—Joseph Robinson was charged with stealing three live fowls valued 7s. 6.3., the property of ‘Villiam Dunbobbin, on the previous day.—Wm. Dunbobbin identified the fowls, but Robin- son strenuously denied the theft.—Superintendent Hig- ginbotham said that there had not. beers sufficient time to go into the matter and he applied for a remand. The remand was granted, the defendant being allowed bail.
RUNCORN PETIY SESSIONS. MONDAY.—Before Messrs. Philip Speakman, C.C., and F.
J. Norman.

LICENSING.—James Ravenscroft was granted the tem- porary transfer of the license of the '' Lord Rodney," Church-street, recently possessed by John Walker ; and George Stevens, the license of a beer-house in Stan- ley-street, lately held by John Lyon. DRITNHENNESS.—JOhII Kilgrass was fined ss. for being drunk and disorderly in Heath-road, Weston, on the 22nd September. AFRAID OF lIIS LlFD.—Peter O`Niel, of Water-street, was charged with committing an assault upon Joseph Morris, of the same locality, on the 28th of September,

NEGLECT OF EnucATioN.—The following persons were fined 53. PROFANE LANGUAGE.—Thomas Woods, Cooper-street, was fined ss. and costs or seven days' imprisonment tor making use of obscene and profane language on the J.& h ult.

AN UNSIISTAINED CHARGE OF C RIIELTY. —Thomas Woolgar, of Wivern-place, was summoned for cruelly ill-treatin,, a h9rt4e by beating the &Arne on the 21st ult. in Waterloo-road.—Mr. Burton, solicitor, defended, and contended that there was no evidence of cruelty against his client inasmuch as he was doing his best to get his horse and cart out of a rut and was forced to use his whip.—Evidence was called and eventually the case was dismissed.
A JUVENILE OFFENDER.—Thomas Elsby, 63 Percival- lane, fifteen years ot age, was summoned for setting off fireworks in Gilbert-street, on the 24th September and was dismissed with a caution.

A YOUNG THlEF.—Thomas Gresty (12) residing at Wickstone Hills, was charged with stealing four lead pencils valued id. from the stall of Mr. Charles Bird, of Warrington, on Saturday.—The offence having been proved, Superindendent Atherton said the boy was a very bad one. Only on the 19th September he, and ancther lad were charged with stealing clothing and were convicted. Gresty was then ordered to have six strokes with the birch rd but that punishment had not apparently had any good effect upon him.—The Bench ordered that the prisoner should have another six strokes with the rod and cautioned him that if he again was seen in that box on a similar charge, he would be more severely dealt with. HE WAS DISAGREEABLY ASSISTED.—WiIIiam Callan was fined ss. or seven days in gal for begging alms on the previous Sunday night in High-street.—Superintend- ent Atherton said that the prisoner met him and asked if he could assist him. He (the superintendent) said " yes," and took him to the lock-up. The prisoner had just emerged from a puhlic-hcuse and was far advanced in drink. He would have allowed the man to go on Monday morning if h. hal behaved himself in a proper manner but owing to his impudence he had now brought him for the bench to deal with as they pleased. THEFT or 'rum—Enoch Walker,ll years of age, was charged with stealing two pieces of iron value 10s. be- longinc, to John Hughes.—The evidence showed that the defendant had entered the yard adjoining 24 Suffolk-it. and had taken away the two iron sides of a wringing and mangling machine thus rendering it unfit for further use. The machine sides were then sold by the defend- ant for 104 d. to a marine store dealer.—Defendant was sentenced to fourteen days' hard labour. NON-PAYMENT OF GAS RATE.—Several persons were summon:A for neglecting to pay their gas rate, and in those cases where settlements had not been arrived at, orders were made for the speedy payment of the amounts.

Bridge-street, Go'borne. Thompson was fined is., and Bate and Wright who had been previously cautioned were fined is. and costs. P.C.'s Simpson and McKay proved the cases. AssAuvr.---John Dunn, was charged with heating and assaulting Ann Collins at Golborne on the 23rd Septem- ber. The complainant steed that thr defendant wanted to fight her son on the previous Sunday night. She went out to them and the defendant struck her in the face. Christopher and Mary Collins each corroborated this statement. The defendant was ordered to pay the costs.
ST. JOHN'S PRESBYTERIAN CHURCH BAZAAR, RUNCORN.
SPEECH BY MR. BR,UNNER, M.P.

This long-looked-for event has now happened. The bazaar has been opened and by this time is hasten- ing to its close; and there is every reason to believe that the results of the undertaking will prove immensely satisfactory. The under-inc-ntioned gentlemen have been responsible for the various arrangements z iar Committee : Rev. J. Pulford Williams (Pastor), chairman ; Messrs. John Pritchard, treasurer ; William Carroll and Frank Littler, secretaries. Building Committee : Messrs. James Pritchard, chairman ; James Steele, treasurer; James Richardson and W. G. Jackson, secretaries. The direct obj.cts of the bazaar were : Ist.—The liquidating of the balave of debt reinaining on the land, schoolrooms and classrooms ; 20d.—The raising of sufficient funds to justify the building committee in proceeding with the erection of the church. The promoters appealed for at least £6OO, and therefore hoped that generous and hearty responses would be made. The hazaar took a " national " form and was opened for three days, commencing on Wednesday, in the newly erected schoolroom. In the neighbourhood of the build- ing a profuse supply of bunting and flags was flying ; whilst over the main gateway in Victoria-road, leading to the schoolroom, an arch composed of foliage plants had been constructed. Upon entering the room a scene both delightful and artistic was presented. Tnere were ten stalls, four of which represented the nations of the United Kingdom. These had been fitted up and adorned with art muslins of various pretty and pleasing tints by Mr. James Steele,and many of the young men connected with the chapel. Considerable attention had also been paid to the platform, at the front of which was placed a large number of fine plants. The roof of the chapel was also adorned flags and bunting hanging from every : corner. Ths following is a list of stalls and stallholders : —English Stall :—Miss Pritchard,Mrs. Philip Booth,Mrs. Richardson, Mrs. Wynne Humphreys, Mrs. Lister, Miss Rovalantls,Mrs. W. G. Jackson. Irish Stall :—Mrs. War- burton, Mrs. Robinson, Miss Stringer, Miss E. Cameron, Miss Warburton, Miss M. Booth,Miss Robinson. Scotch stall it. McLeod, Miss E. Hewitt, Miss C. Kirk- ham, Mrs. Branch, Mrs. Carroll, Miss Jessie Dutton. Welsh Stall :—Miss Williams, Mrs. Fred Jones, Miss E. Dobson' Miss Maggie Jones, Miss Unsworth, Miss Lillie Streets,Nliss M. Davies. Refreshment Stall :—Mesdames Harrop, C. Kirkham, D. Jones, M. Thomas, R. Bax- ter, J Leach, J. Timperley. China Stall :—Mrs. Tickle, Mrs. J. Hewitt, Mrs. Burn, Miss Parr, Miss G itley. Young Men's stall :—Messrs. Rudd, Platt, James Jones, G. Parr, A. Booth, G. Gatley, and others. Flower and Fruit stall :—Misses A. Dobsan F. Dutton, B. Harrop, Pope, Marion Jones. Sweet stall :—Mrs. J. Booth, and Misses A. Booth, Dutton, Hough,ltnd Forrester. There was also a salt stall erected and given by the Salt Union Company. It was constructed in the form of an arch by large hlocks of salt. Inside the arch were various kinds of salt. there was also a model of the Eiffel Tower made of salt, and it was a very delicate piece of work. Among the other attractions were a museum of fine art, and a museum of curiosities. In the last named place were several articles of great antiquity and value, all of which were sent by local ladies and gentlemen for exhibition. Messrs. Harrop, Richardson, and Thomas superintended this room, whilst Mrs. Timp,nley, Miss E iwards, and Mr. Charlestown were in charge of the museum of fine art. The Bazaar Committee were in- debted to Mrs. Charles Hazlehurst for plants ; to Mr. Wiswall for so excellently lighting up the exterior of the building; to Mr. P. Speakman for boles; Mr. William Shaw, missionary, and Mr. Cooper, Widnes, for hunting. Other ladies and gentleman also generously assisted the Committee in acquiring necessary fixtures, &c.

_ SATURDAY.—Before Mr. T. J. Gillespie (chairman), Captains Withington and Wood, Messrs. T. H. Pear- son, N. McCorquodale and R. Stone. APPLICATIONS FOR ALTERATIONS TO LICENSED PREMISES. —Mr. Caunce, solicitor, made an application on behalf of the proprietors of the Prince of Wales Inn, Gol borne, for alterAtion of premises. He submitted plans showing the proposed alterations, and stated that they proposed to build up the present corner entrance at the back of the premises and erect a new one. They were giving two feet of laud to enlarge the footpath—Mr. Sandon, architect, explained to the magistrates the alterations that were proposed to be made —Superintendent Bras- sington stated that he had an objection to the plans in their present state. The magistrates would notice that the back door of the premises would open out, without any tack yard, close to some cottage Property. The police would not have the same control as at present unless a yard was provided. The magistrates granted the application, subject to a back yard being provided as suggested by Superintendent Brassington.—Mr. Stuart, solici:upr, said he had an application to make on behalf of the proprietors of the Sir Charles Napier Inn, High-st., Golborne, which was right opposite the Prince of Wales Inn: They proposed to enlarge the club room and also to provide additional room. downstairs.— Superintendent Brassington raised no objection and the application was granted. The magistrates then disposed of the cases in two courts, one being held in an ante-room.
FIRST COURT. Before Captain Withington (chairman), 'Messrs. N. McCorcploda'e and.T. H. Pearson. . _ _
LICENSE TRANSFERS.—Thp license of the Black Swan Inn, Collins Green, was transferred from Peter Antwiss to T. P. Rhodes, and that of the Millstone Inn,Golnorne, to William Gordon.

MINES EXPLOSIVES.—Messre. R. Evans and Co., Limited, were granted permission to store mines explo- sives at the Wood" and " Princes.," pits. DRUNK.—Michael Smith, for being drunk on the high- way at Newtin was fined ss. and costs; Thomas Mason was mulcted in a fine of 2s. 6d. and costs for a similar offence on the 13th ult. DRUNK AND DFORDERLY.—For being drunk and dis- orderly the following were dealt with : Michael flig,,ins at Newton on the 10th August, ss. and costs ; John Ball at Newton on September 8,2 s. 61. .and costs; James Bennett on the same date and place, 2s. 6d. and costs. Dous AT LARGE, —George Griffiths and Charles Collier were each fined 7s. 61. including costs for allowing their dogs to be at large unmuzzlert. " HP: DIDN'T WANT TO BREAK THEM."—John Le, Warrington, was charged with riding a bicycle on the footpath at Winwick on September 20. Defendant pleaded guilts', but added that he was carrying a box of cakes at the time and did not want to break them. He was 'fin, d is. and costs.

„ A SHOPICEF:PER FlNED.—Christina Haigh, grocer, gur- tonwood, was c!iarged with having in her posAession pair of scales. which were umtamped.—lnspector Spencer who proved the case stated that the scales were correct but had not been .stamped. Defendant who had been previously convicted was fined 10s. and costs.
SFC,-,ND COURT.
Before Mr. T. J. Gillespie (chairman) and Captain Wood.

DRUNKENNESS .—Joseph Otymshaw,drunk at Golborne, 2. 6d. and costs ; Henry Ince drunk at Haydock, ss. and costs; Joseph Harrison drunk and disorderly at Harclock.2s. 6 I. and costs; Thomas Bond similar offence at Havdoek, 2s. 6.1. and ,-!,;ists ; Robert Bolan drunk and disorderly at Golborne, 2s. 6-1. and costs ; John Thomp- son drunk at Golborne, 2s. 61. and costs. DRUNK ON LICENSED PREMISES.—James Hayes, Hay- dock, was charged with being drunk on the licensed pre- mises ot Wiliam Tunstall, HAydock on the 23rd ult. P. C. Gresty stated that at a quarter to four the previous Sunday he was called to the premises of Mr. Tunstall respecting the defendant's con- duct. He proceeded there and found the defendant drunk. The man was ordered out in witness's presence, by the landlord. Mr. Tunstall, landlord, stated that he had given orders for the defendant not to be served at all. When he entered the house the previous Sunday he was drunk, and when they refused to serve him he com- menced to create a disturbance. The magistrates fined him ss. and costs.

BREACFI OF THE PEACE.—John Bartley, David Boniton, and Alfred Horrobin of Newton, were charged wirh committing a breach of the peace at Golhrarne. P.C. Simpson stated that at about twelve o'clock on Satur- day night, the Bth inst. the thre defeniants were shouting, brawling, and using bad language in Park- mad, Golborne. They also gave wrong names. Mr. Stuart, solicitor, who defended, stated that the three defendants were returning from Golborne, when to keep their spirits up along the lonely road, they commenced singing, and perhaps they shouted. But it was no offence to sing or shout on the highway at night. The three defendants each stated that they were singing S tivation Army songs. Gorrobin on being cross-ex- mainerl as to the songs they were singing said one was "At the end of our journey we shall wear a crown." Mr. Stuart : " Not a fine of 59. I hope" (laughter.) The magistrates dismissed the case on payment of costa. CHARGE OF BREAKING A WINDOW.—TWO girls named Kate Orrighan, and Kate Waugh were charged with do- ing damage to the window of Sarah Hart, Goiborne, on the 10th ult, to the extent of one shilling. Mr. Stuart, solicitor, prosecuted. No evidence was given showing that the defendants did break the window, but they were seen running away after the occurrence. Three witnesses were called for the defence, one named Tforro- bin stating that she saw a little lad break it. The magis- trates thought there was a doubt in the case and dis- missed it. OBSTRUCTING THE FOOTPATTI.—JosPph Hatch, Peter Churton' Arthur Russell, and Michael O'Donnell were each fined a shilling including costs for obstructing the free passage of the footpath in Legh-street, Golborne on the 23rd September.—John W. Bate, IV. Wright, and Isaac Thompson were charged with a similar offence in

div.head: FI RST DAY.
div.p: FI RST DAY.

Towards eleven o'clock on Wednesday the attendance began to increase rapidly and in the space of almost half-an-hour after Mr. Brunner's arrival the interior of the large room was filled with persons, amongst whom were the following :—Mr. and Mrs. Brenner. the Rev. Dr. and Mrs. Preston, the ReY.John Stafford, Ellesmere- street ; the Rev. J. P. Williams (pastor), the Rev. Jno. Williams (Chester), and the Rev. Thomas Bramhall (Greenway-road), Messrs, P Speakman, J.P.C.C., Jas. Pritchard, John Pritchard, J. Steele, John Simpson; J. R. Frith, J. Harrison (Liverpool), W. Carroll, J. Kirk- ham, senior, J. D. Jones, J. Temperley, J. Robinson, G. Hayes, Wesley Cooke, J. Walton, C. Kirkham, &c., &c. 'rue proceedings opened by the singing of a hymn after which the Rev. John Williams offered prayer. Mr. Carroll made a brief statement showing that the scheme into which the congregation had entered was estimated to cost £4,500. Of this about £2,000 had Wen expended upon the site and schools, and they hoped to realize by that undertaking £6OO which would clear off the debt already ineurred and encourage the congrega- tion to proceed with the provision of the church they so much required. Mr. Pritchard in introducing Mr. Brunner s aid that that gentleman held a very high position and was very popular its that part; of Cheshire. They were all glad to see that Mr. Ilrunner had not, like some members of Parliament, resolved not to open bazaars, or they would not have had the pleasure of his presence that. day. Their pleasure was enhanced by the presence of Mrs. Brunner amongst them. Ho was sure they all appreciated the kindness of Mr. and Mrs. Brunner in thus assisting them in the undertaking. Mr.Brunner,M.P.,who was warmly applauded on rising said he was glad to be with them that day, and to give them encouragement as far as he could, and to bid them God speed. (Applause.) He had had a rather more intimate connection with the movement than was usual for a man occupying the position he did for the reason that it was somewhat in consequence of the action taken by him that a move had been taken at so early a date. He was cordially thankful to those who were responsible as trustEes for the care of the property they had given him an opportunity to acquire. They had left their building with a feeline of thankfulness and reverence for the good work that had been done in it,and at the same time holding a high hope for the work they were going to do in the futuie. The building had come into his possession but he trusted they would not look upon him as an evicting landlord. (Laughter.) He saw in the programme an admonition to him which had been put in by a man of business, and he was rather inclined to suspect Mr. Carroll. On the page headed the " Opening ceremony " appeared the quotation " Deeds not words." That was a reproof to him for the long speech he was inflicting upon them. (Laughter.) He had been led to think that morning by the history of the chapel that many another place of worship in this country had a cor- responding history. They had moved the scene of their labours from a neighbourhood which was found no longer suitahle for the work they had to do, as it had been in generations gone by. He thought they were entitled to say, as many another congregation had said, that the pastors had educated them to a pitch somewhat above the neighbourhood in which the chapel was situated. He thought all present were well-wishers of the Church of England, and if the Established Church was only able to pssese the same facility the scandal of so many empty churches richly endowed, in the centre of London and other large towns, would very quickly vanish and the churches would be removed to places where they were wanted. To put it in a few words, if the Church ot Englaml possessed the facility their denomina- tion did it would add greatly to the benefit of the church He saw another quotation on the programme" I have a bag of money that troubles me." He gave the ladies fair notice that he had handed that hag to his wile—(latieh- ter)—.A rid therefore it. did not trouble him. He did not think that the possession of a bag of money ever troubled him except in those cases where so many folks liked him because they wanted to dip their hands into it. (Re- newed lauehter.) Mr. Speakman proposed a vote of thanks to Mr. and Mrs. Bruner for their presence at the bazaar. He con- sidered it was very fortunate when an organization like theirs showed that individually they were ready to per- form good work. He remarked that although Mr. Brunner had handed his bag of money be his wife he had a cheque book and was well able to write, and they weuld be pleased to receive assistance in that way. (Laughter.) Dr. Preston, in a speech abounsling with humour, seconded the vote of thanks. He had been termed a bigot, tut he did not think that he was so bigoted as he was given credit for. He trusted the undertaking would ho attended with success. The motion was carried unanimously. • Mr. Brunner, in responding, thanked Mr. Speakman and Dr. Preston for their kind sentiments. He remarked that the latter gentleman was at times a thoroughly frank enemy of his, but he was glad that on the present occasion he was one of his supporters. He hoped the time would come when they would agree in their opin- ions. He then declared the bazaar open,and that every- one with money was at liberty to spend it. Each one could go to work in his or her sphere with the satisfac- tion of their approval. Mise Clara Teylor, R.A.M. sang the solo " The Flight of ages "in a manner greatly appreciated by the audi- ence. The business of the sale was then proceeded with.

ORNAMENTATION OF ST. rtiARY'S (R.C.). BUTTERMARKET-ST. Another small group of .figures carved in Caen stone has been placed in one of the recesses in the interior of St. Mary's, representing Jesus falling the first time under the weight of the cross. Th e carving is in keeping with the other fine work of the church. Messrs.Boulton and Sous,art sculptors, ein-Atenham,have executed the work. Ten recesses are now filled, leaving four still to be completed.
