RUGBY. WARRINGTON v. OLDHAM.

The first meeting of the above teams took place at the Watersheddiugs enclosure, Oldham, on Saturday after- noon. It is a singular fact that at every previous meeting of Warrington and Oldham,at Oldhatn,the game has either been played under the most wretched con- ditions, either in a snowstorm or something almost as bad,or else the mach has had to be cancelled altogether. However, on Saturday, the weather was at its best, and as a result, upwards of 10,000 spectators were present on the caplcious ground, to watch the game. Almost a thousand of these came from Warrington. The game was commenced with commendable punctuality, Mr. Slevin acting as referee. The following were the teams :

Warrington : Full back, Heesom ; three-quarter backs, Carey, Lawless, Potts, and Cunningtam ; half backs, James T. Bate and Clark ; forwards, Turner, Jolley, Nevins, Dakin, Taylor, Berry, Buckley and Thorniley. Oldham Full back, Eagland ; three-quarter backs, Burst, Taylor, S. Lees, and McCutcheon ; half backs, Varley and A. Lees ; forwards, Barnes,Furness. Newby, D,iwson, Bonsor, Moore, Hughes, and Corscadden. Warrington lost the toss,and during the first half they had to face a stiffish breeze. Turner's kick off was re- turned well to near half way by A.Lees. The well known backs of Oldham early showed that they were in fine form for S. Lees securing, he raced down the field but when a score seemed inevitable, he spoiled it by a bad pass to Hurst. From this fright the Warringtonians plucked up their courage, and by dribbles among the forwards, play was taken to half way. Lawless here made a punt which went too far,and Hurst securing ran to the quarter flag and passed to Taylor, who, however, was promptly floored. Corscadden then had a dribble on his own account but he also came to grief. The War- rington forwards again changed the scene of operations to half way,and a strong punt by Bate took play to the Oldham quarter flag, and the same player afterwards by a too strong punt sent up the first minor. From the drop out Clark returned well and Bate by a feint at pas- sing fairly baffled Varley and he was not stopped until he was near the posts. From the ensuing scrimmage, McCutcheon secured, and kicking when in diaiculties followed his kick so 'well that Heesom had only just time to make his mark before McCutcheon was upon him. From the ensuing kick the ball was quickly taken by the Oldham backs, and passing between Hurst, S. Lees, and Taylor ended in the latter's pass being well taken by Potts who was tackled after a good run,by Varley. The latter then took the ball smartly from the scrimmage, and quickly passing to Hurst, that player passed all opposition until he reached Heesom, who floored him on the line. This let off did not last long, for McCutcheon eluding his opponents got over, but S. Lees was unsuc- cessful with the place kick. Dawson was almost over by a dribble after the kick out, and McCutcheon a minute afterwards was floored on the line by Heesom, who had all his work cut out for him at this stage. At length the danger was cleared by a combined rush of the forwards, conspicuous among whom were Turner, Taylor, and Dakin. Lees, however, got away, only to find Cunningham too good for him. A passing movement between Varley, S. Lees, and Hurst immediately after- wards ended in the latter getting overtire line by eluding Carey and Heesom. His kick at goal was a failure. After the restart Varley was hurt, and play was stopped for n few minutes, and after his injuries being attended to, a scrimmage took place, which Warrington ecrewed finely and took play to the half way line. Cunningham then secured the ball, but unfortunately let it drop, and Varley like a hawk was upon it in a moment,and Heesom just collarel him in time, when the game was again stopped owing to the latter being hurt. His injury was not, however, serious, and the game was again started, when McCutcheon taking a pass from Varley got over the line again, carrying Heesom over with him. Hurst's kick at goal was a failure. Oldham pressed from now to half time, and Hurst got over again amid thundering applause from the Oldham spectators. The score at half time was—Oldham four tries, Warrington nil.

The play after the interval was of a more promising character to the Warrington supporters for a short time. The Warrington forwards appeared to have profited con- siderably from the slight rest they had, and the dribbling was fine indeed. Shortly after the start, the ball was dribbled more than half the length of the field, and Cunningham also made a grand run to the line. A series of exciting scrimmages took place on the line, and Bate was held whilst grounding. The visitors were at length rewarded by Clark securing a pass from Bate and grounding over the line. Turner failed to augment, his kick falling short. Warrington again pressed and Law- less spoiled a good run by a long pass. The hopes of the Warringtonians were speedily dashed to the ground, for Oldham commenced playing in the old sweet way and Taylor, of Oldham, roused great enthusiasm by a run through the thick of his opponents and successfully grounding. Hurst was still nsuccessful with the place. Turner's kick out was called back, and from the next kick, Hurst raced away and was tackled just on the line. A combined rush cf the Oldham forwards was stopped by Bate but this was of short duration and another scrimmage took place under the Warrington posts. A series of passing between Hurst, S. Lees, Taylor, and McCutcheon,ended in the latter being pushed into touch by Cunningham. Warrington recovered a little after this, but Hurst had a try at association football, and by this means dodged the Warrington backs, and although Potts for a short time averted the danger, S. Lees made a dart and got in between the posts, and this time the place kick was successful. Warrington pressed after the kick out, but the last spark of hope for Warrington died out when Potts, in trying to stop a rush by Hurst was PO seriously hurt that he was obliged to leave the field. His place was taken by Nevins who played very well in that position. With a man taken out of the forwards, the Oldham men were able to overcome them, and a bout of passing between Varley, S. Lees, Taylor and Hurst enabled the latter to get in without any opposition and ground under the posts. S. Lees increased the try to a goal. This was followed immediately afterwards by another try by Furness, this being the first not scored by the three-quarter backs. Moore failed to convert. War- rington had another spurt afterwards, but Oldham returned to the attack and Bonsor ag,ain got over, but ho was called back to half way owing to him going into touch. From the line out, Hurst got the ball, and made cue of his usual runs, but this time he was unsuccessful. A grand dribble now ensued and the Warrington for- wards transferred play to the opposite and and a scrim- mage took place on the Oldham line without any tangible result. The whistle soon afterwards blew for full time with the teams in mid-field, when the score ran, Oldham, two goats, six tries, to Warrington one try. WABRINdTON IA " v. OLDHAM "A ".

There was a large:attendance on the Wilderspool en- closure on Saturday afternoon to witness this match, it being the first engagement in the Lancashire club cham- pionship for "A" teams. The Warrington team had undergone several changes, Mannion taking the place of Boscow at full back, and the three-quarter and half- backs were also different from the advertised team with the exception of Moores. Oldham placed a strong fifteen in the field, several of the players having played in first team matches for Oidham. When the teams lined up for, the kick-off they were composed as follows : Warrington, full-back, Mannion ; three-quarter backs, Cresswell, Jackson. Gibson, and MoGres ; half-backs, Foster and Foden ; forwards, Bailey, Savage, Handles, Andrews, Houghton, Burrows, Donoghue, and Fairhurst; Oldham full back, Lamondv ; three quarter backs. Fillingliam, Wright, Mills and -Dunkerley ; half-backs, Lawton and Rhodes ; forwards, Philips, Whittle, Ballard, Sellars, Wilde, Speak, Murrel, and Lees. Handles, captain of the Warrington team, set the ball in motion; and play for some time continued in Oldham territory. Warring- ton here gained a free kick in an alvantageous position for notching a goal but the kick was a failure. Some interesting play followed in which the Oldham men forced their way into the home quarters hut without result. Wartisr.,ton again attacked and carried the ball near to the Oldham line. Success soon afterwards at- tended their efforts for Foster accepted a pass is: the nick of time and scored the first try of the match. The kick at goal failed. Spurred on by this reverse the Old- ham men played up with determination, and play was of an exciting nature. At length Fillingham by one of the best runs which has been seen on the ground for some time, crossed the Warrington line, scoring a try. The visitors were further successful at the goal kick, which gave them a lead of two points. Half-time shortly afterwards arrived with the score standing: Warrington, one try ; Oldham, one goal. After the restart strong efforts were made by both teams to augment the score. Each goal was visited again and again but no scoring resulted and an evenly contested game was witnessed. The visitors secured a free kick opposite the Warrington goal almost at the call of time but were unsuccessful, and the whistle sounded with the score standing as at half-time,Oldham thus winning by two peints. Mannion for Warrington played a good game at full back, but Moor-s was greatly impeded by having his foot hurt early in the second half of the game.
WARRINGTON T. MARY'S 2ND V. BEDFORD ST. JosErn's 2ND.—Played on the ground of the former, and resulted in a win for the home team by two tries to nil.

RUNCORN v. BRADFORD.—A match was played on Sat- urday sfternoon between these teams on the Irwell-lane enclosure before a good attendance of spectators. The toatns were : Runcorn: Houghton, back ; Richardson, Warder, W. Gayter, and Butterworth, three-quarters ; Robinson and J. Faulkner, half backs ; W. Faulkner, J. Langley, A. Taylor, H. Farmer, J. Davies, R. Li2latfoot, J. Pendlebury, and F. Gayter, forwards. Bradford : Ward, back ; Cooper, Crompton, Dobson, and Murga- troyd, three-quarters; Duckett and Blacow, half hacks ; Dewhurst, Suglen, Marshall, Jenkinson, Bates, Wilson, Hutton, and Robertson, forwards. Both, as will be seen, were fairly well representative,among the Bradford men being Crompton, who will at once be recognized as a Runcornian, and whose fame, in the football would, is still a subject of interest to Runcorn lovers of the sport. The visitors, who won the toss, elected to play with the sun at their rear, and Faulkner kicked off. After a little bye play Runcorn besieged their opponents quarters and made much work for the backs. Buttarworth secured a penalty kick, but it fell short and a similar kick by Bradford was answered by Houghton finding tuach beautifully. Play remained for some time in Bradford territory until Dobson, Cooper, and Crompton relieved. By an expert bit of passing Murgatroyd bore down upon the home goal but was stopped jtv,lt in time by El nigh- ton, Runcorn retaliated and the outcome of some capital passing was a good try, scored by Warder. The goal kick was unsuccessful. The homeAters still maintained the pressure and shortly afterwards Gayter scored a secomd try, half-time arriving with Runcorn leading by two tries to Bradford nil. On the resumption of play Bradford began to press but were well withstood by the Cheshire men who gradually secured the mastery. The visiting forwards made some grand efforts to retrieve their fortunes, and after Crompton had all but scored, Dobson secured possession of the leather, and making a splendid run down field obtained a try which Cooper converted into a goal. Both sides now did their best to improve their positions, but although for the most of the time Runcorn were the aggressors, they could not score, so superb was the visiting defence. The game, therefore, end-11 in a well-earned win for Runcorn, by two tries (six points), to Bradford one goal (five points).

div.head: LIVERPOOL 'RUGBY JUNIOR -LEAGUE
div.p: LIVERPOOL 'RUGBY JUNIOR -LEAGUE

RUNCORN "A " T. ST. JAMES'S WEST DER-BY.—The home juniors journeyed. on Saturcla.y to West Derby to engage St. James's in the first fixture of the League. The teams were as follows :—Runcorn : J. Jolley, full back; B. West, H. Myers, J. Lightfoot, and Dunbavand, three-quarter backs ; W. Penilebury and E. Woodward, half backs ; J. Stubbs, S. Johnson, A. Clarke, T. Antro- bus, J. Moores, G. Shaw, W. Tatlock, and G. Derby- shire, forwards. St. James's : Bailey, full back ; Herrin, Meek, Roberts and Hengler, three-quarter backs; Turner and Pendleton, half backs ; Bennett. Yardley, Wool!, McGeorge, McKnight, Goss; Mollineaux, and Barlow, forwards. There was a numerous attendance of specta- t2rs, and the greatest interest was manifested in the movements of the respective teams. Runcorn had the best of matters right through the game, and did not allow their opponents to gain a single advantage. The game ended in a win for the visitors, the score being Runcorn, two goals, two tries, ten minors ;St. James's, nil.

WARRINGTON ST. MART'S V. LOSTOCIL—On Saturday the Saints journeyed to Lostock, minus the services of Burton, who was away owing to an injury to his foot. Lostock won the toss,and elected to play with the wind. G. Hampson started the ball for the Saints, Reece mak- ing a good return. The Saints were the first to show up, and a smart passing movement by F. Hampson and O'Brien resulted in the latter scoring, F. Hammon doing the needful. Their forwards played a good game, and a rush headed by S,,nders, G. Hampson and Swift gave Neckar trouble, a minor accruing. Good passing by the visiting backs :-a,w Bennett walking in under the posts, there being no attempt made to stop him, F. Hampson landing a goal. Lostock, however, tried ha rd but to no avail, when Sanders only a few minutes later scored, F. Hampson failing. Nothing daunted, St. Mary's returned to the attack, and by a dodgy run G. Hampson got over and Roughley converted. At half- time St. Mary's led by three gals, one try, to nil. On changing ends Lostock tried hard,their forwards playing a smart game, and the visitors' defence was menaced for a few minutes. The Saints now had another innings, when Higginbottom accepted a pass from Warburton. who ran fn a splendid try, the effort being cheered, Rou,ghley took the place kick, and succeeded in register- ing another goat. St. Mary's held the upper hand to the finish, and when time was called they were returned victors of a rather one-sided game by four goals two tries (26 points) to nil.

LATCHFORD RANGERS V. WARRINGTON RANGERS 2ND.— This match was played on the Latchford ground on Saturday. The visitors started the oval, White charg- ing the kick-off down. Play waged in the visitors' quarters. Massey and Newton got through a lot of work, but it was left to Buckley to clear, which he did with a good kick. Gradually the ball was taken into the visitors' quarters, and from a scrimmage Warburton got over, but the point was disallowed. No relief was offorded the visitors, and Warburton got over, the try being again disallowed. Half-time was then called, with the snore sheet blank. On the restart Fox and S. Spencer dribbled well to the line, and Warburton scored an unimproved try. From the drop-out Warburton again got hold and drApped a splendid goal. Some good work by Newton, Rigby, Read, and White reached the visitors' lines, a try resulting, which was, however, dis- allowed. Time was then called, leaving Latchford the winners of a hard-fought game by one goal (dropped) and one try to nil.

RUNCORN RECREATION V. WARRINGTON ST. PETER'S.— These clubs m.-t at Runcorn, on Saturday, in a St. Helens and district league match. On account of the players arranging to see the Runcorn v. Bradford match it was after five o'clock when the home side kicked off. The Recreation were short of four of their usual team,but were much too strong for the St. Peter's, and playing UD hill had the best of mitters, Hearne and Dixon scoring tries, one of which was converted into a goal. In the second half the game was not interesting, as the visitors played in a very loose fashion, and the home side added a couple more tries and won a one-sided game. The final score was Runcorn Recreation two goals, two tries, and four minors, Warrington St. Peter's nil.

WIDNES ST. MARY'S V. STOCKTON HEATH.—St, Mary's journeyed to Warrington on Saturday to meet Stockton Heath. This team at present is stronger than ever it has been before, including such men as Boscow (formerly of Lancashire County), Barber, Cross, Webster, Broady, Lally, and Higham, all of whom have formerly played for Warrington. Sr. Mar' s pl yed against the wind in the first half, and after about 15 minutes' play Webster got away with the ball at his toes, and by his superior speed succeeded in getting over the line. At half time nothing further had been scored. After the interval Cross scored another point, but the 'goal-kick failed. Murphy now injured his ankle, and had to retire. St. Mary's were now more pressed, and owing t] a miskick by McElroy, who had talc-,n Murphy's place at three- quarter, Glover scored under the posts, Barber adding the major point. Nothing further was added, and the final score was—Stcckton Heath, one goal, two tries; St. Mary's, nil.

div.head: ASSOCIATION.
div.p: ASSOCIATION.

PENHETH V. WARRINGTON.—This match VAS played at Penketh on Saturday,in typical football weather. There was a good number of spectators on the ground, many e.ominir from Warrington. Williamson kicked off for Warrington, and was very soon afterwards compelled to save on behalf of his team. Boswell and Bowyer then made the play for Penketh, and Williamson saved twice in a splendid manner. Linaker also was pressed hard,but kicked very judiciously. Half time was called with nothing scored. The second half was much the same, and very evenly contested. Both sides played well, and the game travelled all over the field. After fine bit of play, T. Mather scored in the last ten minutes. This seemed to put fresh energy into the villagers, and four goals were run up in the remaining few minutes, Bowyer scoring two, Dumbell one, and Parsons one. When time was called the score stood :—Penketh, four goals; Warrington,one. The result was very unexpected, even by the most sanguine Penkethites, and until the last few minutes the game was very evenly contested. WARRINGTON Sr. ELPRIN'S V. CHESTER COLLEGE (15T TEAms).—This match was played at Chester on Satur- day. Both sides were fully represented, and the Rev. T. W. Cook, the founder of the St. Elphin's team, ap- peared as left fullback for the home team. The visitors won the toss, and Chester kicked off. A corner was soon forced by Horsley, but this was well cleared by Robson, and the Saints went down to the Chester goal and remained there for some time, but the shooting was very weak. Soon after from a breakaway by their left wing the College scored. Both sides then took up the attack, but nothing further was scored till half-time when the College were leading by one goal to nil. In the second half, the visitors did most of the attacking, but Cook and his colleagues gave them little chance to shoot, and when they did get a shot the ball was always sent over the bar or outside. In the last ten minutes the College came with a rush, and scored twice. The ' first goal went through off one of the visiting backs, and the second came from a shot which hit the upright and was rushed through, Robson having no chance with either. Time then arrived with the score—College three, St. Elphin's nil.

1 ST. ELPHIN'S T. CHESTER COLLEGE (RESERTT TEAMS).-- The above match was played at Dalton Bank on Satin.- day afternoon. The Saints kicked off, and immediately ran the ball down to their opponents' end, a goal-hick resulting. After some even play in mid-fe Id the College came away, and experienced hard lines in not scoring. • For some time the game wag evenly contested, bat the College team showed grand combination, and before half time added two goals to neir total. It was generally • thought that the Saints would show up better in the second half, hut the visitors started in fine style and the opposing backs were placed on the defence. 'Though St.. Elphins played a good game the College could not be kept from scoring, and in the end ran out winners by six goals to nil. RUNCORN ASSOCIATION T. WAVERTREE.—The return match between these organisations was played off en Saturday afternoon at Runcorn in grand weather. 0 wine to the great attraction on the Irwell-lane enclosure there was but a sparse attendance. The home ream had been greatly altered since these clubs met on the Ist September last there being only four playing cm , Saturday who had taken part in the previous engage- ment at Wavertree where the light blues were so decisively beaten in their first turn out. I've again donned the shirt for Runcorn as centre fofward for the first time for about two years. Casson was played, centre half and Richards partnered Carter at full hack. The visitors winning the toss they elected to play with the strong wind in their favour and the sun in their faces. Pye set the ball in motion, and the heme forward; were soon in the visitors quarters and Mercer was called upon to clear. The home forwards kept up the pressure arid ultimately Bell relieved, and Johnson gettingposses- sion raced off down the right until pulled up by Richards. The visitors backs had their work cut out to keep the homesters from scoring. Pye made some splendid efforts to score but failed to get the ball past M-rcer who kicked out of danger. Johnson and Broughton next tried to get away but Barlow and Carter sent them to the right about. The homesters played up pluckily,. Wavertree rarely getting in the Runcorn quarters during the first half hour. Wavertree now ineuleecl in long kicking, Carter and Richards replying wth interest. The home forwards again got away nicely but W.Walker failed in the final effort, the bail going wide. The goal kick gave the visiting forwards posuessien and they were not slow in taking advantage of the opportunity. 'They ran well down field and Johnson kicaed past the home back. The custodian attempted to clear by kicking out hut the ball, striking Little on the hands, rebounded through the goal. The referee allowed the point much to disgust of the homesters and surprise of the visitors This appeared to discourage the Runeorniana who for the remainder of the first half were anything but bril- liant. Half-time arrived with the visitors leading by one goal to nil. On resuming the homesters tried their utmost to equalise rye putting in some good work and several times Mercer was called upon to save. Smith and Hanley at last relieved and the play was kept in mid-field, Barlow eventually giving Peacock possession. The visitors now attacked vigorously, and from a corner placed well in goal Broughton scored. Wavertree still continued to hold the upper hand, and the borne hacks had plenty of work. Finally from a grand centre by the visitors' left wing, Bell scored with a splendid shot. This seemed to arouse the homesters and they played hard. Pye made a strong shot and S. Walker, meeting the feeble clearance of Mercer, scored first for Runcorn. Peacock soon followed with another. The home front rank kept up the attack and experienced very hard lines in not scoring again. Smith intercepting and serrling the ball up field, Little and Bell made tracks for goal but could not break through the home defence. Several scrimmages took place in front of the home goal and Bell again scored for Wavertree. Nothing more was scored and the game ended in a win for Wavertree by four goals to two. The home team played better than they have previously this season, and Pye gave strong evidence that he had not forgotten many of his old tricks. The forwards with a little more practice to- gether will acquire that combination which is the foundation of success. Next Saturday the team will journey to Riinhill to play off the fixture with tf.e3 club of that name. The following team represented Run- corn :—Goal, Hough ; full backs. Richards and Carter ; half backs, Hulse. Casson and Barlow ; forwards, W. Walker, J. Jones, H. rye, S. Walker, W. Peacock (cap- tain). EARLESTOWN V. MIDDLETON LANCASHIRE ALLIANCE.— Before a large number of spectators the above Al- liance match was played at Earlestota n on Saturday. Earlestown won the toss and elected to play up hill, Middleton having the advantage of the wind. Hall kicked off, and after some desultory play, Birdta led a rush on the home goal,the final effort being nicely saved. Earles- town then forced the pace, which became very fast, but both teams proved equal to it for a time. Birch was again prominent for the visitors, and his centreing was remarkable for its accuracy,but he was badly supported. Earlestown pressed, and made several attacks on the Middleton goal,but Holt proved a formidable stumbling block. From a penalty kick Earlestown had a chance, but Holt smartly cleared. After a grand run down the left Birch centred, but Hall failed to improve, and the ball went behind. A corner kick fell to Middleton, but Laurence saved, and the visitors began to press a little, but they could not break through the defence of Peat and Wilkinson. The pace now eased somewhat, and Earlestown attacked, but Holt cleared. A return was made and from a centre by Jenkins Conway scored, and shortly afterwards half time was called. On turning round Earlestewn had the the advantage of the hill,and at once took the game in hand for a time pinning their opponents in their own quarters. Hughes getting hold centred, and Topping scored. From the kick off a visit was made to the Earlestown goal,but Peat cleared,and a rush was at once made to the visitors' end, where Con- why scored from a centre by Hughes. A bombardment of the Middleton goal was kept up fur a short time. but Holt proved equal to all efforts to lower his charge. A. splendid bit of hard play ensued, which placed the visi- tors' goal in danger, but Holt managed to save. Again Earlestown returned to the attack,and from a scrimmage the hall was worked through. Middleton after kicking off ru-hed up and made a desperate charge on the home goal, which resulted in the defeat of Laurenee,the game shortly after ending as follows—Earlestown 4 goals,Mid- dleton 1. . • •

OCTOBER. FROM WARRINUTON TO
FRO the
ANNUAL MEETING OF THE RUNCORN
NURSE FUND SUBSCRIBERS.
INTERESTING REPORT.

The annual meeting of the subscribers to the Runcorn District Nurse Fund took place in the Board room of the Town Hall, Runcorn, on Monday afternoon, the Rev. Canon A. Maitland Wood pre- siding. There were also present—Messrs. S. Taylor, J.P., treasurer; J. W. Lightburn, Thomas Cooke, Mesdames A. M. Wood,Joule,Barker, Fisher,Preston, lmison, and Misses Andrews and Taylor.

THE ANNUAL REPORr. The Chairman read the report of the committee which was as follows :-=The work of your committee has now been carried on uninterruptedly for five years, and has reached that stage when such enterprises,having became familiar, commonly encounter the danger of being taken for granted. There is first the stage of opposition,next the stage of popularity, then the dull level of admitted though criticized usefulness. It is gratifying to your committee to know that the subscription list is not de- creasing ; it would be more gratifying to recognise a healthy growth. Nurse Potter, who came to us in April, 1893. left us in July, 1894, after more than a year's woik in the town ; she made many friends, hut her physique hardly sufficed for the continued arduous labours of so large a district. She has gone to other work pro- vided by the South London Nursing Instituion,and your committee had no hesitation in giving her a testimonial. Nurse Buckenham has settled down to her difficult task, and your committee have every confidence in her success. The number of visita paid by the nurse makes a t„tal of 2,874 for eleven months, which compared with the eleven corresponding months of last year, when 4,000 visits were made, shows a decrease of 1,126 visits. The number of cases (typhoid, medical, surgical and chronic) visited during the eleven months was 201, and 43 persens have received occasional visits, making a total of 244. Of these, 8 have been sent to hospitals, 1 to the asylum, 1 to the union, 32 have died, and there are on the books, 21 cases, and 18 patients receiving occasional visits. In moving its adoption the Chairman said that to an impar- tial observer a singularly large amount of good work had been done; an immense amount of sorrow and pain had been alleviated, and that without any great display or fuss. The work had been carried on quietly, inside the housea of theie humbler brethren, and it was very much appreciated. For his own part if the work ended at that moment he should try to keep it going himself for the benefit of their poorer brethren. No waste had taken place in the expending of the money; everything had been nut to a good practical use. They would see from the list that the subscriptions were bettor, than in the previous year. The amount collected last year was £79 17s. 9d., against £74 133. the previous one,showing an increase of about five guineas. The increase was not very great, but it was encouraging. An effort this year by the Runcorn Football Club 'had resulted in £l7 17s. 6i. being obtained on behalf ot the fund, of which the committee were very glad and grateful. The reasons why the visits had decreased in number were firstly,that the health of the town had improved; and secondly, that Nurse Potter had not enjoyed such good health to- wards the close of her connection with the town as she had at the beginning. They had increased, however, under the new nurse,who had at present as much as she could pessibly do. For the information of the public something might be said about the nature of the nurse's work. She very often went to Liverpool with patients when they were journeying to the hospital ttlire to un- dergo any operation, and rendered valuable assistance. This greatly augmented her labours as well as the ex- penses. The expenditure for these journeys had to be defrayed out of the private sources, as they had no fund for them. In other directions the nurse had proved most useful, especially in typhoid fever cases. She was employed unceasingly. For an instance he might cite one case where in one house there had been five.typhoid cases. In this particular house he knew that the nurse's labours had been of a most devoted natare. The Chair- man in concluding, regretted that at the present time there was no place to take these typhoid patients, who greatly increased the work of the nurse. It was also a serious thing for her to go to a house where there were so many ill, especially two or three times a day which she had been known to do often. This might possibly be the means of spreading the disease which would be very unfortunate. He had been informed that in one house where typhoid had existed, the slops had been poured down the ordinary gutters in the street and that as a result two cases of infection had occurred there. (Mrs. Preston: A similar ease has occurred in Mill Brow). The Chairman hoped the evil would be remedied, and added that had it not been for the nurse some of these poor people would have died He had much pleasure in moving the adopti .n of the report. The proposition was seconded by Mr. J. W. Lighthurn who remarked that with reference to the Vicar's obser- vations about there being no place for typhoid fever cases, such a conclusion ought not to have been arrived at. At present there was a dispute between medical men as to whether typhoid was an infectious disease. It had been scheduled by the Local Government Board as a notifiable disease, so they evidently considered it infeclous. However, he did not think it was altogether right to state that there was no place to take these cases. But he hoped that the necessity would be met by the authority with a place of isolation. Mr. Cooke, who intimated that he was present, not as .he representative of any society but in his own private capacity, at the request of Canon Wood, also spoke m. the vast amount of good work performed by the nurse. He made reference to certain cases where he had known that nurse Buckenham had been in attendance before eight o'clock in the morning. He had also known the nurse to procure cast-off clothing from ladies of the town for patients, when they had become convalescent and were without wearing apparel. He might now mention that if any lady present had any clothing which they no longer required, nurse Buckenham would be pleased to receive it. He thought also that it should be widely known that the nurse made no distinction of persons' whether of sect or creed. She attended persons of all denominations.—The report was adopted.
MARKET ROBBERIES AT ST, HELENS.
A TRADESMAN CHARGED WITH RECEIVING.

At St. Helens, on Saturday, before Alderman Harrison, Mr. Oppenheim, and Nix% J. B. Leach, the two boys Arthur Slater, aged eleven, and William Henry Mather, eleven, were brought up under remand charged with stealing several pocket-knives and brooches from a stall in the St. Helens Market, the property of Messrs. Lyon and Cross, and Mr. George Benson, watchmaker and repairer, Church-street, was charged with receiving one of the brooct4ei knowing it to have neon stolen. Miss Boardman, who had chirge of the stall, said the brooches were sold at not less than 2s. 6d. ea(th. She did not know the wholesale price. The brooches were on a card.—lnspector Steel stated that in consequence of what Slater said while in custody he took him to Mr. Benson's shop. Slater in the presence of Mr. Benson said "On Tuesday night last week I went into Mr. Bensons shop and sold a brooch for 3d. Mather fe. "
t )1d Benson he had found it behind the People's Palace. of any society but in his own priv,— quest of Ginon Wood, also spoke of I Mr. Benson thehlit7,diTide'irthe brooch from a drawer

;one') TrMix and Slater said, "That i the one I sold to him, but it was not bruised like that when I sold it to him." The Inspector asked Mr. Benson to go to the police office,and he there charged him with receiving the brooch knowing it to have been stolen. Mr. Benson said, "I didn't know anything afout it having been stolen. The boy said he found it near the People's Palace. lam in the habit of buying all kinds of old jewellery and broken things ; it is part of my business." M. Benson was then admitted to bail. In reply to Mr. H. L. Riley, who defended, the inspector said Mr. Benson voluntarily produced the brooch.—Mr. Riley then addressed the magistrates for the defence. Be said Mr. Benson had lived in St.Helens for forty-nine years,and had been in business for twenty- five years. The brooch in question was of trivial value, and such as might well appear to have been found. On two occasions valuable property which had been found was brought to Mr. Benson. and through his efforts in advertising, &c. ,the property was restored to its rightful owner.—Mr. Pritchard, ironfounder, said he lost a portion of a valuable chain and guinea attached, and it was restored to him through Mr. Benson.—The two boys were further charged with stealing three shirts, value 2s. from a stall in the market. —The magistrates ordered the boys to be whipped, and censured the mothers for their carelessness in watching the' conduct of the boys. As regarded Mr. Benson, the Chairman said the bench thought that, considerin,, the high character he had always borne in the town, and the respectable manner in which lie had conducted his business, it was a matter of carelessness mare than anything else. The case would be dismissed.

div.p: TREASoRER'S REPORT.

Mr. Taylor's report showed that the subscriptions had realised £79 173. 91.; which with the proceeds from the football match and interest brought the receipts up to £lO7 12s. 91. The year began with an adverse balance of £8 us. 21., but after paving all expenses they had a balance in hand of £l9 123. 4d. The beef tea receipts amounted to £l2 10s., of which £l2 had been spent.— The treasurer in proposing the ad iption of the report, intimated that in reality they were in debt about £5, as he had forwarded recently several cheques which had exhausted their balance. In view of the fact that they did not begin to collect until February,lie thought some- thing should be done. He afterwards spoke ofthe worthiness of the work,and expressed a hope that the public would extend to them more help in the future.— The proposition was seconded by Miss Andrews and carried. The vacancies on the committee were filled by Mrs. Wood and Mrs. Lightburn being re-elected, 'and Mrs. Abel selected in the place of Mrs. Meadowcroft who had retired.—Mr. Taylor was re-appointed treasurer. It was moved by Miss Andrews and seconded by Mrs. Preston, that the following gentlemen serve as an Anxil- iary Committee to acquire funds :—Messrs. Poole, Imison, Mellor, Lighthurn, Frith, Woodland, Cooke, Evans, Weston, Holt, Nickson. Collier, Scott, Moore, F. J. Norman, Kay, Callender, Pope, Posnett, Diggps and Bridgewater. Votes of thanks were accorded the commissioners for the use of the room and to the Chairman, after which the proceedings closed.

div.head: BOWLING.
div.p: BOWLING.
LANCASHIRE AND CFIE'zIIIRE COUNTY ASSOCIATION.

The second annual tournament by representatives of affiliated districts and last county competition of the season took place over the Midland Green at Withieg- ton on Saturday, for prizes presented by the Council. The president and vice-president acted as referees. The competing organizations were Old Trafford, Cheetham Bill, Sefton Park, Didsbury, Titnperley, Warrington, flarpurhey, and Douglas. The great surprise of the afternoota was the defeat of Warrington by flarpurhey. That the Warringtonians were distinctly unlucky in losing the tie is round in the fact that four of their members gained victories out of a possible six, whilst the remaining two had left such a leeway to be made up that in the end Warrington could only tie, and in the decider our local representative was decisively beaten. After the tournament had concluded about one hundred players assembled in the large dining-room, where a banquet was held. Mr. J. J. Meakin (Broughton) presided at the "social" afterwards, whilst among others present were Councillors Nlorecroit and Oilier ; Mr. R. Anderton (Warrington), Mr. J. W. G. Coombs (Midland), Mr. J. Singleton, hon. secretary (Newton-le-Willows) ,&c. The usual patriotic toasts were drunk, and in responding to the tomt of " Success to the Lancashire and Cheshire Bowling Association," the President said the aim of • the association was to promote a better feeling amongst bowlers in general than had hitherto existed. The various prizes were then distributed, and in the individual merit competition the first prize was secured by Mr. W. FiAding and consisted of a massive silver cup. The second prize. a case of cutlery was received by Mr. J. Harrison,of flindsford. Mr. F. Berry, of Warrington, took third honours, the prize taking the shape of a handsome gold al bee-, whilst the same player was also to the fore in securing the gold medal Oven by the vice-president (Mr. J. W. G. Coombs, Withington) for the largest aggreglte majority secured in the county matches against Yorkshire. The success of the War- ringtonian was immensly popular amongst the bowlers in this district-. The evening was enlivened by songs given by Messrs. Anderton, P. Fielding, and Wells, and the gath-ering stands out as being one of the most enjoy- able in the history of the association. Credit is due to Mr. Sineleton for the admirable arrangements made, the whole proceedings passing off without the least hitch.

div.head: ?Lettero to tbe ebitor.
div.p: ?Lettero to tbe ebitor.

- - - THE NEEL FOR PUBLIC ABATTOIRS. Sir,—Some time ago I occupied several columns of the " Examiner" with a series of papers advocating the establishment of an abattoir under the management of the Corporation to take the place of the numerous private slaughter-houses situated in various and crowded parts of the borough. In one article I pointed out the ready, facilities offered to the slaughter-house men to perpe- trate excessive and unnecessary pain to the animals,and in another I instanced examples which had come under my own observation of the depravity to which many boys were exposed by the almost free access to some of the slaughter-houses. The following are two paragraphs which I have culled from the newspapers this week :—" Colonel Coulson, of Fourstones-on-Tyne, has re-printed in a booklet some correspondence which lately appeared in one of the the morning papers on cruelty in slaughter-houses. I am glad to see that he is endeavouring to further arouse public opinion on the subject. The correspondence arose on a case in which a man was convicted of flaying a bul- lock alive, and there can be no doubt that the butcher's work is too often carried out with the most ghastly and atrocious cruelty. As one means of preventing this, all slaughtering ought to be done in municipal abattoirs, and there should be an efficient system of inspection bs Corporation or Government officials. What is needed as much as anything else, however, is un- ceasing vigilance on the part of the E.S.P.C.A." The case against the three little boys who killed and mutilated three pigs because, accerding to their state- ment, they "wanted to get the bladders out," was dealt with by the Worthing magistrates on the 28fh inst. Tha children were ordered to receive six strvkes each with the birch rod. The father of one of the boys said he thßught the occurence was due to the encouragement given to boys to go into slaughter-houses and witness the killing of cattle." Is it not about time that English Corporations were left no option in the matter but were cotripelled by law, to establish stir h an abattoir and close all so-called priv- ate slaughter-houses P—Yours truly, " CL EO." Warrington, Sept. 28, 1894.

div.head: THREE MONTHS' IMPRISONMENT FOR STEALING COAL.
div.p: THREE MONTHS' IMPRISONMENT FOR STEALING COAL.

At the Warrington Borough Court, on Friday, Samue Leigh, Watkin-st..was charged with having stolen from the L. and N.W. Railway siding in Dallam-lane, at half past two on Wednesday last week, a quantity of coal, value Is. 6d. Mr. Browne appeared for the prisoner The Chief Constable stated that at about half-past two on Wednesday morning,Constahle Bell saw the prisoner come out of the railway sidings in Dallam-la,ne, opposite Stamford-st..with a bag of coal. As he passed,Constable Bell said to him, "It is you, is it ?" The prisoner then dropped the coal and Jan up Stamford-st. Inspector Dipple said he appeared on behalf of the L. and N.W. Railway Company. From inquiries he found that a waggon of coal was put in D illam-lane siding at 730 p.m. on the 25th inst. The following morning it was found that a quantity of coal had been removed from it, and some bits were an the floor. They had had serious complaints about coal being taken from waggons. P.C. Bell stated that at the time stated on the date named he was standing at the end of Stamford-stree, near Dallam-lane, when he saw the prisoner earring a bag, which appeared to be very heavy, on his shoulders. He was in his stocking feet. Witness stood in the dark, and prisoner walked close by him. Witness said "It is you, is it "? He then dropped the bag and ran away. Witness ran after him a short distance, but returned and got possession of the bag, which was found to contain coal, and put it in the lodge at Dallam. Sergeant Smith subsequently went to the prisoner's house and knocked at the door, which was immediately opened by the prisoner, who said " You have come again have you ?" He shouted upstairs that the "bobbies" had come again for him. His hands seemed as if they had been lately washed They also found a pair of stockings in the kitchen which were wet and dirty. Sergeant Smith also gave evidence. corrnoora.ting the latter Dart of P.C. Bell's statement. A witness named James Haves also spoke as to a man ! rushing past him in his stocking feet,.in Stamford-street, at 2.30 on Wednesday morning. He could not recoenise the man again. Mr. Browne said he would call several witnesses who slept in the same house as the defendant on the night in question and who would prove that the defendant never left the house during the night. The only evidence against the defendant was that of P.C. Bell. That officer might be perfectly consciencious in thinking that the defendant was the man he saw, but he might have been mistaken, espocially as it, was dark at the time. Thre witnesses named Daniel Ward, J. Ward, and Florenee Ward gave evidence that the deft- ndant was in bed at the time stated.—Samuel Davies. 25. Watkin-street, stated that he was in Watkin-st. at 2.30 on Wednesday mornine,but he never saw anythina of the defendant.—The mav,is- trates considered that the defendant did take the coal and committed him to gaol for three months' hard labour.

div.head: STOCKTOg HEAT ET.
div.p: STOCKTOg HEAT ET.

THE PAROCHIAL AND SANITARY COMMITTEES .—A t the last meeting of the Runcorn Rural Sanitary Authority held at Dutton Workhouse on Tuesday afternoon. Mr.J. Mclntyre in the chair, the minutes of the Appleton Parochial Committee's previous meeting, held on Mon- day evening at the London Bridge Inn, Stockton Heath, were submitted for confirmation.—They showed that a letter had been received from the Local Government I Board acknowledging the receipt of the Committee's letter of the sth September, enclosing draft of the con- tract into which the Authority had entered with Mr. Newton for the removal of house refuse, and the cleans- ing of ashpits, &c., in the Stockton Heath ward. The Local Government Board notified that the contract did not require the Board's approval but they observed that it was unsatisfactory from three points of view.—lst, the absence of scavenging at regular periods : 2nd, the deposit of filth in the streets; and 3rd, the performance of the work of scavenging under cover of darkness, that is between the hours of 10 p.m. and 9 a.m. The Board also pointed out that the work shnuH extend to the cleansing of earth closets, and that the description of the duties devolving upon the contractor should be in the words of 42 of the Public Health Act, 1875.—The Committee resolved that the Clerk acknowledge the receipt of the letter and that the agreement with Mr. Newton be completed, and to also inform this gentle- man that duties will commence as from the 2nd inst.— The Clerk read a letter from the Town Clerk of Warring- ton re the water sunplv to Stockton Heath. and enclos- ing a report from Mr. Rose thereon. The letter stated that the Corporation had not yet determined what to do in the matter, and that the idea of spending £16,000 for the purpose of supplying twenty houses seemed alto- gether out of the question. A letter from Mr. Robert Davies, of Warrington, relative to the same subject was read saying that he had not heard that anything was being done with respect to the supply to his house. It had been better since the weather had broken about St. Swithin's day, on account of the rain that had fallen, hut should dry weather follow the supply would be just as bad as ever. He had heard that something had been said about a tower, but suggested that it would perhaps be better if the reservoir at Winwick was raised, which would benefit the whole of the area.—The Clerk was instructed to reply to both letters.—A letter was sub- mitted from Messrs. Percy Davies and Forshaw. War- rington, which stated that Mr. Pike was quite I:silting to bear the expense of the sewering co-extensive with his land fronting Gaskell-street. The nuisance inspector was instructed to see Messrs. Davies and Forshaw and take their instructions.—On the motion of Mr. Keowles the minutes of the Committee were approved and -adopted

The team has been altered considerably to meet the Rangers from Broughton to-day at Wilderspool. It is composed as follows: full back, Boscow; three-quarter backs, Nevins, Heesom. Potts,Cunninzham ; half backs, James T. Bate, and Clark; forwards,Fair Turner, Jolley, Thorniley,Taylor,Berry,Buckley, Bailey, and Dakin. It will he noticed that Boscow re-appears in the team, and that Heesom goes to his old post of three-quarter back. The teams have already met this season at Broughton when the game ended in a pointless draw. G)ing on the principle that home teams have the best chance, War- rington should therefore win.

Our local" A" team on Saturday were unsuccessful in their first engagement in the Lancashire Club Champion- ship for" A" teams, they being beaten by Oldham, who scored a goal, to Wairington one try. As the score indicates the match was a close contest for supremacy, and the victory of the visitors was due to a successful goal kick, after the scoring of a try. This result should have a beneficial effect upon Warrington players in caus- ing them to give more attention to goal kicking. More practice is needed in "place-kicking." Had Warrington been as successful as their opnonents in the place-kick, the result would have been a drawn game. But it is no use crying over spilled milk, and it is to be hoped that to-day Warrington will make up for their defeat by giv- ing the Broughton Rangers "A" team a taste of it. Mannion at full-back was a success on Saturday, and he will no doubt be often called upon to fill that position. In the three-quarter backs there was room for improve- ment.

While our senior team were havingsuch a bitter experi- ence at Oldham, several of the junior teems were enjoy- ing themselves at the expense of "foreigners." Stockton Heath for instance, took it out of Widnes St. Mary's by a goal and three tries to nil, while Warrington St. Mary's were piling it on at Lostock to the extent of four goals, two tries to nil. It goes without saying that many of our so-called junior teams are looked upon with great respect by many good clubs round about. Agat._

CYCLING.

On Saturday afternoon- about 20 members of the War-, rington Cycling Ciub, in conjunction with a dozen mem- bers of the Widnes Cycling Club, had a pleasant run to Knutsford. On the Kuutsford heath a friendly football match was played between the two clubs. Tea was partaken of at the Red Cow, Knutsford, after which a social evening was spent, the songs and toasts being enthusiastically received. The weather was beautifully fine and rendered perfect, the afternoon's outing. This is the final official run of the season, but it is hoped that there will be a few more opportunities for friendly runs.

div.head: EXAMINER, SAT URDA-Y OCTOBER 6, 1894. NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SAT URDA-Y OCTOBER 6, 1894. NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
RUGBY FOOTBALL.

The match with Oldham to which so many have been looking forward to during the past few weeks, has now been lost and won, and the result is a matter of history instead of speculation. The result confirmed the worst fears of the pessimists wlro were expecting a bi,-; score nct in favour of Warrington. There is now nothing for it but to wait until the return match in February, and in the meantime get a team which will combine well together, and then give the Oldham men a good slating 'in return. Now, gentle reader, don't think that this is all nonsense, for when a severe defeat is suffered by a team a large number of its supporters are at once seiz-d with the disease known as " down in the dumps." It will, perhaps, comfort those people by informing them that last year the Oldham team came to Warricgton on October 21, and then rubbed it into our local champions to the tune of a goal and five tries to a goal in the Lan- cashire competitien, and the Warrington team forthwith pulled themselves together; and did not suffer defeat again in the competition until they again met Oldham on February 17, when they were only I.eaten by a try. it is pretty evident, therefore, that if past history is anything to go by, the Warrington team is not finished with yet by a long chalk.

The match on Saturday was fought in glorious weather, and as:a result there was a tremendous "gate," about 1,000 of whom came with the team from Warring- ton. By the way,is it not strange that at every previous visit of the "wirepullers" tc "Spindledom," the weather has beer of the most wretched description? In fact,the " Owdamers "were beginning to look upon the Warring- ton team with similar feelings to which the sailors loi,ll upon the stormy petrel—as harbingers of bad weather. However, the spell was broken on Saturday, and let us hope that it is broken altogether, although truth to say, a wet day would have been a godsend to Warrington.

The ground at Watershectdings is an excellent ground, and is also well patronised, and it is pretty evident that Warrington was a popular fixture, for almost every- where was packed. As to the game itself, it showed to what perfection it was possible to get the backs into. The way the ball was worked from one player to another was a treat to watch, and if every Rugby match were played in a similar fashion, it would become far more popular than the Association game, as it is far more ex- citing even than the expositions of the League teams.

The department in which Oldham so completely over- shadowed their opponents was the tkreequarters. There was absolutely no comparison between the two. The way Hurst, Lees, Taylor, and McCutcheon worked in unison was marvellous. If the ball once was fairly in their pos- session, there was an almost certain try. The opposing quartette were unable to cope with them at all. Potts was the t.est for tackling, and Cunningham made some good runs,but he could not resist the sturdyML:Cutcheon. Lawless, who was called upon in place of Evans, also made a few good rushes,but Carey appeared to be afraid of Hurst, and he was of very little use. The Oldham team went to Yorkshire for their full back,but they have not captured a very first-class one to judge from Satur- day. He had very little to do it is true, but he did not do that little very well. He appeared to be too clumsy. Heesom, on the contrary, had a tremendous amount of work to do, and con- sidering that fact, he came out of the ordeal very creditably. It was totally impossible to stop the Oldham backs from scoring when he got so little assist- ance from the threequarters. Bate was about the best man on the defeated side. He was instrumental in re- pelling numerous invasions, and it was chiefly through his instrumentality that the solitary try for Warrington was obtained—with the asss:..stance of the forwards, of course. Clark, his colleague, had the honour of scoring the try, but his play in general was outshone by Leesand Varle.. The Yorkshire international was all there on Saturday, and let Warrington know it, too.

The Warrinaton forwards unlike the rest of the team, Proved the equal'of their opponents. In the scrimmages, they were equal, but in the loose dribbling, they were the superior of the Oldham forwards and every invasior of Oldham territory during the game was through their instrumentality. It would be invidiQus to single any out of the eight, for they all played exceedingly well.

In all their acquisitions from all parts of the kingdom, it is very strange that Oldham cannot alight upon a goal kicker. More of the tries scored on Saturday could be called difficult "places," but they could only convert two into goals,and those two were right under the posts. Warrington are not so well off in this rcspect,but I think that if they had the same chances as Oldham, there would have been a few more goals.

On Saturday, Miss Nellie Bennett, of Pear Tree House. took the the girls attending her Bible Class, which is held at the Wesleyan School, to Frodsham. Miss Mary Bennett also took the boys attending her Sunday school class on the same day, The children were conveyed by special carriages from Bank Quay station, Frodsham being reached about 12.45 p.m. Games were indulged in on the hills, after which tea was provided at the expense of the Nlisses Bennett, at Mersey View. Warrington was reached about half-past seven o'clock, where a 'bus was in attendance to convey the children to Pad- gate.

WRSLEYIN DISTRICT SYNOD. According to the current number of the " IV arrington Wesleyan Methodist Church Record" it was decided at. the Synod held at Liverpool in September to accept the invitation of the Warring- ton Circuit to hold the Synod at Warrington in May next. Mr. W. Bennett, who was present, gave the invitation in the name of the quarterly meetiag,and together with the Rev. John Kirtlan assured the meeting of the circuit's desire to do everything possible to ensure the comfort of the ministers and gentlemen who will attend. There are upwards of 120 ministers in the district, for whom hospitality will be provided, and on the layman's day there are probably more than 200 laymen eligible to attend. 'lt will therefore be seen that the Synod is a great and important gathering.

TEMPERANCE MEETING. * A gospel temperance meeting was held in the Workingmen's Gospel Temperance Mission Hall, on Sunday evening, conducted by Mr. John Drury. Mr. Sandford rejoiced to know that that temperance mission was a power for good in Warrington. The work of the past week was cheering. All men must see that there were too many public-houses in War- rington; therefore more ought to be closed. Chris- tians ought to do all they could to help the temper- ance cause. If teetotallers and Christians would do their duty next month they would not vote for any publican being returned to the Town Council. Nir. James Rigby briefly addressed the meeting. Mr. 11. Taylor (Police Court Missionary) also spoke, and said the Rev. D. W. Roberts, in bringing to light the conduct of certain publicans in Warrington,was worthy of all praise for his moral courage. He need not be troubled at the mean abuse those interested in, and tied to, the drink trade had spitefully , used.

STRANGE ACCIDENT AT PADGATE. On Saturday aftPrnoon a singular accident occurred at Padgate. Whilst two horses belonging to Mr. Thomas Sankey, of Culcheth, and attached to lurry loaded with cinders, were passing over the Padgate railway bridge towards the church a little before one o'clock they were startled by a passing brain and became restive. The leading horse dashed thrlugh the hedge on the right side of the roadway, followed by the other horse and the lurry. This portion of the roadway is some distance above the entrance to the railway station, and is on an embankment. As soon as the horses had gone through the hedge they at once dragged the lurry after them down the incline, horses and lurry roll- ing one after the other. During the descent the shafts of the lurry broke,or the consequences might have been more Serious. Strange to say neither of the horses was injured. Fortunately, the driver, who had been riding on the shafts of the lurry previous to the accident, jumped down on to the roadway as soon as the horses became restive. The news of the accident spread, and a large number of persons were soon on the spot. A contingent of railway employes was summoned and they took up the railings dividing the foot of the embankment from the approach to the station, and the horses I were liberated.

FORTHCOMING PEOPLE'S MEETING. A people's meeting will be held in Wycliffe Church, Bewsey-St., on Thursday evening next in connection with the autumnal session of the Con- gregational Union of England and Wales. The gen- tlemen announced to speak occupy a foremost posi- tion in. the Congregational denomination, and the topics to be touched upon at the meeting will apper- tain to the welfare of the people. The chairman wi:l he Mr. Wm. Crosfield, M.P., who was at one time Liberal candidate for this borough. The Epeakers include Mr. A. Spicer, M.P., Revs. J. D. Jores, M.A., 8.D., and J. Guiness Rogers, B.A. Mr. Spicer, who has been described as the "model deacon" is member of Parliament for a working class constituency in South Wales, and was chair- man of the Congregational Union last year. The Rev. J. D. Jones, M.A.. 8.D., of Lincoln, is a rising man in the Congregational denomination, and is a capital speaker, The Rev. J. Guineas Rogers, 8.A., of London, the veteran champion of religious liberty, has previously preached and lectured in Warrington. The chair is to be taken at eight o'clock prompt, and a large gathering is anti- ated.
NOTES BY THE WAY AT EARLESTOWN.

div.p: SNVDIXMei.

Mr. George E. Corbett, a son of Mr. T. Corbett, of Orford, and who is at present at business in London, has been successful ln obtaining the 100 yards champion- ship of the West Eud Swimming Association. The race took place the other evening at the St. George's iths, Buckingham Palace-road, Lyndon. The programme in- cluded a polo match and a team race, &c., but the event of the evening was the above-mentioned race far the championship of the association, which saw the defeat, for the first time since the institution of the contest, of E. York, the Magpie Swimming Club's Champion who was just "pipped " on the post by Mr. G. E. Corbett, who is a memher of the Kildare S. C. The time was 1 minute 22 4-5 seconds.

WYCLIFI4E YO.U.Net PEOPLE 3 SOCIETY. This society commenced its seventh winter ses- sion with a most successfol conversozione on Mon- day evening, held in the upper schoolroom. There was a large attendance, and the proceedings were presided over by the Rev. J. Yonge. An attractitia programme of readings and vocal and instrumental music was submitted. div.head: BY AN OCCASIONAL CORRESPONDENT.
div.p: BY AN OCCASIONAL CORRESPONDENT.

We have been very free in this neighbourhood for some time past of anything in the sensational line, but whether this is due to the higher educatinn of the people I am not in a position to say. The fact remains, however, that in the way of suicides and such like diversions, the local columns have been remarkably free. We were congratulating ourselves upon this tact when suddenly, in one day in fact, a sensation is sprung upon us. It was only a rumour, but still a sensational one, and involved nothing more nor less than two alleged suicides, and an equal number of murders. If this was not enough to make the mouth of the most indifferent reporter ' water, then I pity him. The most unfortunate part of the business, to the reporter, was that there was not a word of truth in either statement. One con- sisted of a domestic disagreement, snd the wife had so little respect for herself that she must needs drown herself and two children. Just about the time however that the woman was said to be lying beneath so many feet of water, she and the children were alive and well in Haydock. The other case was that of a man who was said to have drowned him- self, but in this case no reliable statement could be obtained. These are silly rumours, and I cannot see that they do any good to anyone.

I see Colonel McCorquodale has consented to fall in with the wishes of his colleagues, and agreed to serve, nominally it must be owned, as a Commis- sioner, until the Board goes out of office. Of course this relievee the Commissioners of the necessity of tilling a vacancy, for the short time they will be together, but I am under the impression that legally Colonel McCorquodale is no more a Commissioner than I am, as I think I am correct in saying he has not attended a Board meeting for more than the disqualifying period of six months. However, per- haps it is as well that he be allowed to die natur- ally along with his brother Commissioners, in the ordinary course.

Now that the time is rapidly approaching when the Board upon which so much ignominy has been heaped trom one end of the township, will have ceased to exist, the officers appear to be very effec- tionately and regretfully bidding it a long adieu. Dr. Watkins presented his report on the health of the township on Monday, and he was thanked by the members of the Board for the satisfactory nature of the contents, which they attributed (quite naturally) to the perfect state of the sanitary conditions. Dr. Watkins did not appear to be in a very happy frame of mind, when he expressed the hope that his successor to the new Board would have as satisfactory report to make as he had just presented. Of course the Board hoped so too,but I am afraid if some of those hypochondriacs on the sewage question get on the Board, the new medical officer of health will have a lively time. However I trust we are not going to part with our old friends in this wholesale manner.

Wonders never cease. and I am inclined to think, if the Board of Commissioners go on in this extrav- agant fashion, we shall soon be in the bankruptcy court—at least this will be the cry of some of our friends at a certain end of the township. To think that the Commissioners should in the middle of the 19th century, have gone the length of declaring that we ratepayers when meeting on town's busi- ness, can have the use of the Town Hall "free, gratis for nothing." Things come upon us so sud- denly that "we dunno' where we are," and I shall not be at all surprised if I hear some day that extra threepence has been knocked off the gas, and that the foundation stone for the new post office has been secretly laid. But this is sarcastic ; seri- ously I think the Commissioners have done wisely and well, no matter what their detractors may think.

div.head: EARLESTOWN SONS OF TEMPERANCE.
div.p: EARLESTOWN SONS OF TEMPERANCE.

The 23rd anniversary of the Britain's Need division of the Sons of Temperance was held in the Co-operative Hall, Earlestown on Wednesday even- ing. The proceedings were initiated by a tea to which about 70 persons sat down, the tables being presided over by Mesdames Peareon, Judson. Misses Pickett, Dickson, Prescott and Robinson. After tea a public meeting was held in the large hall, presided over by Bro. W. Clare, in the unavoidable absence of Bro. Thos. Molyneux. and he was supported by Bro. W. Pearson, G.S. ; 0. Pickett, and Martin of Manchester, and other officers of the society. Bro. Pearson after reading a letter of apology from Mr. Molyneux, who should have presided, said it would scarcely be right at that maeting, to give any statement before referring to the decease of one who he believed had at those annual gatherings, been on that platform in the past. Their late Brother Prescott so long the secretary of that Society, and who as G.S. of the district had been one of the most untiring members of the order of tile Sons of Temperance. They knew how he had shown at those meetings awl all other meetings in which he had taken part, and he had done his work thoroughly and not by halves. They represented that night the Order of the Sons of Temperance, which was a friendly society worked on total abstinence principles. All their members had taken a pledge not to make, buy, sell or use, as a beverage any spirituous or malt liquors or cider. They thought, or rightly. so, that their order was one of the best Societies, called friendly Societies. He believed their order stood second to none, and that they could come out equal to any, if they did not surpass the rest. He had such a firm belief in the Order he represented that night, that he could recommend it. One of the reasons for considering they were one of the best, was that they were comparatively modern, and had the experience of other societies to work upon. ' They belonged to the branch of the order known as the Britains Need, the 23rd anniversary of which they were celebrating that alight, and they were proud to be known as members of the division. They were looking iorward to a greater and nobler future; their members were greater and were daily increasing, and during the Past the division had proved worthy of its objects. During the past 10 rears, they had paid to numbers in sick claims £479 4•;. 6d , and for funeral claim £ll2, and this had been done without having to impose an extra levy. After paying out these claims, they had the sum of £220, in that branch, as their own private money. The grand division of which they were a part had a fund of over £6OO, which they might fall back upon in time of need, so that they might say they were worth to-day between £BOO and £9oJ—(hear, hear)—and that had been got together by a handful of working determined men. And seeing that they had achieved so much in the past, with increased members, increased zeal and energy, he was not prepared to say what they would attain in the future, hut they expected to go forward by bounds. Their rate of sickness for the past 10 years had averaged six days per year, which was lower than the bulk of other Societies. The death 'rate of the Order was 8.03 per 1,000, which went to prove that their members were healthy and longer lived than other ordinary public-house clubs. In connection with the Britain's Need, they had a juvenile section called cadets, which was oce of the principal features of the society. He trusted that in the future the Britain's Need would ever be to tte fore in all temperance work, and as a friendly society, still prove itself to be second to none. (Applause.)—Bro. Martin, of Manchester, also delivered an interesting address, and a neatly framed emblem of the Order was presented to Bro. S. Marsh, P.W.P., for his services during the year. During the evening several songs and recitations were given.

div.head: DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.
div.p: DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.

At the To;;;; Hall, Newton-, on Monday morning, before Colonel J. L. Wood, Patrick llanley, of Lawrence-st., collier; and John Mahoney, Clarence- St., were charged with being drunk and disorderly and fighting in Market-st., Rarlestown.—Hanley was fined 5,1. and costs, and Mahoney 2s. 6d. and costs, the latter going to gaol for 14 days.—Mary Reynolds, of Crewe, was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Market-at., at midnight, on Satur- day. She left a lodging-house in Back Market-st. and was in a nude state, carrying her clothes under her arm, and was screaming and making a noise. She got into Market-at, where P.C. Burns took charge of her, but she resisted, and with the assist- ance of another constable she wee ronvevad to the police aation.—She was fined 2s. 61, and costs or 14 days.

A SUCCESSFUL STUDENT.

Mr. F. H. Gornali, a Lorimer member of the War- rington Grammar School, has been successful in obtaining a Cheshire County Council major scholar- ship to Owens College, Manchester, for a candidate about to engage in chemistry._

div.head: INVITATION TO THE TOWN CLERK.
div.p: INVITATION TO THE TOWN CLERK.

The Town Clerk (Mr. Lyon Whittle) was amongst those invited to attend the luncheon at St. Helens on Tuesday in connection with the laying of the foundation stone of the new Free Library and Technical School.

div.head: PARK Music.
div.p: PARK Music.

On Sunday afternoon the League of the Cross Band played a selection of music on the band-stand before a good attendance, no doubt owing to the fact that this was the last of a aeries of pleasant performances. The efforts of the Bands Committee have been very successful, and they are to be con- gratulated upon the excellent programmes of music which have been provided. P.S.A. AT THE Y.M.C.A.

The usual Sunday afternoon meetingof the above was held at the Y.M.C.S. rooms on Sunday after- noon, Mr. H. Taylor in the chair. Au interesting address on "Christian Citizenship, its aims and its responsibilities" was delivered by Mr. W. Roberts. Mr. A. Jowett effectively rendered a flute solo, and Mr. W. H. Bayley also Look part in the meeting which was very well attended. TILE " PELICAN " LICENSE.

Mr. Herbert Hatton, solicitor, appeared at the Warrington Borough Court on Tuesday, to give notice of appeal against the decision of the magis- trates at the adjourned licensing sessions, in which they refused the renewal of the license of the "Pelican." The following persons atTeared as sureties: Fairfield l'. Turner, John Henry, J. H. Clarke and Herbert Hatton. S. PETER'S CHTIRoiI BOUNDARY WALL.

At a meeting of the sub-committee for the build- ing of the boundary wall of St. Peter's Church, the Vicar (Rev. B.Percival) reported that Mrs. Beamont had very generously sent him a cheque for £25 to- wards the fund. It was stated that the fund now amounted to nearly £7O. The committee, thanks principally to the liberality of Mrs.Beamont,decided to at once proceed with the building of the front portion of the boundary wall.
